speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are concerns about rising costs of living and great discomfort with the uncertain times ahead and the changes that Singaporeans are expecting to go through.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think it is clear to Singaporeans that it is not business as usual.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: People are more aware of the deep shifts in the world with the advances in technology and the disruptions to traditional businesses and jobs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The shopkeepers in my estate know that business is dwindling partly because people now buy online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Most of them are old and their children are generally not interested in taking over the business.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They are not sure whether to continue to invest in the business, especially as they are uncertain as to how long more they can sustain the lease.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A resident I met recently sought help to re-enter a course he signed up for to upgrade himself.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He failed to meet the grades required of the school and was terminated a few months into the course.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He knows he has to work hard to keep up, but picking up a new skill and studying while still working are challenging.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also know of a young couple with seven young children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He is keen to find a better paying job and his wife is also keen to work to supplement the family's income.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, they are saddled with bills and debts and have no alternative options for childcare.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They are, therefore, struggling to survive and have difficulties making the time to upskill so that they can participate actively in the future economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These are some real day-to-day concerns and struggles faced by our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I do not intend to paint a gloomy picture.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the cases I mentioned, some guidance and support are being given to the individuals and families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also know of a lot of people who have overcome difficulties and I believe that people do need to take personal responsibility to improve their circumstances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But the point I would like to make is that we will always have to keep in mind the day-to-day issues people face and ensure that the translation of our policies can alleviate these concerns.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He added that our bonds will help us develop greater resilience in the face of unexpected shifts and improve our ability to adapt.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are gems within the Budget with regard to the plans to re-energise the economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have faith that the efforts in industry transformation, internationalisation, improving capabilities of businesses and workers will go a long way in building a stronger economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, the Budget is not just about the economy and fiscal needs but should also be a roadmap on society's values and support network.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that it is important that we give a little more attention to this aspect and consider the development of our social policies in light of the changing trends in the world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, there are three main areas I wish to address.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One, how do we help the vulnerable and disadvantaged in our community survive in the competitive economy?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Two, how do we rally people to care about one another and the environment while they face their own challenges?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Three, how can we harness existing resources within the community, in particular, amongst the young, to work together to build Singapore's future?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My first point relates to those who may be vulnerable or disadvantaged in our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important for us to ensure that they do not get left behind in our race to develop our economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This may sound cliche, but it is real.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am referring to the elderly who have to struggle with the technological and digital developments; the children from low-income families whose parents may not have the time and money to send them to enrichment classes; persons with disabilities which may inhibit them from participating actively in the competitive job market; caregivers of the elderly who have to stay home to care for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a whole spectrum of people with varying needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government needs to ensure that it does not lose sight of them in crafting policies and programmes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The reality though is that it is unrealistic to expect the Government to extend help to every single individual.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A more feasible way is to encourage the growth of a community network of support, with organised voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) as well as organic groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important to extend the support and funding to organic groups as well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Last year, there was mention of Our Singapore Fund.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This leads me to my second point, about rallying people to help one another.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is very easy for people to forget about others when they are caught up with their own issues and difficulties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Most times though, people can support one another and there are always avenues to pay it forward.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There should be efforts to create and promote a culture of giving back to the community through education and conversations with people in the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I laud efforts like SGCares and hope it gains stronger momentum amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On the ground, we can continue to develop platforms for people to give a little time and support to others.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is basically a platform for residents to make Requests and Offers and the Community Club will assist to match the needs and offers of support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: People should also be encouraged to continue taking care of the environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In keeping with the theme of a Budget for the future, I am happy to see the initiatives which pave the way towards a greener Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I trust there will be further efforts introduced to continue encouraging environmental consciousness.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At this juncture, I declare that I am a board member of the Singapore Environmental Council.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am of the view that any future efforts need to be realistic and sustainable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The programmes need to connect with the people on the ground.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My third point relates to harnessing our existing resources in the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the past one and a half years as a Member of Parliament, I have been approached by several young people, some of them living in my estate and who are looking to do projects to help the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is heartening and such enthusiasm should be nurtured and encouraged.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note there are many existing programmes for youths and platforms for them to express their views and obtain grants to carry out community projects.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At the local level, more can be done.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Grassroots organisations, VWOs and charities can work together with youths within the neighbourhood to create solutions that can benefit the local community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Over the past year, I had the chance to chat with and engage many people, including students, grassroots leaders, professionals, volunteers and housewives from the Malay-Muslim community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Initially, I was worried because I observed a lack of concern or sense of urgency about the ever-changing economic situation and the need to upskill to tackle the new economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, recently, I have seen a change in the mindsets and attitudes of our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many of them frequently asked about opportunities to upgrade themselves and many have taken the step to acquire new skills.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This awareness should be increased and guidelines to understand and use the available resources should be made clear.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I feel that the Malay-Muslim bodies can play an important role in providing the assistance and platform for our community to prepare themselves in acquiring the knowledge and skills to face the new economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My view is that every Malay-Muslim body needs to be aware of our nation's development and direction at the national level.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Programme planning and framework structuring must be in line with the direction that our country is heading to, so that we can help our community progress and be able to compete together with the other communities in this large family that we call Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Singapore is unlike other countries because our society is different.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a society, we treasure the harmony among the different races and religions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, we cannot take this sense of comfort for granted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Constant effort is required to foster inter-racial relations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We must always maintain a good relationship with our neighbours and colleagues so that we can rely on the strong bond that we built when we are faced with challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): I note that Minister Heng had said that we will take a learning and adaptive approach, try new methods, continue with them when they work well, cut losses when they do not and draw on feedback and experience to adjust and refine our plans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe this would also refer to our social policies as well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is a practical approach and it is important in ensuring that we keep pace with the uncertain and changing world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am grateful to be given the opportunity to serve on the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE), whose recommendations are broadly reflected in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This era is marked by rapid changes in technology, which is exciting because this presents many new possibilities for productivity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, this bright spot is, unfortunately, slightly clouded by the growing push from globalisation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It was the emblem of the United States (US) Presidential Elections.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We may see more of it when other European countries go to the polls later this year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Concerns were raised of their impact on an already dull economic forecast.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For Singapore, the policies of the Trump Administration may contribute to a slowdown in foreign direct investments from the US.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thus, it is good that we look at other areas for growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: CFE has rightly shifted its focus from just productivity to healthy sustainable growth by looking at new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would now like to discuss three areas where we can add to these maps, particularly from a social point of view.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Equality is key to promoting inclusive and sustainable growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The political lessons from the US and United Kingdom elections point to a failure to reconcile the vast differences between the voters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Globally, policymakers will be hampered by widening chasms, how to meet the needs and aspirations of the middle class and the rise of populism.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is vital that we recognise and prioritise the need to reduce gaps in living standards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In order to sustain public confidence in the various Government schemes, like the SkillsFuture Credit, that promote upscaling skills and continuing education, as well as various technological advancements, we must assure everyday Singaporeans that the Government is working to support the aspirations of all Singaporeans to have higher living standards and no erosion in social mobility.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The World Economic Forum commends Singapore for faring well in many areas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we ranked low in gender equality in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are still struggling to improve female participation in the labour force and narrowing the gender pay gap.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Measures were introduced to encourage men to play a more active role in fatherhood, through paternity leave, for example.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, parenthood does not stop at the baby stage.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More needs to be done in this area.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Tax reliefs for working mothers are well and good but, ultimately, the root problem must be solved − in my view − by creating a family-friendly working environment, without compromising overall productivity and growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should lift some of the load off the mother's shoulders, so that she does not feel the need to resign or compromise her work to care for the child.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Other forms of assistance to alleviate childcare costs and measures to encourage enhanced flexible work arrangements in the corporate and public sectors for all mothers, including working single mothers with children, will go a long way to alleviate childcare concerns as they struggle to also bring food to the table.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My next point in this area is with regard to the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even as we talk about help for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) over the past one day − SkillsFuture training, job matching and others − I believe one basic bedrock and core business of Government that we need to enhance further is TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As it is, most of us in Singapore or Singaporeans are employed, and not business owners.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am an active advocate for a stronger TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe it has greater potential to further eliminate workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Due to the changing social and global labour trends, we have a few groups of people vulnerable to workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to ensure that these contract or part-time staff are treated fairly and are not exploited by employers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, as we raise the retirement age for the older workers, we must also look into how in this age of digital transformation, they can be retrained to stay relevant to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are a country that thrives on meritocracy, and this must be reflected in our labour market and labour laws, which is one of our most crucial propellers for growth for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The next point I want to talk about is on helping employees − still within inclusive growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Minister Iswaran has elaborated at length yesterday that SMEs are our central focus in transforming our economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Minister Iswaran's speech yesterday has reassured SMEs, in my view.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, some of the short-term relief and targeted help for some sectors were made in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, broad social transfers to businesses are taking a backseat this year, as we all know, but I hope more can be introduced.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope that, in the future, some of these one-off measures can be rolled out to help SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the past year, social transfer to SMEs has also been generous.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some SMEs are still struggling to make sense of the schemes though, and some do not have the prerequisites to qualify for the schemes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, a lack of SME cash-flow visibility forces some of the banks and financial institutions to place greater emphasis on collateral requirements when assessing SME credit risk, but very often, SMEs are not able to provide such collateral, leading to their loan applications being rejected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I applaud the new International Partnership Fund to help SMEs scale up and internationalise, which is good.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the concern is that it would tend to invest in more established or initial public offering-ready firms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It may not benefit smaller, less-established SMEs which are capable of going into the region as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the relevant authorities can work closely with SMEs to help them realise their full potential.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The next point is about the tax system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has been a while since we last reviewed our tax system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Tax incentives should perhaps be given to the sectors that are favourable for our growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One question I have in relation to the tax review is the concern whether we are taxing the current generation disproportionately, relative to the savings set aside for future generations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The tax review mentioned in this Budget is timely as our funding for social spending is expected to continue to rise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In that sense, I hope the tax review will incorporate all options on the table.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, the review should broadly not just include more taxes but also Reserves accumulation and formulation of the net investment income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, how much flow or revenue is going into Reserves each year and whether it is falling sharply?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the possibility of considering a proportion of land sales and recurrent revenue from extension of leases of leasehold land into operating revenue rather than into Reserves, a situation we are seeing now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will more jobs be generated in these sectors, especially for the younger generation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How about the older employees who are not technology- or computer-savvy, but wish to do a mid-career switch?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second area is professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMET) stress.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moving on to the next topic, there have been a number of high-profile cases these couple of years whereby large companies have had to retrench some of their staff.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Undoubtedly, there must have been more in smaller companies that flew under the radar.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are certainly tough times for businesses, but even more so for the retrenched employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our tax filing season is just around the corner, and this brings to mind that those who have just lost a reasonably well-paying job due to retrenchment may find it tough paying for the income tax and other forms of taxes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Alternatively, allow the period for tax payments to be spread out over a longer period of time and allow for income tax payments to be deferred for unique circumstances.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My final area of focus is on overcoming global protectionist tides and having diversity in policies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the more advanced western countries coping with problems of their own and turning inwards, I am, hence, pleased to note that the economic focus is shifting back to our immediate neighbourhood − countries like Indonesia and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Now that the cards have been shuffled, we need to examine our approach and explore enhancing our various language policy options to make us the true global trader that we are in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we look at the protectionist rhetoric coming out of Washington, then the Indonesian economy is likely to be the least affected in the region, as they are not heavily dependent on the US.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Malay connection as in the context of reinforcing the relationship with our neighbours, through language and cultural ties, by learning the Malay language.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Compared to the older generation, the younger generation are also becoming less adept at the Malay language and understanding the culture as an extra option.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As for India, if we tap on the Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement, we could do well to also expose our students to learning Tamil and Hindi as a third language.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   For Singapore to remain adaptable and competitive, diversity in education and proficiency in three languages may be necessary.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And starting the learning process from a young age is one of the keys to proficiency.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Government will encourage the availability of more language options in schools.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Society is at the stage where we increasingly recognise and encourage many different pathways to success and many students who select these institutions have high aspirations and career paths that they would like to pursue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some are even more confident and clear about their future compared to their GCE "A" level counterparts from the same cohort, for instance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Those who have studied abroad would appreciate that through our interactions overseas, we would benefit from cultural diversity and this would help to open our minds as a community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are all aware that if we want to broaden and deepen our perspectives on a particular topic, there is value in reading books by different authors on the same subject, and the same thing also applies in terms of policy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Madam, we are expecting difficult, unpredictable times ahead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we do not make changes now, many workers may find a bee in their bonnet, worrying about having a job tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have a bright future and this Budget puts us in good stead.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But in time to come, it will become a worrying concern in the minds of all Singaporeans, young and old.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What the future holds for our jobs, careers and cost of living upon retirement are questions that will creep up eventually.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Budget 2017 is a reflection of the uncertain times we are living in today.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Although this Budget attempts to address some of the concerns and outlines measures for our economy and society to weather the uncertainties, there is just no certainty in dealing with uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some measures may work and some may not.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some measures are judgement calls, calculated at best, clutching at straws at worst, all in the hope that some of them will bear fruits for the economy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of the previous Budget measures have gone on to become permanent features of the fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some were given a makeover, hoping that the result will work better this time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What does the Government hope to see at the end of this initiative?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We have seen this initiative introduced in the past under different packaging.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What did the Government learn from the results of the past initiative?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Why are the targeted SMEs not embracing the digital revolution, despite the many opportunities to do so in the past?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Does the Government want every SME to go digital?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And is it even necessary to do so?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One of the measures introduced in 2010, the Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) scheme, has impacted the food services sector positively.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The tablet computer has replaced the hardcopy menu in many restaurants.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Customers no longer need to wait to be served to place their orders.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The use of technology in this instance is motivated and meaningful.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In 2006, then Second Minister for Information, Communication and the Arts, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, highlighted an example of a local businessman who had embraced infocomm to improve his business.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He shared that the dessert stall owner has invested in the touchscreen system to allow customers to place their dining in or take-out orders at the Peoples' Park Complex Food Centre.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He cited that the use of technology had brought the owner new business and improved productivity in tracking the stock of the dessert sold and the amount of ingredients left.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I visited the dessert shop at the old food centre to see for myself why the shop was worthy of a mention by the Minister at the Opening of 10th InfoComm Commerce Conference in 2006.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The dessert shop was manned by two persons: a lady at the counter and a gentleman to prepare the dessert right behind her.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Both of them could easily take orders from customers, as the shop was very small.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For those who have been to Peoples' Park Complex, you will know what I mean.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I proceeded to order via the touchscreen and waited.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I looked back at her and tried to hint with my eyes that I have just ordered my dessert at the touchscreen system.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: There was a queue forming and she snapped suddenly and said, "Ai see mi", which means "What do you want?" So, the touchscreen system was not broken but it was not much of a use.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A decade on, and the use of the touchscreen technology in hawker centres has not caught on.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It was more of a novelty than an enterprising productivity tool, as highlighted by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It can be a productivity tool or a glorified novelty.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This Government should not waste public fund on the latter.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The fact of the matter is, for some sectors, going digital may not be the sole solution to improving productivity.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Beyond automation and going digital, the cleaning sector, for example, needs a redesign in the way refuse and waste are being collected.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The design of old HDB estates needs a serious relook because it takes too long to clear the many bin chutes for just one block of flats.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Going digital alone is not going to help the cleaning sector.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It also needs the whole-of-Government (WoG) approach to educate or incentivise the public to generate less waste, because no amount of productivity improvements is going to help if we keep on generating waste at the current rate.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is important to embrace the digital economy, but going digital alone is not going to resolve the productivity issue.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The digital economy needs "brick and mortar" support.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It may need the Government to relook into all the compliance processes and to remove them if necessary.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Getting SMEs to go digital is only one part of the equation.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It needs a collective effort for the digital economy to function and flourish.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, most of the measures introduced under the objective to sustain a quality environment for the future will impact Singaporeans and the aggregate of their impact will add to the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Since the Government has taken the approach to incentivise users to reduce consumption and manufacturers to develop more energy-efficient vehicles, the special tax on diesel cars and taxis should be scrapped completely upon the implementation of the volume-based diesel tax.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Likewise, now that the tax structure for all motor fuels is harmonised, the road tax for vehicles should also be scrapped in favour of the more equitable volume-based usage tax, which was already in place for the longest time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Road usage is tied to the consumption of fuel.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The more road you travel, the more fuel you burn and the more tax you will pay, be it petrol duty or diesel tax.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, why are motorists being slapped with a road tax that is based on the engine capacity of the vehicles?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What has engine capacity got to do with road usage?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The current road tax regime is beyond a misnomer to begin with.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Let us compare two cars of the same engine capacity.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If one owner uses his vehicle seven days a week while the other utilises his vehicle three times a week, why are both drivers paying the same road tax when one is obviously contributing more to road congestion and pollution?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What is the relevance and purpose of keeping an engine capacity-based road tax which has no relation to road usage, on top of the volume-based fuel duty which, in my opinion, is the actual and fairer road tax?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Last, the quantum of the water price hike is perhaps the most puzzling measure in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Minister Masagos has stated in his reply to my Parliamentary Question that the current national average water consumption has dropped about 11% as compared to 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If we look at the per capita usage, water consumption in Singapore is about 5% to 70% lower than that of London, Melbourne, Tokyo, Hong Kong and New York.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They basically say Singaporeans understand the scarcity of water and we have been doing our part to conserve this precious element all this while.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Minister also acknowledged that and he cautioned Singaporeans not to be complacent and to save more water wherever possible.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Public Utilities Board (PUB) said this cost included water treatment, reservoir operation, NEWater production, desalination, used water collection and treatment, and the maintenance of water pipelines.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Using simple ratio, the share of the cost of supplying water to households should be 45% of $1.3 billion or $585 million.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This will roughly translate to an average cost of about $40 per month to supply water to each household in 2015.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This is well below the average monthly water bill paid by households of 4-room flats and above and, I am sure, for most private housing as well, before the proposed price hike.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As highlighted by the Government, water prices have remained unchanged since 2000.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What that means is that the margin of supplying water to households could be even higher in 2000 than what I have estimated for 2015.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Using the same assumption, it costs about $21 per month to supply water to each household in 2000, since water consumption per household was fairly stable the past decade and water prices have not changed since 2000 and, based on available data, the Government could not have lost money supplying water to households for the past 15 years.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Resident households are already facing price pressure in carpark charges, transportation to food.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: From the proposed carbon tax, volume-based diesel tax and the 30% hike in water prices, the knock-on effect will be felt by Singaporeans eventually one way or another.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, why I think the revised water tariffs are a fairer mechanism than our current pricing system and should, therefore, be supported; and, second, why I think water pricing is a limited instrument in reflecting the true value of water, especially in the high uncertain future which lies ahead.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The last time we raised the water price, it was against the background of an intense price negotiation with Malaysia over the price of water.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the time, it was truly an existential issue.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I would argue it has been so since our Independence and will be so as long as Singapore remains a small island of no more than 700-plus square kilometres with not enough land for the graves of our ancestors, the training of our armed forces, and, yes, the large catchment areas needed to store water.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In 1963, we were dependent on Malaysia for three-quarters of our water supply.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In that year, in his Fullerton Rally speech before the General Elections, then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew spoke of water.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He had to because it was a hot issue during the elections, which were held in the middle of a drought.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: His opponents at the time accused him of not doing enough to provide for water and promised to solve the problem by quickly expanding pipelines to run more water from Johor − disregarding the fact that it takes years to build pipes and that thirst kills in those days.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Of course, the fact that we live in the tropics also means that rains are likely to come before the pipes were completed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: During the speech, Mr Lee also spoke about engineering works, reservoirs and the need to ensure a long-term supply of water by negotiating water agreements.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It was only after the agreements had been signed, he said, that works on expanding the pipelines began.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Water was, and remains, a long-term engineering and infrastructural public good but its impact can be felt in the very short term and is, in fact, a highly political good.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the time since the announcement of the water price, detractors have lost no time in politicising the issue.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I will address the two myths that have come up in the past two weeks, show how they are false and state my support for raising the water price, with the corresponding help extended to various households through the U-Save and Goods and Services Tax (GST) vouchers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, there have been accusations that the Government is making money off water.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some of us may have received messages that PUB is making $166 million of profits a year.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In 2012, the then-Environment Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan had said that the Government pays $1.3 billion a year to run the system but collects only about $1 billion in water tariffs − marginal charges − and water borne and sanitary fees − these are fixed charges.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In simple terms, we could say that water is thus subsidised by at least 30%.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At least 30% because prices charged do not reflect the capital costs of the water and the wastewater system.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The second objection is tied to the first − that raising the water price will hit the poor heavily while the rich will still be able to use as much water as they want.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, raising the price of water to reflect its true cost, I believe, is a fairer system than subsidising it willy-nilly.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But we can and should raise tariffs without burdening the poor.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this case, the Government has proposed increasing prices in such a way that ensures burdens fall lightest on the poorest.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One- and 2-room HDB flat owners will, in fact, see no increase in their bills at all.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Last, I want to address the limits of water pricing.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As policymakers, we use price for many things − we use it as an incentive, as a tax, as a signal on how much we value things.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A household of five in Singapore pays $30 a month for water − 0.04% of the median income.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Each month, for many of us, our handphone bill costs more than our water bill.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Using price alone to motivate people to save water, I believe, is not going to work.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Water consumption per capita has stayed roughly the same since the last price increase.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It was 165 litres in 2003 and it has gone down a little bit to 151 litres today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It may be that the increase in price may reduce water consumption but I believe we would need something else to bring home the value of water.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I started my speech by referring to the 1963 speech by Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The year after, in 1964, Singapore held a water rationing exercise.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It was to be our last such exercise.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Since then, we have had no water rationing, not because we have not had severe droughts but because our systems are now far more resilient.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But research at the Institute of Water Policy at the National University of Singapore (NUS) has shown that such "resilience" should be interpreted with care.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It was more severe, in fact, than 1964.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, that month of February was the driest month since 1869, with near-zero rainfall.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In neighbouring Malaysia, water rationing was implemented in Johor, Selangor, Negri Sembilan, Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In nearby Thailand, 20 provinces were declared drought disaster areas.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, there was no rationing and, in fact, water consumption increased by 5%.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Extreme weather events, including heavy rainfall and exceptionally dry periods, are projected to occur more frequently for the Southeast Asia region as a whole.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Historical data has shown that Malaysia and Singapore, as a region, has experienced severe droughts in 19 of the past 150 years.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need, therefore, not just to prepare for everyday scenarios, but to ensure that our people are psychologically strong.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Resilience, therefore, not just in systems but in our people.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singaporeans born after 1964 have never experienced water rationing.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think there are a few Members of Parliament who have not gone through that experience.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They do not know the experience of having to go without water or bear the weight of 130 litres of water that we would need if we take a long shower of 15 minutes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is not a new suggestion but one that has a special salience in the light of this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I suggest we do this, not during droughts, but during "peace time" as it were, following the footsteps of countries, such as Australia, where they are called "water restrictions".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is an inoculation against the environmental realities that are to come.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In 2016, Singapore joined more than 120 countries to ratify the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It was a formal commitment to combat global warming and reduce climate change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this Budget, the carbon tax can be seen as part of a larger movement towards addressing the effects of climate change and other environmental challenges.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Being densely populated and urbanised, Singapore is highly vulnerable to abrupt changes in the environment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The carbon tax brings Singapore in line with other countries as well as our regulatory environment for businesses.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I urge the Finance Minister to think also of the impact of mass human behaviour in this and bring into play the Sustainable Singapore Blueprint two years ago.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These include embedding towns and homes with smart technology and eco-friendly features, reducing reliance on cars by building up the public transport system and encouraging cycling, encouraging sustainable business practices and achieving zero-waste by encouraging recycling and reducing consumption.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many countries have had to balance a trade-off between development and environmental sustainability.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In China, decades of rapid growth have been accompanied by severe air pollution.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore appears to have achieved both economic development and environmental sustainability at the same time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But as our Prime Minister noted during its launch, a large part of the Blueprint's success will depend on the collective action among individuals to adopt green practices in their daily lives, as well as build up new norms of sustainability within their communities.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The environment is a common pool enjoyed by everyone.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It can only be protected through the efforts of everyone.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Environmental sustainability is truly a collective effort that begins with the individual but has important implications for our collective future as a community.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must take the first steps in order to ensure a cleaner, greener and more comfortable living environment for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Water can be priced, but clean air cannot.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot expect our children to grow up respecting nature and being willing to pay for clean air, clean water, to live together with trees and wild animals and insects if we do not, in our policy decisions, underline the importance of these voiceless stakeholders in the use of our public spaces and financial resources.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Finance Minister has said that he will set aside funds for "diverse social spaces where people can come together, create shared experiences and forge stronger bonds." In that, money must go towards large projects, such as Jurong Lake Gardens.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I suggest that we also think of small spaces, of giving support to community green clubs, of allowing social groups and civil societies to flourish within their own homes, towns and districts, and to educate residents on the need to make room for trees, birds and wildlife within our urban environment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the age of the Anthropocene, where human activity can be seen as the dominant influence on climate and the environment, we need to grow even greener, to keep our waters even bluer.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The alternative is to be breathing in more polluted air, greenery around us turning to brown dirt, and sweating in the heat of global warming.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We should be ready to pay the price for our industrial actions, whether it be in the form of increased water tariffs or by changing the way we live and behave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: They address ongoing challenges in the economic restructuring process and, despite the changes the last year has brought, reiterate the vision of a secure future that Minister Heng has set out from last year's Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The circumstances we face are undoubtedly unique, but there are important lessons from the experience of other countries that we only ignore at our peril.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We could just as easily become trapped in our own lost decade, exhausting our limited resources on a dispersed agenda without heed to strengthening our economic foundations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Our priority, therefore, should be to provide a footing for future generations that is even more secure than the one we now have.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget takes a strong lead in shaping the environmental agenda.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We have enjoyed our entitlements of clean air and clean water for as long as we remember.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But the unwelcome reality brought about by changes in our world is that not only are both in short supply, the two are growing sources of contention in an increasingly fractious world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has developed a lead in clean water technology and we can do the same with green technologies in general.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A fundamental element in managing the competing access to clean water and air is to correctly price their availability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The long-term consequences of mispricing water and pollution are severe and incompatible with the direction we intend to take for our future economy, as well as for our society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We should not leave future generations unprepared to confront a problem that is developing now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The issue is not how much clean water we still have or where the current threats to our environmental air quality lie.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The issue is much broader and has to do with our collective responsibility for the environment and societal development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I would like to urge the Minister to consider price corrections in other areas in urgent need of attention as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Areas, such as electronic waste generation, should be incorporated into a comprehensive strategy for responsible environmental advocacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: By ensuring that pricing is imposed on both water and pollution, Singapore is not just taking a responsible leadership role in pushing forward the agenda for dealing with climate change, we will also be putting in place incentives for nurturing the development of technologies whose global economic potential is rapidly expanding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: These lie in the path of our future economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The first of these is our manpower policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We should strengthen the connection between our manpower policy and our skills framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although the recent weakening in demand has been partly due to economic conditions, there is little doubt that the primary mechanism bringing about this shift is the system of levies and dependency ratio ceilings (DRCs).

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Our policy on foreign manpower should not just be about restrictions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It should be about promoting long-term economic competitiveness for the benefit of our overall workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In order to realise this objective, we must be open to the type of skills we lack and incorporate foreign manpower contributions into a comprehensive strategy for filling our skills gaps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The indications are that we have made promising improvements in this direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, labour productivity measures depict improving performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What is reassuring is that these changes occurred gradually, despite the fluid environment and turbulent global backdrop.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The work is far from done and the productivity challenge is an ongoing one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The delicate balance of maintaining robust domestic employment, ensuring global standards of openness to deep and diverse skills, and injecting momentum into the productivity drive is a challenge that all countries face.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Given the limitations of our domestic labour market, the magnitude of the challenge we face in Singapore is far greater.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: That is why robust yet flexible policy instruments are so important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There is no doubt that our foreign manpower management policy has encountered enormous challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This should not detract from the tremendous success it represents as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Compared to many other countries, we have taken a lead in this area and we should recognise its effectiveness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, we should reorientate our policy to move away from restricting inflows and focus on growing skills sets that our domestic workforce alone will be too slow to achieve on its own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The "triple weak" system promulgated by the Minister for Manpower for monitoring companies' with poor hiring practices already contains essentially the same key ingredients, which is that companies should be assessed on a multi-dimensional metric, rather than a single-dimensional measure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The predecessor to CFE, the Economic Strategies Committee, originally proposed the system of levies and DRCs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In its report, it recognises the need for foreign talent with specialised skillsets and calls to develop a more differentiated foreign workforce policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The measurement of skillsets and skills levels should be carried out in coordination with the skills framework constructs being developed by SkillsFuture Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The resulting system should be validated by the needs of the ITMs, merged with the current levels of foreign workforce passes, and used to assess the extent to which gaps at the company as well as sectoral level can or cannot be filled by the existing local workforce supply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Such a system can also be used to track whether the gaps are effectively closed over time through training, and how fast this is occurring.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The system of foreign manpower levies and DRCs forms a clear set of rules for managing foreign manpower participation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, including the current Budget proposal, the system has been used to moderate the impact of manpower cost pressures when economic conditions are poor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As a counter-cyclical tool, the system of levies and DRCs can be adjusted by sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And compared to alternatives, such as the Central Provident Fund (CPF) cuts that were used in the past, this approach is much more amenable to finetuning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My second concern is about the challenges of scale that we, in Singapore, almost uniquely in world, face.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Whether we are prepared for the reality of competing against countries much larger than us, this is something that we will have to deal with as a result of the proposals set out in this Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget makes a significant push for internationalisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This will increase the companies and local talent being given greater exposure to global competition and will serve us well in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: While programmes, such as the Global Innovation Alliance (GIA), can help Singaporeans gain a foothold in overseas markets, as well as a better appreciation of our global competition, there are adjustments that individuals have to make.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the transformative impact of the GIA will take some years to become visible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The issue of scale has always been something of a challenge for Singapore's economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We have pushed near to saturation point in many of our efforts, but the competition can harness vastly larger numbers without batting an eyelid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This fact is visible in every aspect in which we compete internationally, from trade figures to our workforce composition, to even our robot density.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Our share, of course, has also grown, more than doubling to 2.3%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Between 1984 and 2015, the share of the US in world manufacturing exports fell by a third.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: These developments have redefined the global economic balance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: They have also brought about the tremendous groundswell of reaction that ranges from the Brexit vote outcome to the repudiation of the Trans-Pacific Partnership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In 2015, world manufacturing exports shrank more than 8% in nominal terms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The options we have in reacting to these changes are determined not just by our preference, but also by the choices made by the countries we compete against.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: China is also the world leader in high-technology manufacturing exports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, Singapore's share of global high-technology exports is about a quarter of China's, which makes this sector more important to us than general manufacturing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Across all regions of the world and in many countries, the proportion of manufacturing classified as high technological activity is on the rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A comparison across countries reveals a visible correlation between this rise and the increasing use of robotics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister for Finance Mr Heng had already pointed out last year, China is the world's largest buyer of robots.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And other countries are keeping pace, including Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: According to a recent update from the International Federation of Robotics, between 2010 and 2015, the operational stock of industrial robots in Asia rose 70%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Robotics and artificial intelligence (AI) are just two of the things that are often mentioned in the same breath as Uber and Grab when discussing technological changes and disruption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, what concerns those who cite them as examples in the same breath is not necessarily their economic or technological novelty but the loss of control workers feel in facing the rise of these innovations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This fear of loss of control is the most important reason why ordinary workers today identify with the notion of being caught up in an industrial revolution beyond their control, no different from the original one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Research supported by the International Federation of Robotics argues that while there have been job losses, their magnitudes are small, compared to the increase in employment over the same period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless of whether one believes in net gain or loss of jobs due to the introduction of new technologies, such as robotics, there is little doubt that existing jobs will have to give way to new ones and the workforce must, therefore, be prepared to adjust to this reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although we cannot be certain about the precise rate and impact of the change on all jobs, the pattern of change and the nature of jobs of the future are becoming increasingly evident.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Job creation is increasingly concentrated in domains requiring high intensity of knowledge and skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In research and development (R&D), for instance, across countries and with very few exceptions, the number of personnel has seen strong upward trends.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is true both in absolute terms and as a ratio of the population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore, of course, as usual, faces the limitation of size that our competitors do not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: To remain competitive despite our limitations, our workforce must be prepared for a continuing process of advancement and workplace transformation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporean workers, many of whom juggle their regular jobs with important roles, such as family caregivers, will have to add regular overseas postings to the list.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is what we have to do as an innovation in order to overcome the limits of scale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Given our size, we are already at the boundaries of what we can reasonably achieve if we go by norms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Both in R&D personnel and in robot density, we are already at the limits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Countries whose sizes are multiples of ours have a lot more scope for expansion in absolute terms and will reap further economies of scale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Internationalisation will, therefore, expand the potential space within which our companies and workers operate, but not completely overcome the fundamental disadvantage of scale that Singapore has always faced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just workers who will be challenged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs will also feel the discomfort in operating outside of their comfort zones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The question I am trying to ask is: are the internationalisation initiatives a realistic option for local companies which do not have the basic capacity to scale up beyond their setup in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The timeline this time around will, I believe, turn out to be the greatest challenge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Many of the past restructuring efforts had tangible endpoints, such as the challenge of a recession, that it could take reference from.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This particular restructuring is a long drawn-out process and it is going to be challenging to focus minds on the intangible aspects of the strategy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although the restructuring is aimed at addressing the challenges caused by disruption, as the timeline for restructuring lengthens, it will heighten uncertainty among companies and workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For some, the distinction between restructuring and disruption could begin to blur.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The completion of this restructuring will not be readily marked by new buildings or highways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Success will probably mean not just an endpoint but an ongoing process of change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, in closing, I would like to thank Finance Minister Heng for staying the course in this restructuring journey as well as for providing a personal model of resilience through adversity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While it improves the way work is done and alleviates the issue of manpower shortage, it will have implications on our workers and they could become tomorrow's unemployed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The challenge is whether we can help tomorrow's unemployed today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How technology impacts our work can be broken down into three broad categories: "Known-Known", "Known-Unknown" and "Unknown-Unknown".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The first refers to a situation where we know the technology and know its impact.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One such example is the self-checkout kiosks found in supermarkets today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other supermarkets, such as Cold Storage and Sheng Siong, have also implemented such "do-it-yourself" services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The job of the traditional cashier is slowly replaced by new technology.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The next category is where we know the technology, but we are not sure when and how it will impact our current work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we speak, trials of autonomous vehicles, like cars, buses and even trucks, are ongoing at different parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While we know that such driverless technology exists and is developing at a rapid pace, what we are uncertain of is when it can be adopted and how extensive will the adoption be.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will certainly change the modus operandi within the transport industry and have a direct downstream impact on our workers who depend on driving as a livelihood.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another example is additive manufacturing, commonly known as 3D printing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the rapid development of 3D printing technology in recent years, many applications have been developed in the food, medical, fast-moving consumer goods and other industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With 3D printing, if our child outgrows his or her shoes, we can simply print out a brand new pair in a larger size!

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The potential disruption that 3D printing may have on our industries is significant.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How and which industries would be affected by 3D printing?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The last category refers to an unknown technology that may change our work in the future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Here, we could take reference and learn from the past "Unknown-Unknown", such as Uber and Grab.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, Uber and Grab are providing new transport options to commuters but have disrupted the traditional taxi business.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Did we expect Uber and Grab, which are mobile applications, to enter, disrupt and even revolutionise the transport industry?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The three situations above illustrate the challenges we face in the current economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Be it "Known-Known", "Known-Unknown" or even "Unknown-Unknown", there is an urgent need for both our workers and companies to brace themselves for the next wave of disruption, as business cycles get shorter and changes happen more rapidly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, our workers need to remain competitive amidst the changes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to embrace the concept of lifelong learning, continuously train and upskill ourselves and start preparing for future jobs even before the current one becomes obsolete.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To do so, companies, unions and Government agencies need to get together to identify future jobs, determine skills gaps and establish structured training programmes for workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Industry partners can collaborate and develop sectoral level training to collectively raise standards across the industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But the Academy has the potential to provide continuous training for all bus captains, keep them updated with industry and technological changes, help existing drivers multiskill and be better prepared for tomorrow's driverless world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should explore setting up centralised training centres to promote training through the respective Sectoral Tripartite Committees even beyond the transport industry, like the lift, aviation and precision engineering sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He left the infocomm technology (IT) sector amid the global recession in 2009 and enrolled himself into a PCP to join the early childhood education sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although the transition was tough as he sought to overcome job challenges in a female-dominated industry, Wayne persevered through his traineeship, took up a diploma and subsequently completed his Masters in Early Childhood.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Wayne did well and is now the acting principal of My First Skool preschool centre in Sengkang.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hopefully, with the newly announced Attach and Train programme, we can look forward to hear more of such stories of success.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If employers proclaim that their employees are the company's most valuable assets, they should step up training investments to upskill their workers and not view manpower as simply a cost.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While some companies are afraid that workers might leave after acquiring new skills, other companies have established training centres, set aside dedicated training hours and sponsored training courses to support their employees in their upgrading efforts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, the Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation (OCBC) is one such company that is pro-training.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By grooming a competitive workforce can our companies remain competitive, productive and prepared for the next wave of change.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to their small scale of business, SMEs sometimes find it onerous to go through the process of applying for productivity grants.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the labour market expected to tighten further, businesses need to be supported in their efforts to raise productivity while adopting less labour-intensive practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In a fast-changing world, we can no longer depend on "one-size-fits-all" solutions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Industry-based roadmaps are very much needed to provide clarity to both our workers and companies on the new jobs and the direction in which the specific industry is moving towards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Japan, 58-year-old Mr Kenji Takemura harnessed a wearable robot technology to help him lift 40-kilogramme boxes with ease.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Like Mr Takemura, we need to learn to work with technology, collectively leverage new technologies, upskill ourselves and be forward thinking.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The success of the CFE report lies in its implementation and I am confident that with our strong tripartite partnership, we can overcome current and future challenges just as how we have done so in the past decades.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through tripartism at the national and sectoral levels, we must help our workers upskill ahead of time as our economy and our industries transform.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to help tomorrow's unemployed today and ensure that no one would be left behind.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One of our young couples in Clementi had a baby girl at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A beautiful baby with a proud mommy and daddy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But when it was time for the HDB's Home Improvement Programme − upgrading within the home − the parents were worried about noise and dust during the construction.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The next-door neighbours opened their home, offered their own home as a place to babysit the baby girl.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Baby is happy and the neighbours have grown closer together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am also moved, during times of sadness, when I meet with my residents at funeral wakes at the void deck, whether it is a breadwinner who passed away and the family is wondering what to do in economic challenge or whether it is an old parent who has passed on after a long illness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But I also see neighbours coming together in this moment looking out for one and another, supporting one another in this time of need.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But I also hear stories from residents about how society is changing and how newer HDB estates seem to make it harder to meet neighbours and new friends.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our multiracial society is very special, very precious.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It also helps us, as a country, connect economically to the West and to many parts of Asia.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But in many societies around the world, social cohesion is being eroded.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A child growing up in a one-child family has a different experience and may not learn the same social skills to get on with others until preschool or school begins.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, if we lose our cohesion, Mdm Speaker, we are finished.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because we will not be able to organise to meet challenges, we will not be able to move as one, we will be less than the sum of our parts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Without social cohesion, we are less than a dot.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
