text: Even as we transform for the future economy and watch our bottom line, our fiscal sustainability, we need to keep on paying attention to social cohesion in all our policies across the whole-of-Government.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is an important issue because design changes in public housing can be revenue-neutral, but they shape an entire generation of society and our heartlands.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But in the modern era of globalisation and wealth inequality, our Ministries should also look at closer integration of Singaporeans from different economic backgrounds within the same block.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The design, proportion and distribution can be studied by the agencies, so that the effect is salubrious rather than divisive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is something that I believe the Ministries should look into.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of my residents feel sad that newer estates are devoid of void decks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or the void deck is shaped such that people do not meet one another as naturally as before.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I suggest, Mdm Speaker, that HDB should revive the older-style void decks or at least think of ways to channel people together, so that people meet naturally, grow to know one another, build friendships.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, the shape of our HDB blocks matters, too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of my residents said that our blocks today are not shaped the way they used to be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In some precincts, including award-winning precincts, the common corridors branch off.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It means fewer lines of sight for neighbours to meet one another, look at one another, start that conversation in the morning on the way to the lift; fewer chances for people to get to know one another spontaneously, day by day.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is something our agencies should look at, Mdm Speaker.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Urban design shapes who we live with; who we know; who we meet.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How we build our homes, how we build our heartlands affect our social cohesion.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our estates are our home today, but they shape our society tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have seen many legal innovations in recent years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, people can do independent work for multiple hirers, using online marketplaces to match supply and demand.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have raised it in this House and elsewhere.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are opportunities in this brave new world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The gig economy can unlock skills and experience not yet tapped from the labour market.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is important, given our ageing population, demographic constraints and smaller families.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I remember a retired nurse I met on my home visit in Clementi.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She is 65 years old, or rather 65 years young, full of energy, still wants to make use of her skills.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But because her husband is sick, she needs to spend extra time looking after him, which makes it harder for her to work a full shift or even a partial shift.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Singaporeans with caregiving duties can also work more flexible hours − a retired nurse can keep active, does not have to work a full shift, maybe helping at a clinic near her home or as a private nurse to fellow residents in the neighbourhood, changing a catheter, changing a wound dressing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Micro-jobs, but they add up to skills that can be tapped.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Additional income, helping people who receive the service, helping the person who is earning.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It also helps SMEs which may not be able to afford a full-time department, whether it is a legal department, graphic design department, copywriting department.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, Madam, there are also big challenges when the nature of work changes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For decades, the relationship has been very much between the employer and the employee at the workplace.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For a long time, this has been a focus for legislation, sick leave benefits, healthcare coverage or CPF.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A delivery driver may be doing the same work as before.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But instead of being a payroll employee, he is now called to be doing a contract for service.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But Madam, this shifts responsibility and risk to the worker.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Home ownership, healthcare because of MediSave, retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And all these, if they come to a head, will affect our fiscal policies as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some have said that the market alone is enough.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But Madam, I believe the market is not enough to impose discipline.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even in the tightest of labour markets, there can be segmentation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some workers having a more difficult time than others.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And it is the vulnerable workers who are not able to find a job in the regular labour market who will have the least bargaining power in the gig economy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At my Meet-the-People Session, I met a resident in his 50s.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He used to be on an employment contract.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But recently, his employer called him in and said, "We are changing you to a new contract".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, he asked what is this new contract about?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Same work, different contract; less benefits, more vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, this is a real issue affecting our workers, especially vulnerable workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And as more jobs become part of the gig economy, I worry more Singaporeans will be affected.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I believe we need to address this sooner rather than later, before the labour market norms reach a tipping point as more companies join the gig and there is a race to the bottom.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, we risk having a cohort of gig workers who have been disadvantaged by this market failure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our policies must keep up, so that our workers are not left behind.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Singapore is small enough, nimble enough and organised enough that we can reinvent our policies for a new century.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can build a better understanding of the job market to improve opportunities for all our workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Imagine if our Ministries apply big data analytics to the job market, pulling data from multiple databases, getting data on how training leads to jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Which course helps to find work fastest and best?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How many people are using the skills they were trained for?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Was the training provider selling hope or helping our workers to gain skills and opportunities?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This can also help us understand how underemployment arises and how to prevent it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our Ministries can also pull big data to have better sensing of market trends.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are people from some backgrounds having more difficulty than others?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are there areas which need to be looked into through deep dives, drilling down to understand where and how best to intervene?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Better data, Mdm Speaker, also opens the door to new policy responses.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This could be done on a testbed basis in sandboxed sectors of the gig economy where you can clearly define the nature of the firm and how the workers are being contracted.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We could have a formula that looks at the total wages from the gig employer or the number of hours spent on gig jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We could find new ways to measure a unit of labour.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The same online platforms that create an Uber, Deliveroo, Foodpanda, all these can provide new ways to measure and ensure that workers have the same protection and benefits they did in the traditional economy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Together, the Ministries could develop an operating system to specify employers' responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or even risk pooling among the gig employers so that the worker has insurance coverage for health benefits or sick leave, rather than falling between the cracks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A strong society is a prerequisite for sustainable economic development.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It gives us the resolve and courage needed to overcome uncertainty, instead of waiting and seeing, and stepping forward, moving ahead, making a difference, moving faster than the competition.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A strong society also gives us the social consensus for fiscal redistribution, for broad centrist policies, for a fair and equitable society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many expressed concerns on the possibility of a major global impact these two events may pose, especially on the economic front.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We rely heavily on our human resource to generate a strong and robust economy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, we are also very aware that human resource is a challenging factor in the near future due to the drop in our total fertility rate (TFR) in a rapidly ageing population.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Apart from making efforts to increase our TFR, we should also find ways to empower Singaporeans, in particular, our workforce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With an empowered nation only can we achieve our objective of, one, a compassionate and inclusive society and, two, an innovative and connected economy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In addition to improving individual skills of the workforce through training, schemes, such as Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) and others, have also been introduced to equip companies and employers with technologies to further enhance innovation and productivity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, enhancement is also very much needed in the aspect of software or heartware.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Technology, by itself, is not able to achieve better innovation and productivity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Its effectiveness relies on employees who use the technology.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Only with a motivated workforce can we work towards enhancing our innovation and productivity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A motivated employee is obviously more innovative and productive and many studies have proven this.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The same study also found that workers who are otherwise unhappy show a decline of 10% in their productivity level.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many internationally renowned companies and corporations practise employee-centric work culture.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Mr Richard Branson, Founder of Virgin Group, in an interview in 2014, mentioned that one business strategy that he used is employee-centric management, giving priority to employees.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He said, and I quote, "It should go without saying if a person who works at your company is 100% proud of the brand, and you give them the tools to do a good job and they are treated well, they are going to be happy." In the same interview, Mr Branson also said, and I quote, "If a person who works at your company is not appreciated, they are not going to do things with a smile." Mr Branson further shared that the first priority is his employees, customers second and shareholders third.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Google, a giant Internet company, emphasises on organisational and work culture that focuses on satisfaction and happiness of employees.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a result, Google has consistently received the top spot in the list of Fortune's Best Companies to work for.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Google believes that, on average, a person spends most of his time in the workplace and, hence, it is important to feel happy and calm.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They believe, with joy and peace, it will spark innovation and productivity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Amongst Google's initiatives are: one, their offices are designed with an open concept that allows the employees to interact openly in order to stimulate the mind and spark innovation; two, to provide facilities, such as gymnasium, fitness centre and games room.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Google believes that a healthy workplace produces joy and happiness and, hence, this will further spark innovation and productivity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Google's office in Malaysia houses a cafe© that provides free food to employees.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Google believes that spending on such is part of their investment cost because everyone knows that good food can boost employees' morale.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: What is the situation of our organisational and work culture in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Do they feel their employer cares for them?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Are our employers making the employees as their top priority?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To answer these questions, I will cite findings of a couple of studies conducted, addressing the issues of Singapore's employees' level of happiness.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Their findings indicated that employees in Singapore are not so happy with their workplace.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The index obtained is 59 out of 100 fell in the category under "happy".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The study used a scientific method that contains 20 factors which were categorised into four main categories ‒ satisfaction, alignment, engagement and well-being.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The survey also found that happiness is related to employees' perception of their work and experience in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The report also stated that the ability of companies or employers in promoting pride, positive emotions, a sense of accomplishment and enhancing work culture will affect how happy their employees may feel.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In September 2016, JobStreet issued a report on a survey, Job Happiness Index, which was conducted in seven ASEAN countries.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The report further mentioned that, given such circumstances, employers have been advised to revisit and review their human resource (HR) practices and address the factors that caused employees to feel less satisfaction.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Overall, if we look at the studies and surveys conducted on Singapore's workforce for the last couple of years, our workers are unhappy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Arguably, the main cause is our organisational and work culture that does not give job satisfaction.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The consequences of not being able to provide job satisfaction are hampering our productivity and innovation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is a process that needs collective and continuous effort and participation of the Government, employers and employees, spanning over a period of time.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government must take the lead in changing the organisational and work cultures through programmes, its schemes and other initiatives.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Programmes should be conducted for employers to enhance their knowledge on how to establish a conducive work culture that can make employees feel appreciated and, thus, feel more motivated to innovate and be more productive.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Employers have an important task in ensuring that the Government's schemes and initiatives are being implemented and practised in the most extensive manner to bring about an employee-centric culture.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As for employees, they must strive to manifest the best work values.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One way of doing so is to attend more programmes and training to improve both the hard and soft skills.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am of the view that we need to cater more programmes and training focusing on the development of soft skills.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The reason is that self-awareness, as well as awareness and a better understanding of others around us, will allow the development of more positive and effective intra- and interpersonal skills.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We need not teach the whole spectrum on the subject of psychology.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The learning of these three components will allow our younger generation to develop better awareness of themselves, family members, friends and others in our society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With such better awareness, our young ones will be able to establish good social and community values.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And with such good values, and equipped together with skills and knowledge, our young Singaporeans will be more empowered when entering our workforce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Madam, the organisational and work culture has an impact on the level of happiness of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many internationally renowned companies like Google and Virgin Group and corporations, practise employee-centric work culture that gives priority to workers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Are our workers happy when they perform their tasks?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Do they feel that their employers care or give priority to them?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Due to the absence of job satisfaction, the level of productivity and innovation cannot be improved.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is a process that will take a long time as well as a collective, comprehensive and continuous effort.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It will need the participation of all parties: the Government, employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The increase in the price of water, compounded with the increase in diesel prices, will result in increases in the cost of operations and doing business.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe that this additional cost will, in turn, be channeled towards consumers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For instance, the increase in the price of water will likely result in an increase in prices at coffee shops as well as hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The increase in the price of diesel will likely cause an increase in bus and taxi fares.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In English): Madam, I will conclude my speech in English.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Our nation's goals are to achieve: one, a caring and inclusive society; and two, an innovative and connected economy relies heavily on both components ‒ hardware, that is, technologies, and heartware, our values.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Comparing both, the latter is more crucial and requires a tremendous and continuous effort as well as commitment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Mindset and culture need to evolve and be developed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As a small country, Singapore cannot afford to ignore the progression and challenges around us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The external environment will not slow down or stop in its tracks for us while we try to keep pace or reinvent ourselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I see three key trends that are here to stay and will continue to shape the world.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To some extent, Singapore, as a country, we may have little influence on these global trends, but we must take actions to remain relevant.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We must recognise the presence of these trends, be willing to change, adapt and always prepared to ride the wave.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, the global political situations have altered significantly over the past two years.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: More of these changes are likely to follow.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There is potential shift of economies towards protectionism and mercantilism.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: All these will create new challenges to global free trade and globalisation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The key difference between today's disruptive technologies is the frequency and nature in which the disruption presents itself.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Intensive emergence of the new technologies renders less predictability in our future markets, but it is also able to bring about new economies and business opportunities for us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With digitalisation, the impact and reach of any new technology will be much larger as the market can react more responsively.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: New technologies that constantly emerge begin to dominate the market spaces within a short span of months, not years, unlike in the past.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, time is of the essence in the process of us restructuring any industry as the clock speed of economic changes has accelerated.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, structural changes within industries and how our companies operate.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: A key topic to adaptation and change is: can we be competitive?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Competitiveness has been and remains critical to all businesses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In current times, it becomes even more prevalent.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Only those with the ability to differentiate and create value out of the basic solutions that address needs and generate demand will survive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I believe a key question on many minds is: can Singapore transform and continue to create future economic opportunities and employment?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I feel that we need to be realistic and not expect there is a silver bullet that can provide this possibility.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Moving forward, I see the role of our Government shifting to one that facilitates and enables, instead of prescribing an end solution to everything.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This does not mean our Government should stop forward-thinking, planning or putting elements in place for the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Instead, with increasing dynamism of our economy, we need all the stakeholders as active contributors, be involved and play a part in shaping the requirements that we need to make things work for Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While it is widely discussed and we know that changes have to take place, but I believe we must focus on three areas to make a difference in the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It has to be reflected through our education system, the social environment and our workplace.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is not an object or a target that we create for a specified period of time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I think the reason is that we still lack innovation and value creation deeply entrenched as a culture in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If we review where this stems from, I think it begins from our education.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I definitely agree that it is important to have an adequate foundation and understanding of fundamentals in all that we learn.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But often, rigorous practice to manage examinations is not indicators that we have learnt.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Usually, the most effective results are seen in our ability to actively learn and apply the knowledge that is learnt to real-life situations and challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Being adaptive, thinking out-of-the-box, accepting different ideas and challenges are all part of a process to innovate.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We need to allow our younger generation to do so.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The challenge is: do we have the appetite to experiment and will the society accept different pathways in our education?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Our education and societal norms will eventually shape the workers in our workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The ability to continue learning and take risks reflect the will of our individuals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Without the culture, can we see the jewel in the rocks?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Take, for example, we often claim that technologies have replaced and made humans redundant or made businesses sunset industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Looking deeper, does the issue lie with a person's inability to transform with time or the emergence of improvements in the world?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the most traditional industries, like the automotive industry, it has not disappeared and continues to bring about growth opportunities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With technology evolvement, the processes involved and the product variety that is available certainly has changed our views of possibilities in traditional forms of manufacturing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Producing different car components can now be done using additive or what we call 3D manufacturing, and less of moulding, welding and casting as in the past.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The industry does not go away, but the technology involved has advanced.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Likewise, if we cannot foresee, innovate and integrate new pathways in our economy, it is unlikely for growth to be sustained or even for new jobs to be created.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The second area, develop T-skills in lifelong learning.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As the industries and economy undergo restructuring, workers who have skills mismatch due to inexperience or lack of training opportunities must now try to pick up new skills.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is not easy to learn new skills, especially when one is used to some level of comfort or in the way of how we do things.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: SkillsFuture is a good starting point for people to embrace the need to learn, but that cannot be the only reason why we are learning.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Everyone must recognise the need to continuously learn as they study and work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is the only way to remain relevant throughout our changing environment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Realistically, it is impossible for everyone to learn and shift to every new industry as a new industry emerges.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I do not think that is what we are trying to achieve with SkillsFuture.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In my opinion, every individual worker has core capabilities and basic skills.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Through our lifetime, it is critical for us to develop two sets of skills: (a) to deepen our core capabilities that further enable our expertise or develop fortes; (b) to develop broad-based skills that are transferable regardless of industry.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Only with these T-skills will we be able to add on incrementally at each stage of our career and capture the new opportunities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On the part of the Government, I would ask that moving forward, more focus be put on internships, encourage our public sector and our private companies to develop a learning culture, have more on-the-job training and for schemes to support the companies to enable job rotations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is heartening to see this Budget enhancing the Adapt and Grow initiative and providing more accessibility for training.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These resources would eventually be valuable to facilitate their staff to broaden and deepen their skills.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The term "iron rice bowl", does it still exist?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The fact of the matter is that there is no job guarantee in today's world.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Real jobs are what we make the best of it when it is available.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The Minister for Finance has called for more partnerships in the workplace and I fully support that.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is absolutely necessary for the long haul, where especially the impact it has on the generation of our older workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With time, our older workers will face different sets of challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Before the Baby Boomers become seniors, something has to be done now.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The challenges that the older workers face are: (a) preconceived mindset of our employers; (b) learning new skills over a short timeframe and adapting to the changing business landscape; and (c) accepting the new concept of productivity where less is more and being different is to value-add.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To effect any change, I feel that it has to take place at all levels, employers, employees and the Government, and in partnerships.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Employers must be open and ready to accept helping our older workers through training, refitting their job and scope, and value each worker for their abilities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Employees have to keep learning and upskilling through their career and not only when the need arises.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They must be participative and not hope to be valued due to seniority.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I hope the Government can streamline their processes and review some existing exceptions with certain flexibility and enable new rules to adapt to the new economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Apart from our culture and economy, I am encouraged that this Budget continues to look at strengthening our social safety net, in particular, persons with disabilities (PWDs).

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Mental health awareness is an area that we cannot neglect in urban cities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Dementia is one category of such mental health issues and the most common being Alzheimer's disease.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As dementia has no cure, this has long-term implications on the caregivers and our society as well.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, it is inevitable that Singapore will continue to face different challenges amidst the dynamic global landscape.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The willingness to change, adapt and be always prepared has to take place across generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We must get our younger and the future generations ready to think and act for themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On this note, Mdm Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In Singapore, water is unlike any other ordinary commodity.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We subsidise housing, healthcare, education, but not water consumption.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Even as we give targeted assistance to households, such as U-Save vouchers, to help them pay for their utilities bills, we must price water correctly.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The consumer must feel the price of water.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Consumers must realise how valuable water is to us in Singapore, every time he or she turns on the tap, right from the first drop.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We had not revised water prices for some time then.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Elements in Malaysia were threatening to block our water supply from Johor.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We were embarking on desalination to secure our water supply.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We needed to register with Singaporeans the strategic importance of water and the importance of saving every drop possible.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: If we needed any additional water, where would it come from?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: That is the cost which consumers must see.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At that time and even today, the Johor supply was fixed.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Local reservoirs had been almost fully developed, maybe except for Marina Reservoir.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Apart from conventional methods of collecting water or rainwater, the only proven technology then was to produce water through desalination.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But desalination then was very expensive, $3 to $3.50, through what we call multi-stage flash (MSF) distillation.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This number did not even include the cost of pipelines.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There was no way for the Government then to move the water price to the true cost of the next litre, the price of desalination.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: So, it moved instead in steps, over the period of 1997 to 2000, to today's water price.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Public Utilities Board (PUB) itself invested in R&D.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This resulted in NEWater, which was much cheaper than desalination.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Desalination technology has improved from MSF to membranes.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But costs have gone up gradually over the years.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At some point, a price revision became essential.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In the blend with NEWater and desalination, we have depended more on desalination for the next litre as water demand increases.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There is also a limit to recycling used water in our NEWater plants.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, to increase our water supply further, we must build more desalination plants.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Thirdly, Singapore is becoming more urbanised, so it is costing us more to build new and replacement pipes to deliver water.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Here are some figures from our recent expenditures which can give an indication of how it will be in the future.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For conveyance costs, we now tunnel below the road to lay pipelines.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This minimises inconvenience to road users and the public, but it costs two-and-a-half times as much as conventional pipe laying techniques.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: All these point to the need to update LRMC which the 30% price increase has reflected.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are unable to provide details of its computation because of commercial sensitivities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We still need to build more desalination plants and NEWater plants; and as more desalination, NEWater and water reclamation plants are yet to be built or expanded, revealing the specifics of LRMC could prejudice future bids.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But rest assured that LRMC reflects the best the market can offer.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked whether technology is taken into account in the computation of LRMC.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It has always been and is also the case for this review.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Technologically, we have squeezed everything we can from the current water processing technology.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It will take several more years to achieve the next breakthrough and bring it to a deployable scale.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I also thank Members for reminding the House that we have had a serious problem in the depletion of the Linggiu Reservoir in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is not clear whether the current situation is due to climate change, but we cannot discount the possibility of the dry weather to persist.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And in the future, when climate change effects become more pronounced, it would be more severe.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As Members are also aware, Johor is also drawing water from the Johor River, and Singapore is discussing this with Malaysia to ensure that Johor's actions do not compromise our ability to draw the 250 million gallons per day that Singapore is entitled to from the Johor River under the 1962 Water Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: What is clear is that Linggiu is operating today at a level way below what we are comfortable with and it will take years to build up to a reliable capacity again.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Taking all these together, there is, therefore, urgency to have our policies, including right pricing, in place so that we can moderate demand by both businesses and households while also building the infrastructure we need to have a secure water supply.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is the job of my Ministry and PUB to plan and build the infrastructure, which we will do.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But it is only through right pricing that we can have everyone valuing water as a strategic resource and consciously conserving it.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With the 30% increase that we have announced, the price will be close to, though slightly lower than, the price of the next drop, or LRMC, today.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is the best way to emphasise the scarcity value of water.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Members have expressed concerns over the magnitude of 30%.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clearly, this 30% increase has generated a lot of discussion on water.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I hope it also raises awareness of its scarcity, its strategic value where water is concerned.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But in reality, what does 30% translate to?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is less than a dollar a day.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, I am heartened that some businesses have taken this increase in context and have explicitly said that they would not increase prices.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For households, the Government has provided additional U-Save rebates.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: So, that is what 30% price revision translates to, $1 a day for 75% of our businesses, and still within 1% of household income for water expenses.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: (In Malay):   It is clear that people were taken aback by the 30% water price hike.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This has caused a lot of discussion on the price of water and, at the same time, the importance of water in the context of its scarcity in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, this discussion about the increase in the price of water is good because it raises people's awareness about the price and value of water to us.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But eventually, what is the real impact of the 30% increase?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Do we need to scare people about the impact of the 30% increase?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For businesses, 75% of them will be seeing an increase of less than $25 a month, which is less than $1 a day.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I called up Al-Azhar's owner, "Have the prices of beverages gone up?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Will the price of beverages go up?" He said, "It won't increase." So, if there are coffee shops that increase the price of beverages, have your drink at Al-Azhar.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For households living in 1- to 2-room flats, they would not be experiencing an increase, on average.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The rest would experience an increase of between $2 to $11 per month.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But this is still within 1% of their monthly household income.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: So, we should see this 30% increase in the right context, which is to raise the awareness of the importance of water to Singaporeans, to our country.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But we should also see the context in terms of the increase and its impact towards our daily expenditure.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: (In English): Despite our investments in desalination and NEWater plants, the truth is this: we are still a water-stressed nation.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is not a description of what we do.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is a description of who we are.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We hope that through right pricing, everyone will cultivate the habit of water saving as part of our deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), Singapore's DNA, whether we are a household or business.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Just this morning, I attended a water rationing exercise at Woodgrove Secondary School.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Many schools are participating this year to raise awareness of the value of water and the importance of water conservation among our young ones.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Even during the prolonged dry spell in 2014, we did not face serious shortages because we had NEWater and desalination plants.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But water conservation was something earlier generations of Singaporeans had imbibed.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Singaporeans back then knew that every now and then, elements in Malaysia were threatening to turn off the taps.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: So, they bore with water rationing, supported water saving campaigns and even paid the cost of cleaning up rivers and their catchment areas.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, it is because of our obsessive focus on water and the collective determination of the earlier generations and, of course, our PUB officers, that we were able to manage our vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: If we take this same approach, we will secure our water future for ourselves and our children, and that, I think Members will agree, is well worth doing.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh, do you have a clarification?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a few clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Notwithstanding the improvements that are required for the transmission networks and so forth, some clarity on that would be appreciated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question pertains to a point that the Minister made in his speech, which was about the choice of building more desalination plants.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some understanding on that will be helpful as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And to that end, two follow-up clarifications: is PUB considering a proposal which has been discussed in public before, which is to deepen local reservoirs to increase our own local catchment and the possibility of directly supplying NEWater which, I understand, some years ago was raised in this House and the then-Minister clarified that only one country − I believe it was Namibia − which transmits such water directly?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reason is it would save costs by just having NEWater supplied directly, as opposed to going through another processing exercise through the reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few more quick clarifications, and I beg your indulgence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With regard to my suggestion about a differentiated tax regime to encourage savings among Singaporeans, in addition to water rationing that the Minister mentioned, would the Government reconsider how it prices water so as to encourage people to achieve real savings by conserving water?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: On the issue of the books in PUB, I think it is very complicated for me to attempt to simplify what the numbers really mean.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our books are in accruals and our budget is in cash, and we have to reconcile them.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Because there are some parts which are Government-funded and some parts which are PUB-funded, and it does not add up, if we look at each book separately.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: On the desalination plant, why do we choose NEWater versus desalination?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Desalination, as I have mentioned just now, is more costly than NEWater.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, all these cost considerations give us a way to basically evaluate the best cost-effective model and also to spread our risks across technologies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There was a question on whether we can deepen our reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, that was the first question I asked when I joined the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Why can we not just deepen our reservoirs?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Unfortunately, the answer is not as simple as the question.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have done studies and, currently, the studies show that there is a particular yield from the reservoir if you leave it as it is, and there is a risk this yield can be reduced if you start disturbing the bottom of the reservoir.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, we do not want to do something adversely affecting our yield of the reservoir by doing something which looks intuitive.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I have asked our experts to study this further.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are still in the midst of studying this, but, right now, the prospect is not fantastic, unfortunately.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The fourth question which the Member asked is about whether we can directly send NEWater to our homes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Theoretically, we can, but we do not have to right now.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Certainly, when we need to, we will have to put the right processes to ensure this can be done, because we must ensure that it is safe for our house to drink from end to end.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There was also a question on Linggiu Reservoir.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If the Linggiu Reservoir fails and we cannot draw from the reservoir, would the water conservation tax go up because it is associated with not over-consuming water?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And, therefore, for whatever reason, the next drop of water that we need to draw will be coming from desalination as well as NEWater.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The problem is what will we do, what can we do, to prevent that from happening.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Because it is not just an issue of supply; it is a very complicated issue should that situation ever occur to us.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And to give back that cost means we are subsidising the use of water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Any way we change the structure of water that we have today either involves cost or will be counter-intuitive to trying to promote conservation of water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I think what we have today is achieving its objectives, and I am glad that everywhere I go, water is one of the things that Singaporeans are very aware of.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, during the 93.8Live discussion on water, there was a caller who was very upset because one of his colleagues was using water in the shower after work.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It was given for free for, I do not know, half an hour, or for a very long time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And he got very upset because you do not do this at home, why you do this over here?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is the right DNA for Singaporeans − even though it is free, we cannot bear to see water wasted.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And I think that is how we should move forward.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Continue to price it properly to reflect the scarcity value of water and, with that, hopefully, we achieve a DNA of always wanting to conserve the use of water.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: The Minister said that water was never subsidised.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Is it a Day 1 policy or only starting in 2000?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And also the song, "Do you remember? − Times of Your life".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But when Steve Sassoon invented the digital camera and showed it to Kodak, he was told to keep quiet about it as it would kill the company's crucial film industry, Kodak's golden egg.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is likely if you ask your grandchildren and members of Generation Y and beyond, they may never have heard of Kodak.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fuji, on the other hand, realised the world was going digital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With a long-term vision and survival instincts, it invested in digital technology; diversified into new areas; started an in-house expertise development programme; participated in joint ventures, such as Fuji-Xerox; explored and actively innovated in new areas, such as nanotechnology, placing chemicals onto films, which was even later carried into the cosmetic industry till today, and medical imaging technology and equipment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There is really no magic wand but effort, hard work and strategy, with a touch of flexibility and adaptability that is needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Discovery is really seeing what everybody else has seen and thinking what everybody else has not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As one of the smallest nations on the globe, that is how we need to be − changing, transforming, and change has to really be our only constant and it keeps us up there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This mindset must be our value and our gift from one generation to the next generation, just as this quote is from Warren Buffet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: He said: "Someone sitting in the shade of a tree today is because someone planted a tree (with a vision) a long time ago." Budget 2017 must leave us thinking about this, about our survival together, about Singapore's survival.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If one reviews our Budget the last few years, you will notice it is a continuum of change and development, through new schemes, enabling us to adapt to the new world order that is upon us all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It comes from a combination of two elements: firstly, good and in-depth sensing of the changes and the external environment which have impact on our economy, politics and foreign policies, besides other factors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And, secondly, our internal "conversations that matter", heart-to-heart, Singaporean conversations and feedback, which were weighted and considered to effect policies and schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is not just about wait and see.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is really what I would call the five "Ps" − to predict, to have projection, to plan, and then, of course, to progress together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And, finally, it is practical − the fifth "P".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It works and it is not viewed through rose-tinted glasses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It must also make us realise the hard facts and our challenges, and water is one of them, as we have just heard from the Minister, with only people as our resource.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In the words of Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, I quote: "To survive, we need to be exceptional".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our biggest threat is really our mindset and complacency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Together, as one Singapore, putting our heads and hearts together, we have the ability to create choice by deepening and altering our interpretation of the world today, as it moves along so quickly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We have to keep shining, shimmering and glowing as the Little Red Dot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thomas Friedman, in his book, Lexus and The Olive Tree, talks of two countervailing factors in globalisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The "Lexus" stands for modernisation and "The Olive Tree" represents our need for identity and belonging.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Whilst we stay open to trade, talent, ideas and inculcate deep intrinsic and global capabilities, our racial, religious values and cultural identity are just as important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We must learn to balance the two, just as the book states that Lexus has, indeed, provided a means to growing stronger and bigger olive trees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The future of our Singapore identity depends on the right mix that we choose together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   I would like to share the following scenarios.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: When I visited his home, I met him and we had a chat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Since retirement, he is usually at home by himself during the day, waiting for his eldest child to return around 8.00 pm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: When asked whether he does any other activities, Uncle A told me that one of his friends will drop by each evening around 7.00 pm and have a chat with him.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: After speaking to him for a while, I moved on to his neighbour's home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: His neighbour informed me that every evening, Uncle A will stand outside his corridor and speak to himself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We assisted Uncle A with the help of the Silver Ribbon team that collaborated with me in the Geylang Serai area.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Together, we diagnosed and brought Uncle A for counselling and treatment and he is better now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There is also a family of four who lived in an HDB flat, and when I visited them, the wife and mother of that family, who is in her 40s, sorrowfully and tearfully told me about her breast cancer, the pressures that she faces and many other things that are weighing her down.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We spoke for a long while and I did referral for her in terms of counselling, assistance and other activities, and her depression improved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The issue of mental health is becoming more noticeable and prominent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Balancing physical and mental as well as social health is very crucial in creating an individual who wants to function and mingle optimally in society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They have commenced new initiatives and ideas that they will feature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Mental illness in a multi-ethnic and plural country like Singapore is more diverse and there are different interpretations as to why someone is afflicted with mental illness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It should be handled sensitively and tactfully to avoid hurting the feelings of the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So far, this has proven to be very popular and effective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With our Budget announcement recently, I would like to share with the House some of the comments from the global mental health fraternity and leaders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Filipa Palha from Portugal, the World Federation of Mental Health Regional Vice President for Europe said, "In Portugal, we had similar promises from the government, but it never came through." Another person, Hugo Cohen from Argentina, World Federation of Mental Health Regional Vice President for Latin America, said, "Bravo!

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Good example for our own governments." Ellen R Mercer, from the US, President for Government Affairs said, "Fabulous news…an example for other countries." Robert van Voren, World Federation of Mental Health, Vice President for Constituency Development in the Netherlands, said, "Congrats, great news indeed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Wish we could have this back home." And similar comments came from people from South Africa, Taiwan, Pakistan and the Mediterranean countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   The Malay/Muslim community and organisations have organised many dialogue sessions and I find that they have benefited greatly from the schemes under our previous Budgets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They are more confident, reassured and understand our Government's strategies better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If we look around, many countries are unable to come up with this kind of Budget, especially in the midst of a dreary and gloomy economic situation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We are thankful for this vision as well as for the firm, vigilant and prudent approach in the national expenditure, where all activities, projects and enhancements are progressing as announced earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Similarly, our mindset must also change, renew and adapt in order to move with the times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If previously, we were told about this saying "Acquire knowledge everywhere we go", now we can acquire knowledge from laptops, smartphones and SkillsFuture easily from our own homes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): To end, Madam, in the Budget, let us look beyond "just asking what is in it for me".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is beyond just handouts, although there still are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is really about us together as a nation, Singaporeans and Singapore, moving together.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The aim is to identify jobs of the future and preparing and equipping our workforce in deepening their skills, improving productivity with technology and automation, embracing innovation for better business opportunities and business sustainability, and providing market opportunities for internationalisation of businesses, especially for SMEs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is understandable as SMEs employ two-thirds of the workforce today.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, with targeted budget allocation and the introduction of both existing and new schemes, how do we ensure that these SMEs create better jobs for our Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: To what extent will they succeed in improving productivity and, if so, where is the check and balance that SMEs will share the gains with the workers that thereafter translates into sustainable wage increases or profit sharing?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some SMEs or companies are barely keeping themselves afloat with the funding support provided by the Government.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Should these SMEs continue to suffer and prolong its losses, their workers will be adversely affected.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With this in mind, the Government can perhaps work with the Labour Movement to explore ways to assist these potentially affected workers leverage programmes, such as the Adapt and Grow programme, and transit into new employment before the company winds down.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Which part of the expenditure will the 2% cut come from?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As manpower is often the big ticket expenditure of any organisation, will this cut affect the workers' jobs and salaries?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is it the right time to cut the budget for all Ministries, especially for Health, while we are confronted with challenges of an ageing society; and for Home Affairs and Defence with the increasing threat of terrorism globally?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be a fee increase passed down to Singaporeans consequently?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, indeed, heartening to see several schemes made available to families to cope with the cost of living.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, Singaporeans, especially the middle-class families, will feel the brunt of these increases.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, short-term help for such families would be welcomed, especially when companies are expected to be prudent with wage increases and bonuses.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, more should be done to help these middle-income families.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some Singaporeans questioned the sudden huge increase in water price.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Should there be a gradual increase over a period instead?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can there be a systematic way or formula for increasing water price so that it is less painful for Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, the increase would mean some sellers or outlets may take advantage of the circumstances by increasing food and drink prices, amongst many others.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I would strongly urge the Consumers Association of Singapore to help keep tab on this and act swiftly to normalise such behaviour.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As for social enterprises of the Labour Movement, I believe that they will, as always, act to moderate the price increases to safeguard consumers from being exploited by those who often cite a compounded cost increase in the supply chain as an excuse.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: One other industry that would see such impact is the healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will such increase result in an increase in the cost of healthcare services to Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Because in healthcare, we use a lot of water for every step of the procedure.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the respective Ministries will not pass on the cost increases to its consumers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Also, with the increase in water price, will employers use this as a reason to reduce wage increases as well as bonus payouts?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With regard to U-Save rebates, perhaps the Government can consider having different subsidies for multi-generation flats and executive flats, instead of grouping them together and providing them with the same amount of assistance.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is because people living in multi-generation flats get the least U-Save rebates amongst other flat types when many are living as three-generation family units with elderly parents or grandparents and may require more assistance and support from the Government.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are there enhancements extended to existing CPF Housing Grant for couples buying Build-To-Order flats?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, I applaud the Government's Budget inclusion for the expansion of infant care centres.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end, there is support for both businesses and workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will touch on SMEs and their workers, as well as freelance workers and how Budget 2017 will impact them.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Organised by the unit for SMEs at NTUC, I met with SME owners from different sectors at forums and learning journeys.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Trade associations and chambers have also been identified as multipliers to lead industry-level initiatives and can support SMEs scale up and be more competitive.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, recently, the Early Childhood and Education sector announced a centralised meal catering project.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Meals for childcare centres are now prepared in a central kitchen and delivered to participating centres.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this particular instance, the Association of Early Childhood and Training Services worked in collaboration with the NTUC's e2I, Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) and Workforce Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some SMEs may be members of informal groups.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we also allow these groups to be eligible to receive the support if they have an innovative idea that can move and transform their sector?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2015, for example, the Earn and Learn Scheme was rolled out to attract more graduates to join SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The coverage of industries was fairly small with limited places.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope more sectors can be included and more vacancies generated for SMEs to attract more fresh graduates.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recently, I received feedback about the Earn and Learn Scheme for the logistics sector and the results for the polytechnic students have been more than encouraging.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, with more millennials entering the workforce, some SME employers also express the need to be better prepared to guide and communicate with them.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These young workers' perception of work and aspirations vary very differently from their older colleagues.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope SkillsFuture Singapore can provide training support to help line managers to do a better job at helping the workers assimilate into the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Equally important is to help existing staff learn to effectively communicate and work alongside these young workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We heard from many SMEs that they want to do more for training and have asked for some more support.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They hope to see more being done for targeted in-house training programmes with bite-size modules.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will cater to their shortage of time and sometimes inability to release their staff for training at a particular centre.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many SMEs which were early adopters of different Government schemes have benefited.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The next challenge is to reach out to and extend assistance to many other SMEs to help them transform their businesses, innovate and scale up so that their staff at their workplace can also benefit.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Very often, individuals opt for freelance work to pursue their own passion and interests, or simply that is how some of the industries today operate.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the rise of the gig economy, it is timely that we address challenges faced by those who choose freelance work, either on a full-time, part-time or project basis.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially relevant with some of them making it as a career choice.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some graduates I met even consider starting it as their first career, instead of going on the traditional employee/employer model.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have also heard of how traditional sectors, such as transport and services, are also impacted with the convenience of online apps and the sharing economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The way services are delivered is now transformed, with the likes of private hire services, cleaning, grocery shopping or food delivery services gaining traction.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some of these workers, they may hold the title of freelancer or self-employed in name.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, they have little control and/or bargaining power over their work.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
