text: Some even have to put on uniforms of the buyers that they serve while on duty and carry the brand on their bikes or bicycles for the services that they render.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Very often than not, the payment structure and work arrangement are heavily controlled by the service buyers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unlike employed workers, freelancers do not earn a fixed salary and are also, therefore, not entitled to various statutory protections, such as annual leave, medical leave and so on.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we gear up for the future economy, our employment practices and laws need to be robust, inclusive and cover all groups of working people and to ensure that no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can perhaps take a leaf from how the taxi industry has evolved.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Together with LTA, the taxi operator works with the National Taxi Association to start up a mediation centre back in 2014.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This allows the self-employed, such as taxi drivers, to come together to have disputes and issues resolved through mediation rather than through civil suits and other platforms.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a good move by this taxi operator with the other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The union also work with the taxi operators to facilitate training, offer hardship grant and funds to aid taxi drivers in need.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This level of support, while not very extensive and comprehensive, still shows a stark contrast to what other freelancers in the market enjoy.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We hope other sectors can at least take the first step and follow suit.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, various Government agencies work closely with freelancers in their respective industry development plans.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We hope that the Government can also take the lead and work with the freelancers and the various buyers in that community to ensure that measures can be rolled out to better protect and give support to the freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This information will be very helpful because, today, many people are drawing anecdotes and examples they hear and, therefore, we need to rely on official sets of information to guide us.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We hope that the data will help us to monitor the workforce trends, study the needs and issues faced by freelancers, and thereafter effectively put in place appropriate measures to safeguard the interests of freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope we can continue to render targeted support for SMEs and their workers as well as freelancers to help them operate and thrive in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very confident that our SMEs, our SMEs' workers and freelancers can do their part to stay resilient, adaptable and be bold to experiment with new ideas.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, I would like to focus on issues that have not been directly addressed in this Budget but which are, nonetheless, top of mind for many Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From my interactions with residents and their industry, I hear a rising concern about their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the policy level, I am confident that the Government is doing what it can to protect the welfare of our workers for the long term.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, from my discussions, the man on the street has a different perception.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The question is how do we communicate the meticulous efforts in this regard by the Government to the public?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we assure the worker that his welfare is front and centre of the Government's priority?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is a perception on the ground that the Government is not as worried as it should be, that there is a disconnect between the fear that workers are feeling and the optimistic, forward-looking messages that they are hearing.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my view, the Government needs to calibrate the message so that it is empathetic and realistic, that people can relate to, and to also serve as a rallying cry so that people can take the steps to prepare themselves for this future.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not difficult to understand why people are worried about their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Globally, 2016 was a year filled with surprises and, very often, not pleasant ones.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This has created a cloud of uncertainty over global economic growth.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There has been a marked rise in protectionist and anti-trade rhetoric, and this discussion has alarmed Singaporeans who are acutely aware that their prosperity is intricately linked to global trade and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Global uncertainty is not the only thing on their minds.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For years, we have been trying to raise productivity in Singapore companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is the critical step towards building resilience and robust businesses to try to allow businesses to thrive in tough times.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, for many workers, this can sound ominous.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They think that they will be replaced by robots or do double duty as their teams are "downsized".

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Looking ahead, technology will threaten other jobs further up the value chain, and at a much faster pace than anticipated.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Autonomous vehicles will displace drivers, and that we know.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But increasingly, trading algorithms have started to displace trading professionals, many armed with Masters and PhDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And in the future, artificial intelligence might replace human lawyers, doctors, accountants and even civil servants.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Of course, history shows us that as old jobs disappear, new ones will rise to take their place.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But this is cold comfort for each individual worker who worries about his job being replaced by robots.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is a parallel to the rise of protectionism here.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Free trade benefits the economy as a whole, but specific workers lose their jobs, as they see their wages being depressed.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To them, "the greater good" is mere words, whereas their own pain is immediate and tangible.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Given these concerns, it is not surprising that many are turning to what we now term as the gig economy, doing freelance or part-time work to supplement their income.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are even full-time part-timers who do a portfolio of different jobs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore is not there yet, but we are certainly moving in the same direction.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are some local part-time job portals like Freeboh or MyWorkSG that are gaining a lot of traction, as even more workers report their willingness to partake in the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the gig economy increases our resilience of the workforce as a whole by matching workers with new opportunities, there are some concerns.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And we hear Deputy Prime Minister Tharman saying that he is not yet a fan of the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The first is that these freelancers may not develop and grow their skills and end up doing the same role forever.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is nothing to incentivise them or there is nobody looking out for the freelancers in terms of their career progression.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The other concern that I have is that the gig economy essentially transfers the risk from company to individuals.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They also lack group medical insurance that most full-timers enjoy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The trend towards part-time and freelance work is gaining momentum.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The gig economy will allow workers to work in a variety of roles and pick up new skills.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This supplements or bolsters training or retraining like what we are trying to do in the SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But instead of the classroom, the gig economy will let them try and learn in real life.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The role of the Government here is to ensure that worker welfare is sufficiently protected in this brave new world.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As The Straits Times recently argued, we need a future-ready social safety net for the future economy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Heading in this direction will hopefully also dispel some of the cognitive dissonance that we currently perceive on the ground.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As the economy slows down and as we restructure our economy, more Singaporeans will be out of a job and be retrenched in the coming years before we can finally see light at the end of the tunnel.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I understand that MOM, the Workforce Developoment Agency (WDA) and e2i are of the view that they have tried their best to retrain and redeploy displaced workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But the perception on the ground, however, paints a different picture.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When companies move out of Singapore, it can be very challenging to retrain displaced workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When factories close down and production line managers lose their jobs, it can be very difficult for them to switch from supervising processes to supervising people.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some workers are still falling through the cracks and, despite their best efforts, they cannot find jobs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This happened to one of my volunteers, Ross.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She had a high-flying career as a Systems Applications and Products (SAP) specialist, working with Apple in Singapore and the US for about 10 years and she also worked for IBM as a managing consultant.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Her work was valued by big clients like British Petroleum, American International Group and even in the US State Department.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She returned home to Singapore in 2011 at the age of 48.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She believed that there were many jobs in Singapore available for her.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, she only managed to find a part-time contract job as a project lead security consultant with Jemena.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Her contract, unfortunately, ended in 2014 as Jemena was sold off.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But this is not due to a lack of effort.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She has spent the last three years applying for jobs without success.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the few job interviews that she was granted, she felt that she was discriminated against due to her age and race.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In an effort to keep up with change, Ross diligently used her SkillsFuture credits to attend classes and upgrade her IT skills.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She is now 54 and is still holding on to the hope to find a full-time job.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I have come across many similar, heart-wrenching stories on the ground.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We need to do more to help these people.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This committee should catch those falling through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With a holistic overview of job demand and supply, we would be able to better address the anguish, disappointment and needs of the displaced workers, so as to give them hope, help and a new lease of working life.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   In my English speech earlier, I said that Singapore is restructuring its economy and many companies are facing the issue of survival.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Amidst the economic slowdown, the number of workers who were retrenched last year had doubled, compared to 2015.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, there are still many growth sectors, such as healthcare, social services and transport.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Every year, these sectors need to hire a few thousand staff.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is even higher than the $2,500 starting monthly pay of polytechnic graduates and $2,700 starting pay of private universities' graduates.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The $3,000 gross monthly pay of a new bus captain is comparable to graduates from local public funded universities with a median starting pay of $3,400.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While a new bus captain's gross monthly pay is $3,000, the chief bus captain's gross monthly pay can be as high as $6,000.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is a perfect example of "every trade has its master".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Hence, I urge those who are retrenched to seriously consider taking up jobs in the services sectors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Next, I would like to move on to the sports scene, Mdm Speaker.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare my interest as the President of the Volleyball Association of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Every year, in the past, many NSAs have to raise hundreds of thousands to promote our respective sports.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Currently, all of us have to compete for the limited funds from Sports Singapore for the dollar-for-dollar matching grant which is capped at $40,000 per NSA on a first-come-first-serve basis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, I hope that with the new allocation of $50 million, more NSAs can benefit from the matching grant.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, having a higher quantum for the matching grant is not sufficient.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We need Sports Singapore to work with various agencies to make available more training venues for national players and amateur players alike as interest in sports grows.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Volleyball Association has groomed our indoor women's team to win a Southeast Asia (SEA) Games bronze medal in 2015 after a 32-year break.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: And last year, our combined school boys' team won a bronze medal during the Association of Southeast Asian (ASEAN) Schools' Competition for the first time in Singapore's history.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: And our beach volleyball Men's and Women's youth teams were invited to participate in the World Beach Volleyball Competition in Switzerland last year, again the first time in our history.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: During the Singapore National Games in 2014, prior to the SEA Games, the most number of teams that participated in a team-based competition was for volleyball.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This shows the growing popularity of volleyball in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Without a doubt, a lot of effort has been put in to help workers in this transition for them to be future-ready, future-proof and future-forward.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This may hamper our efforts to narrow the income gap between workers in the bottom 20th percentile and those of the median percentile.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When I talk to low-wage workers, all of them would like to have better pay, better jobs, better working conditions and hope for better job security.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the years, the Labour Movement, together with our tripartite partners, advocated and pushed for Progressive Wage Model (PWM), Best Sourcing Initiative (BSI), Inclusive Growth Programme (IGP), Workfare and National Wages Council recommendations to ensure sustainable wage growth for our low-income earners and these are some efforts that have given a hand in helping our workers to future-proof themselves through better training opportunities.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, these efforts are compromised by issues, such as cheap sourcing, wage resetting and high turnover rates.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unless we attempt to tackle these issues as well, we would take one step forward and two steps back.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The low-wage workers will find themselves at the mercy of things beyond their control.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my speech, I will be covering my proposals surrounding protection for our workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we continue to provide opportunities to train our workers for the future, it is also important that we provide protection for their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While many contracts are typically independent of Government influence, the Government itself may want to take the higher moral ground to ensure that all of its contracts are reasonable and fair, based on the principles of proportionality and best sourcing.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The outsourced sectors have long been plagued by low productivity and stagnating wages as a result of irresponsible outsourcing by businesses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Cheap sourcing and the imposition of high liquidated damages which do not commensurate with the non-delivery of specific service have resulted in the industry being caught in a vicious cycle.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Here, service providers find it challenging to embark on productivity efforts, given that their operating margins are very low.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Service buyers are on the receiving end of cheap yet less than ideal service outcomes, and workers' wages are depressed as service providers find ways to cope with the increased cost by compromising on workers' welfare.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In one of my blogs, I have shared about contracts with one-sided clauses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such contracts will impact the workers as the service providers find ways to cut corners, such as not giving workers their 13th month bonus, paying low basic salaries and, in the process, minimising any overtime payments as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some of them also deny workers their medical benefits outside the scope of the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moreover, it could also be challenging for service providers to embark on productivity efforts, given that their operating margins are very low.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Government procurement guidelines generally ensure strong financial governance.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the Government taking the lead, other companies, including Temasek-linked companies, would be encouraged to follow their example and this trend will better the lives of our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am involved in the sectoral ITM committees for the cleaning, landscape and security sectors.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A common challenge identified is the difficulty to attract local workers to join these industries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my engagement with the industry players, one of the things we can do is to improve the wages in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC, with the strong support from the Government and the industry stakeholders, made significant progress in this aspect through PWM.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: PWM is a good start to give some protection to the workers to ensure their salaries are commensurate with the workers' training, productivity and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, moving forward, if PWM is to make a real positive change in the livelihoods of our low-wage workers, we need to be bolder.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was an unprecedented move that required a lot of determination from all the stakeholders involved to see it through.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I hope the tripartite committees in the security and landscape industries would demonstrate the same tenacity to ensure the same for the security and landscape industries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also hope the Government will continue giving its strong support for the future recommendations to improve PWM.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   In the future, it is possible that many jobs will disappear due to disruptive technologies.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, the presence of driverless cars will definitely affect the livelihood of many drivers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Self-help kiosks to make payments at supermarkets and to perform check-ins at the airports will mean that fewer customer service officers will be needed.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, we have made steps towards brightening the future for the Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we cannot afford to rest on our laurels because we have to think beyond tomorrow and ensure all workers have their fair share from gains of our economic growth.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I want our outsourced and vulnerable workers in their silver years to look back and not remember their helplessness but remember how they have contributed in their own special way to the development of the nation and the efforts we have, collectively, put in to better their welfare.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I want them to remember that as they have helped Singapore, Singapore has thought about them, too.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I hope they will no longer be called vulnerable workers but regarded as workers who have played a role as we chart our growth forward.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I recall my experience last year, the first time I stood before the House to speak and about the Budget.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, for the next few minutes, before maybe we go for our break, I would make arts and culture my subject: upheavals, displacements and the art of resilience.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We are all acutely aware that we live in a complex world today.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We have been forewarned that the times ahead will be difficult.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There will be displacements to our seemingly orderly lives.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Last month, I attended a seminar organised by the Salzburg Global Seminar.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This organisation was set up 70 years ago after World War II, gathering thinkers, practitioners and policymakers to consider world issues, articulate problems and propose broad strategies to deal with these problems.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For the 2017 iteration that I went to, 40 fellows from various part of the world participated in the seminar, which was held in a beautiful palace, the Schloss Leopoldskron.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I cannot speak German, but this palace is famous because it is the location site for one of the beloved musical films, "The Sound of Music".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: During the seminar, while overlooking the idyllic lake, we shared and listened to stories and experiences that were at times harrowing, heart-breaking and deeply disturbing.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One fellow from Uganda shared that her brother was abducted by rebels, and how her family had to keep silent, despite knowing that he would become a child soldier.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Another participant shared about the unbearable lightness of existence − the result of her experience of war and bloodshed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our American friends said they feared waking up to another executive order that would bring the US closer to isolation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, within the same country, we heard about another crisis, this time from a Native American, through songs and rituals, demonstrated the solidarity of her relatives in their bid to halt the construction of the Dakota Access Pipeline at Standing Rock Indian Reservation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There were also stories about other urgent global issues, from climate change to social and income inequality.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So many issues, so many crises and so many stories of upheavals, which resulted in a huge sense of loss and displacement.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As I listened to all these sharing, I realised that back in sunny Singapore, although we are cushioned from the immediacy of these crises, we cannot deny that they will undoubtedly impact us.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For many Singaporeans, myself included, the Rohingya crisis seems far away when, in actual fact, it is really close − refugees in Johor needing help and support.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A community that is hurt and injured is a world that is not at peace.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Let us also not be complacent and imagine that such upheavals are too far away or will never happen to us.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For now, while we may not experience such gut-wrenching upheavals, we have our own issues of displacement.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In physics, displacement maps out the relative change of the position of an object, moving from one point to another.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But it does not reflect the total distance travelled and the time taken to reach there, which is just like real life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For some, it is a straight line, quick and fast.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But for others, it is a path with a lot of derailments, ups and downs, and some of them may not even reach there.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Naturally, we want the change that we experience to be good, that it brings us forward and upwards, in a straight line − in other words, positive displacement.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But most of the time, negative displacement within our society is real and undeniable.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, their lack of resources has resulted in derailment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When they are reminded to catch up or be left behind, it sounds as if the problem is that of a personal failing in their lack of trying, rather than a systemic one.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: All of us here are privileged because we have the power to effect change.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In a society that celebrates achievement and progress, no one wants to be seen as a failure.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: People who feel alienated, who feel helpless, become angry.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We see the outcomes of such unhappiness on social media, often resulting in an echo chamber effect, reinforcing collective discontentment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The frustration that stems from material, emotional and psychological insecurity creates a further polarisation of society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the immediate term, pro-business policies retain and create jobs, but it might not ensure a trickle-down effect on the economy to individuals.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But the Government's extended social safety net will help.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But with no substantial increase in income, the reliance on social support may be protracted.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Rather than hoping the safety net is wide enough to catch them, people would generally prefer to lead a self-sustainable, dignified life, earning a respectable wage that ensures their independence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The late British sociologist, Peter Townsend, once said, "It may be worth reflecting, if indeed a little sadly, that possibly the ultimate test of the quality of a free, democratic and prosperous society is to be found in the standards of freedom, democracy and prosperity enjoyed by its weakest members." I and many others believe this to be true.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And in difficult times, we must be even more attentive to those amongst us who fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And this brings me to the next point.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Every economic structural change affects individuals, family, society, politics, infrastructure, economy, environment, the tangible and intangible heritage, and the arts, in other words, the culture of our society and the city state as a whole.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We must take a proactive approach to anticipate the impact of these structural changes, rather than react to them when they arise.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To give an example: technological advancement has progressed so rapidly beyond our imaginations that we, as humans, are trying to grasp hold of the changes and manage them well without falling behind.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Studies of cultural impact of economic strategies will, therefore, put us in good stead to manage changes and their effects on society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would like now to unpack a term I have heard numerous times in the House since our Debate began, "deep skills".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But what is "deep skills" without deep thinking?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What is crucial here is a culture of creative and critical thinking.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Government can create scaffolds and support structures for innovation, but the root source of innovation lies in the people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We often talk about software or heartware, as opposed to hardware.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Software is not just about skills, but it is about human interactions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How lacking are we these days in the art of conversations?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We have reduced our exchanges to monosyllables: "Can", "Want", "K".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we settle a public disagreement in a multiracial and multi-religious society?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we manage the increasing moral panic?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we not see ourselves as helpless individuals, alienated or a powerless observer to surrounding injustice?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we see ourselves as active change agents for our society and the world?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This leads me to my next point on resilience.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To manage change and displacement, we, as a society, must become stronger.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In trying times, resilience in individuals is key in helping us to repulse fear, resist and reject the injustice and oppressive status quo.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It takes courage and conviction; it encourages objective and critical thinking.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, it enables empathy, compassion and a greater sense of hope.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I have attended a number of forums last year and there was always this call for artists to respond to these trying times.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the Salzburg Global Seminar, policymakers, thinkers, non-government organisations (NGOs) and representatives from C40 Cities and so on, made the call for arts to be the active change agent and in building resilience.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In Weimar, a conference on sharing and exchange, political scientists, economists, philosophers stressed the importance of collaboration and intercultural exchanges.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In Malta, NGOs, chief executive officers of Arts Councils around the world made the call for resilience and more arts to heal, repair and imagine.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To give an example: Mr Ong, an audience member of my community forum theatre play, once shared, and I quote, "I used to be a very impatient person.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But after watching your forum theatre play, when I get into a disagreement with my spouse, I will remember you, Heng Leun.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I remember you conducting a forum theatre play and, when a crisis happens, you will say, "Stop!

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Take a moment to think, to reflect." So, now, if I am going to quarrel with my staff, I stop.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It makes me less impatient and, of course, with that, there are fewer arguments and more discussions." For creators, the arts is a means for articulating difficulties otherwise left unvoiced and seething beneath the surface.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for instance, my friend from Uganda, Beatrice Lamwaka, who wrote stories that helped her heal from her pain and trauma of living through arduous times.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I urge you to read her award-winning work "Butterfly Dream", which can be found on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: At home, we have witnessed the lyrical poetry of our migrant workers in Singapore, who have given us an unflinching glimpse into their lives here.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He shared that when he is lonely, I quote, "the pen and paper are my friends.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, when I have the time, I try to write down my feelings." And now, I quote from his award-winning poem, "Why Migrant?": "I long to run back to the warm embrace of my homeland Among loved ones Laugh over a steaming cup of homemade tea to the sound of the impatient strumming of a guitar somewhere Wearing my blue uniform I want to lose myself Back into my childhood Like a stubborn child on a rainy monsoon day Hiding under the safety of taro leaves in the swamp." The arts offer a world of imagination and, in that, the seed of hope.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In art making, an individual encounters the power of art to heal, repair and bring hope in difficult times.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Aside from individual resilience, we need to build on community resilience.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: By that, I mean a community that comes together to listen to differences, mediate and recognise that each differing point of view deserves respect and understanding.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This resilient community will never neglect the individual voice within the sea of voices.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Again, the arts compel us to be engaged through active listening and collaboration, which are essential building blocks that inform creation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond our own communities, we must also build on inter-community resilience, so that we do not become insular and self-serving.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We live in an interconnected world and we, therefore, need to look out for others because their circumstances will have an effect on us.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To develop inter-community resilience, we must create platforms for active engagement among communities that allow for good, honest and deep dialogues.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The arts are one such platform that not only entertains but also educates.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It presents scenarios within safe spaces for the public, making us aware of narratives that are often concealed in our midst, and inspiring us to be the change we want to see in society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This means being politically motivated to gain a better distribution of wealth and success.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It cannot be achieved merely through business-oriented measures or short-term handouts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, an enlightened leadership must respect the differences that exist within our society, not tolerating, not co-existing, but embracing and celebrating diversity and plurality of views, lifestyles and people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In an era where there is increased polarisation sparked off by religion, politics and class, our leaders have ever more important roles as beacons of reason and mediation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To be resilient is to never allow communities to splinter into us versus them ideologies but, rather, to make people see that there is a "u" in "us".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If we are to become a community of hope in these difficult times, we cannot merely focus on straightforward success stories but must engage with those who feel most sidelined and marginalised, so that we can become more robust and resilient together, and never alone.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In Pig Earth, part of the trilogy written by the late John Berger, about peasants trying to survive under capitalism, there is a scene of an old peasant training a mouth organ in his mountain while he was trying to save an old cow.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And John Berger wrote, "All music is about survival, addressed to survivors." Hence, by extension, all arts are about surviving, addressed to survivors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Globally, there are uncertainties, consolidation and key developments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These are fueled by oil prices, the US' political and economic agenda, the future direction of the European Union, the Brexit journey and Asia's growth strategy, in particular, China.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The developments in each will have effects, whether direct or collateral, on economic conditions across the globe and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Locally, Budget 2017 and beyond will have to achieve a balance to address the short-term and long-term needs and challenges of the economy and our working populace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For a start, I am glad the overall Budget has a slight surplus to cater to any uncertainties and exigencies in this financial year and which may impact Singapore and for which we need to respond to.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is largely due to what I have previously mooted or identified as the three mismatches of skills, expectations and jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is also the phenomenon of, what I call, the "slow-burn" or "churn" in several sectors, fortunately not across the board yet, of our local economy, such as in the oil and gas, offshore and marine, foreign financial institutions and retail because of global uncertainties, restrategisation, consolidation, recalibration and the advent of digitisation, robotisation, mechanisation and the Internet of Things.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By the same token, we face the longer-term challenge and need of sustaining inclusive quality growth, bearing in mind we have an ageing workforce, relatively flat productivity in the past five years and a much slower employment growth in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Having heard the Budget and its initiatives fleshed out, I am glad that the Government has considered and adopted several of the key recommendations by the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, all said and done, I submit that the execution and implementation or, what I call, the "follow-through" of each of the initiatives and programmes are most crucial.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In response to Budget 2017's plans and programmes, I have five suggestions and recommendations in the area of future jobs, future skills and future training, with a particular focus on the plight of PMEs, as they are most vulnerable and sandwiched during these times of uncertainty and structural challenges.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, I am glad we are rolling out ITMs for 23 industry clusters and sectors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the course of working out the blueprint, each sector and industry has painted an optimistic future of the new jobs and the jobs growth in each sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: All these sectoral manpower plans paint an extremely optimistic picture of the jobs market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am not sure if there is duplication in the numbers as there may be overlaps, such as between ICT and the financial sector, when we talk of data science, analytics or cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To the person unemployed or retrenched, all these figures mean little to him or her if he or she cannot find a job in any of these sectors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is, therefore, imperative to paint a realistic picture of the jobs market by identifying and sharing where the jobs really are, which companies are hiring and when they are doing so.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Also, what skills and experience are required of these job openings and what training must we embark on to prepare ourselves for these future jobs?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is, therefore, vital for the tripartite partners to work together with the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), industry partners and stakeholders as well as research and consultancy companies to better sense, synthesise and provide a clear signal so as to not just place the current unemployed into current jobs but the future unemployed into future jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To this end, the Labour Movement has started looking into future jobs, skills and training and getting help and support from our extensive Labour Movement network, tripartite partners and various stakeholders and partners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, even as we drive internationalisation and encourage Singapore companies and Singaporeans to venture abroad and be regional and global, it is important that we provide sufficient support and assistance to those who have spent time on overseas stints to assimilate and find jobs back in Singapore when they return.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: My biggest worry is how these Singaporeans who have gone abroad are able to adjust and adapt when they return back to Singapore in the future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I say this because I have met PMEs at our NTUC's U PME Centre, including classmates of mine, who have returned to Singapore after spending some eight to 16 years abroad.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Many have returned due to family commitments, such as because of elderly parents or children's education, or to really come back home.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: One such example is a PME in his 50s who has been working for a European MNC in the oil and gas sector for 20 years in the area of project management.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: He was retrenched and was out of job for a year before finally landing a job as a project manager now based in Saudi Arabia.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I know some who have been back for more than a year and still have not found any job despite lowering their salary expectations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some have resorted to doing freelance work or short-term contract positions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is an area we need to pay particular attention to, and I hope the enhancements to Adapt and Grow and the many SkillsFuture initiatives to be announced will address this problem.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, all the talk on digitisation, the digital divide and disruption is good but what does it mean to the layman or worker?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What does he need to do to stay ready, relevant and resilient?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I, therefore, suggest we come up with a digital disruption awareness or development programme for all workers, all Singaporeans, very much similar to the Basic Education for Skills Training (BEST) and Worker Improvement through Secondary Education (WISE) programmes we had in the 1980s and 1990s where we had to bring all Singaporeans and workers ahead in terms of literacy and numeracy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The future jobs in demand and future skills in demand components can be built into this programme to ensure all Singaporeans stay able, adaptable and agile.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This programme can be spearheaded by the Labour Movement's e2i and NTUC Learning Hub and supported via Government funding.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, the SkillsFuture Credit utilisation has been promising and off to a good start.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have met workers who have shared how they have benefited immensely from picking up new skills via tapping on their SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the rapidly volatile business environment and job obsolescence, workers globally are now concerned that their skills are losing relevance or what I call the "Fear of Skills Erosion".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The credits can go a long way for not just skills acquisition but should also include engaging professional career coach services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Lastly, the Budget has announced proposed enhancements to Adapt and Grow funding, including the "Attach and Learn" programme which I welcome and look forward to hearing more during the MOM Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, I hope as we execute the various fundings, we must bear in mind the need to be flexible, responsive in terms of speed to market and also cater to all segments of the workforce, from low-wage workers to PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am glad that PCP now supports redeployment of PMEs within the company.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, one particular observation I have with PCP is that when PMEs move into a new sector or totally new job, he or she enters at the entry point of that new sector or job.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I find this sometimes unsatisfactory, considering many mature PMEs have accumulated one to as many as three decades of work experience and that their other innate skills are not taken cognisance of.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At our U PME Centre, we observed many PMEs would prefer to stay within their industries where possible or, at the most, move across into any industry by utilising their sets of skills and experience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The public sector has successfully done this for certain job types and I suggest we replicate this to other sectors and companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   With regard to measures introduced in Budget 2017, the key lies in implementation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, our foremost task is to identify where opportunities are, which companies are hiring and what skills, experiences and training are required by these jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, even as we drive internationalisation and encourage companies and workers to venture overseas and gain overseas experience, it is equally important that we provide sufficient support and assistance to those who come back to Singapore to assimilate back into our workforce and find jobs as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, I suggest that we come up with a digital technology development programme to help Singaporeans to improve their skills in the area of digital technology.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This programme will be similar to the BEST and WISE training courses offered in the 1980s and 1990s.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In addition, the usage of the credit should also be expanded to include engaging professional career coaching services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The only difference is the speed at which the treadmill is now moving, compared to previous years.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.22 pm until 4.45 pm.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While a few have expressed concerns with our Budget status, most were concerned with our individual status.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Common questions and comments heard were these: how much do I get?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How much more do I have to pay?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Why the price increase for carbon, diesel or water?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For businesses, their reactions have also been largely similar: how much would I get?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Even amongst some civil servants, they were surprised, "Wow, you mean my Ministry's budget is going to be rebased, which means a cut of 2%?" But what are the core issues for this Budget?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While we can all appreciate the concerns with our individual positions, this Budget must surely be more than these.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our Budget is also, if not more importantly, about our collective future and that of our country, beyond what it means to us individually.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And the core questions that we have to come back to and focus on in this Budget are as follows: how do we earn a living for ourselves and our country?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And how do we take care of one another?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These are the two core issues that we must return to: how do we earn a living for ourselves and for our country, and how do we take care of one another?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many have asked and commented: if the Budget can be a bit more generous; if our Government can spend a bit more.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are, if you like, living on the income of our savings: $1 out of every $5 that we are spending in this Budget comes from the income from our Reserves.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I do not know if Members have also noticed something that is even more significant.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I have been observing this for the last few years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This was not the position a few years ago.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: NII has become the revenue stream that gives us the most to do for our Budget.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And if we think a bit deeper, these top four buckets of revenue stream ‒ NII, corporate tax, GST and income tax ‒ out of these four, how many of them are really under our control?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: NII depends on the status of the world economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Corporate tax and income tax will be similarly cyclical, according to the world economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Even GST, to a lesser extent, will be cyclical.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, the question that we should all pause and think for a while is this: is this a sustainable position, going forward, for our country?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The top four revenue streams of our Budget, of which three are not entirely within our control, even if we do not take into account the competition that we have to face from other cities like Hongkong in how we set our corporate and income tax rates.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I always joke with some friends that our corporate tax rate and income tax rate are not set independently by the Minister for Finance.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Minister for Finance has to watch like a hawk what our competitors are doing.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, this is the context that we are in ‒ $1 in every $5 that we spend today comes from our NII ‒ the four biggest buckets of our revenue stream, three of which are not entirely within our control.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some have commented that we are running a surplus.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The question is this: will we realise this $2 billion surplus?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I hope Mr Leon Perera is right.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will be very happy if we are right and you are right.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: What if the economy turns soft and we do not realise the full amount that we have budgeted for NII but, instead, we need more money to help fellow Singaporeans if the economy turns further south?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How much can we afford and how much more do we have?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, if the revenue comes down and the needs go up, I am not so confident that that $1.9 billion surplus that we have budgeted for will necessarily come true.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But like I said, I hope we are right, I hope you are right.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are some comments by some Members in the House to say that this Budget is a political Budget, that we spend less so that we can time the political cycle.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our system is designed such that every term of Government has to earn its keep.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: At the start of every term of Government, People's Action Party or otherwise, the Government must earn its keep.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We precisely design the system such that no Government will come in and promise to spend before it has earned its keep.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is the reason why we have been able to get $1 out of every $5 to support our Budget.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If our forefathers had done otherwise ‒ to spend first before the term of Government even earned its keep ‒ we can forget about that $1 out of every $5 that we are depending on for our Budget now.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we would rather err on the side of caution, and this is the reason why our forefathers had put in place this system, and this is the reason why this generation will also continue to uphold this system.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Then, there are suggestions that we are ignoring the pains, the short-term pains of the economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If this is so, why did Minister Heng Swee Keat announce targeted measures to help specific sectors like the offshore and marine sector, like the $700 million that we push into the construction sector?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we adopt such a cynical attitude to budgeting, will we have done this?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Just as one of my friends' feedback last night, if, indeed, this is a cynical Government, then we should not be giving anything at all.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Managing an economy is not like turning the thermostat in the air-conditioned room, that when you want it to go up, you just turn it down; when you want it to go down, you just turn it up.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If this Government is not concerned with the short term, and if the economy goes down south, who can guarantee that in two years' time, when we want to turn it up, that it will go up?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We do not have to look too far.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some countries lose their footing, get into a downward spiral ‒ a death spiral, if you like ‒ and never recovered.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our job is to keep ourselves on a steady path, making sure that we address the short-term pains whilst establishing the conditions for our long-term success.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is never either/or; it is always both.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Because if you have managed an economy before, you will know that no one can take a cynical attitude towards whether you can time it to go up or down.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, I would like you all to focus on what this Budget has in terms of what is new.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I would like to remind all of us that it is not just what is new that is important.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some of the tails do not just wind down.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, it is not a small feat for a government, any government of any particular point in time, to make a commitment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While Minister Heng Swee Keat has announced various things that have changed, we must all bear in mind that many things are still ongoing: Workfare, U-Save rebates, the commitment that we have done for SkillsFuture, and so forth.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, it is not just the new things that are important.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is also what has been going on and will continue to go on that define this Budget.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I hope we see that in proper context.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Jobs for those people who are displaced today, and jobs for those people who might be displaced tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Grants and subsidies alone will not create jobs, especially sustainable jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Grants and subsidies, as Minister Iswaran said yesterday, enable and help, but the crux must come from our businesses, our access to markets and our innovation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How good our businesses are depend on the following: how innovative we are; how bold we dare to venture beyond Singapore; how good our workers are to keep pace with the demand for the new skills; how good our regulatory environment is to groom and enable new businesses.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When we look at our Budget, this is what we see.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: MTI, MOM, the Ministry of Education (MOE) and many other agencies are all focused precisely on all these four basic fundamental issues to support our businesses: enable innovation, enable internationalisation, enable SkillsFuture and enable a more progressive regulatory environment for startup businesses.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, the businesses are not alone in this.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And this is where it leads me to CFE.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I found this to be a simple way to remember the seven CFE strategies or, as Minister Heng Swee Keat called them, the seven mutually reinforcing strategies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The two sails are our engines to propel the boat forward.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One of them is SkillsFuture − how good our workers can be.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But SkillsFuture cannot be alone, we need the equivalent on the business side − the EnterpriseFuture as the other sail.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: NTUC, as the apex organisation, will mobilise our workers, work with IHLs, MOM, MOE to make sure that we train up a new generation of workers ready for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I hope that the Singapore Business Federation and the other trade associations will similarly perform the role for businesses, so that not only will we have a SkillsFuture programme, we will couple that with an EnterpriseFuture programme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The three skiffs that make up the trimaran are essentially our three core strategies to make ourselves a more balanced, a more diversified economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The first, how to use our advantage in urban planning and city development as a marketable strategy to sell skillsets and relevant expertise to the rest of the world?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we use internationalisation to broaden our markets to transcend our geography and finite resource limitations?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The challenge is not who comes up with a better plan.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The challenge is who can execute the plan well, who can execute the plan faster, and who can adapt when conditions change.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will get there better than anyone else.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How fast we sail, how good we are able to ride the waves depends on our teamwork, depends on how well we can read the waves of change over and beyond how well the boat is designed, or how well the plan is.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: NTUC will not come to this Budget and ask MOM for more money per se.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MOM, MOE and MOF have been very supportive.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Over and beyond money, what the Labour Movement wants to work with our IHLs and our businesses on are as follows.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, we want to strengthen the job placement system for everyone.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to challenge ourselves, that among NTUC, WSG, the Economic Development Board and all other Government agencies, including our partners in the Singapore National Employers Federation, to form that national database at the backend.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It does not matter which career centre you go to, we will integrate the backend.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are even prepared to work with private agencies like LinkedIn to ensure that we do our placement well and do it faster.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But placement is only for today's job, putting today's employed into today's job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We need to do much better and we can do much better.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have always never been entirely satisfied with our speed-to-market for generating new modules that are relevant to industry needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is a call for the Labour Movement to work closely with the Government agencies and the businesses to come together.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we are not satisfied with the speed-to-market, we work on it, improve and fix it because, at the end of the day, it affects the livelihoods of our workers not just today, but tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we are not going to talk about theories.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Many of the Labour Members have spoken about protection.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are new forms of employment − freelancers, contract workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Labour Movement will fully support the MOM initiative to review our system to make sure that all working people, regardless of workers, freelancers or contractors can have peace of mind for today and tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I visit one to two companies every week.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is no magic bullet to raise productivity just by macro-policy measures.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are the amalgamation of the efforts of the Government, businesses and the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we do not get this right, there will be no productivity gains and no sustainable wage increases for our workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we have to work hard on this, and the Labour Movement will do it with our partners in MOM and the Government agencies and our business partners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Next, let me touch on the kind of society that we aspire to be.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think it is all very good and I am very proud that all Members in this House always mention these two words when it comes to the kind of society we want to be: inclusive and mobile.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to be inclusive to take care of one another, regardless of our starting position in life.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to give everybody a fair chance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want social mobility and that is what defines Singapore, that regardless of ancestry, connections, race, language and religion, we can all succeed, so long as we put in the effort and we have the necessary talent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But every time when we talk about the difficult issue of tax increase or, for the matter, even taxes, we hear a lot of calls from many Members asking: can you give a bit more to some sectors of society?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On one hand, I am very proud that the Members of this House are representing residents in your community and speaking up for them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But on the other hand, we must also all have a care, because remember what we talk about in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we are all politicians, we will all speak up for those who need more.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But if we are political leaders, then we have to face the issues squarely, that in every society, how do we distribute the finite resources that we have?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we make that statement that we, as a society, will lean forward to help those who need a bit more help − the weak, the vulnerable and the poor?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That we do not need to be apologetic.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It takes political leadership to tell our people that we all aspire to a higher goal, beyond "what is in it for me?" Or we can compare this to other countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is no shortage of examples near and far.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When prices go up, or when prices need to go up, everybody pretends that we will subsidise everybody equally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We do not have to look too far.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Where has that gotten some of these countries?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The rich got more subsidies than the poor.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Is that the kind of society that we want?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We say that we let the prices float up to the market price.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I can understand there will always be a quarrel as to who needs it more.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But at least, let us get the principle right, and let us carry the ground.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There will always be somebody who is more in need than us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we can do our part for them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But it is not just about workers, it is not just about businesses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government must do our part as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And this is where the Ministries come in.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Ministries must also lead the way, tighten our belts, make sure that we get the bang for our buck, that we are stewards of the resources given to us, that it is the job of the Government and every civil servant to make sure that every dollar spent on anything achieves the goals that we set and it helps us to bring about a fairer society.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Take it positively, I would encourage all the civil servants.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The best ideas do not always come with resource abundance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In my short little time of 20-over years in the Government, some of the best ideas paradoxically came during times of constraints.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is how we apply our minds to it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having more resources must not lead us to a crutch mentality whereby we throw resources to solve a problem.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have to challenge ourselves constantly to do better.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We say, "Avoid a sedimentation model", and I must attribute this to my comrade Mr Heng Chee How.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First thing comes in, it gets the first bite of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When you do it once, it is an event.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When you do it twice, it is a series.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When you do it three times, it is a tradition, and thou shall not violate thy tradition.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But is that the correct way to do things?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have to look at it afresh every year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What are the most important things that need to be done?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we get it done, even if it needs to be done and done better?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have to ask ourselves, as a Government, how do we challenge ourselves to not ossify?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That every time when a problem happens, we do not have a knee-jerk reaction to clamour for more rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because every rule that we add has a cost − to business, enforcement and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We need to take the approach that everything that we do, we are inevitably managing risk.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is no way to have anything with zero risk.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And if we adopt a mindset like that, we will critically challenge ourselves where we can make not more or less rules, as Lawrence would say, but make smarter rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Smarter rules that lead to better outcomes but not necessarily increasing the enforcement cost.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is a challenge for our Civil Service.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I have touched on businesses, individuals and the Government.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I can understand and appreciate the angst that we all feel if it would feed through and, if so, how would it feed through to the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have heard truths, half-truths and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will be too much for me or the Government to expect everyone to defend the price increase.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will be too much for us to expect that we will speak up for the price increase.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I think we have to get certain basic things right and do what is honourable, regardless of which side of the House we are on.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have to start from this basic premise.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Do we agree that water is existential to our country's survival?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the answer is yes, then we can go on to the next one.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second question: do we agree that we should price water properly?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we agree on these two questions, we can go on to the mechanics of how to price it properly, what should we consider and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It has been so yesterday, it is so today, and it will be so tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For the entire generation who have worn the uniform, you know what this means, including all Members in this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Pritam Singh used to serve with me in the same unit, a classified unit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That has not changed, and that will not change.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Yes, our tremendous efforts over the years have improved our situation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we are nowhere near where we want to be.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We spare no efforts to manage the risk all these years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When I was in primary school and I first looked at the map of Singapore, I was taught to remember the three reservoirs in Singapore: MacRitchie, Seletar, Peirce.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I wonder how many Members in the House today will know how many reservoirs we have today, and how many more of us will be able to name all the reservoirs in Singapore today, without Googling.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How many desalination plants do we have today?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How many NEWater plants do we have today?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How many more desalination plants and how many more NEWater plants we must build in order for water to never be a weapon pointing at our head?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
