text: I dare say no other country has planned it such.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Two-thirds of our entire land area are water catchment areas.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have dammed up every river in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is no river that flows into the sea anymore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The prices for desalination is coming down, but guess what?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our dependence on the higher cost water − NEWater and desalination − is going up.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, yes, technology has helped us and we will be in an even worse position if not for technological progress.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But our demand has gone up the other side.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If in the 1990s our forefathers did not invest in the Linggui Dam, I do not even know where we will be today.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, to expand our water supply, we only have two sources more.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Going forward, we only have two ways to go.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, to depend more on technology, be it desalination, NEWater or any other new technology.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Two, to work with the Johor authorities, the Malaysian authorities, to see whether we can have a win-win solution, because the water needs in Johor are also increasing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some Members might have read that they are extracting water upstream from Linggui Reservoir.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That affects our yield, but we want to and are committed to working with the Malaysian government and the Johor government, the Johor authorities, to see how we can develop the water system for both the benefit of Malaysia and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We spent a lot of money, that Minister Masagos did not say, to make sure that we do not waste any drop of water.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some countries lose up to 5% to 10% of their water supply through leaky pipes.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Minister, if I can just interrupt for a while to ask the Leader to move a Motion to let you speak beyond 40 minutes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This Debate over the last two days has also shown the following, and I agree with the Members of the House: we need to do much more.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We need to do much more to socialise our people to the challenges that we are facing on the water front.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The fact that we have such an intense discussion reflects that we have left this issue off our national psyche for too long.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can do this every year, we can do this every five years, we can do this every 10 years, but regardless which way we choose, we have to make sure that we never forget that water is existential.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In 2012, one year after I entered politics, I returned to the Singapore Armed Forces and talked to some officers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I asked them this question: what was the most significant thing that happened in 2011?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The most obvious choice was the People's Action Party's performance in the 2011 General Elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then, some added, the Presidential Election of 2011.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And some clever ones said, it was the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) breakdown, and there were even some who said that it was the ponding in Orchard Road.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I was disappointed and I let these officers who were with me know that I was disappointed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It was on the front page of The Straits Times, but it was not the headline.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is my hope, this is my challenge, and this is our work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is never easy to talk about price increases.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A responsible government is one that not only takes care of the short-term needs of our people but also the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A responsible government is not one that will raise the price and not take especially greater care of the poor.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A responsible government is not one that pretends that we will make difficult decisions but no one will have to bear the greater part of the responsibility to help those with less.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If this is a political Budget, we do not have to talk about any of these topics.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I submit to the House that this is a government that has the heart of its people at its core.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We know the pressures in the short term.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are doing what we can in a targeted manner.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But more importantly, we know the long-term challenges facing our country and we will do what is right, what is necessary, to leave behind a better state for our future generations to build on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Once again, Finance Minister Heng has delivered a Budget that is squarely aimed at the future.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I commend him for his far-sighted approach and the courage to take measures that might be unpopular.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In this speech, I will first speak about innovation in the Government and industry and then touch on the impact on families.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify what will be the implication of this?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Government ensure this makes it more effective?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will this affect the budget for hiring and retaining civil servants and, thus, the quality of the Civil Service?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think the Civil Service in Singapore is generally corruption-free and competent and much better than many other countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But there is room for improvement in some areas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some civil servants focus more on the rules of their own agency, instead of looking at what outcome will benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I recently visited a newly completed Build-To-Order (BTO) development, Khatib Court, which is beside Khatib MRT.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is a beautiful development, but it has one very strange feature.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It has a covered linkway that is hanging and not completed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It comes from Khatib Court, and here is the MRT station, and there is a gap of 10 metres.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I asked the Housing and Development Board (HDB) what happened.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are you training my residents to be 10-metre sprinters, especially during rainy days?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Then, they shared with me that it is because they faced a lot of challenges and the requirements from the Land Transport Authority which they said they cannot meet.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I called a meeting, both sat together, and I told both parties, "Regardless of what happens, I must have this covered linkway." Everyone forgot about the hassle-free first-mile and last-mile connectivity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I can give you another example, another one of my new BTO developments, Palm Breeze.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As usual, I asked HDB to construct a covered linkway from the nearest block to the nearest bus stop.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: HDB agreed and the consultants submitted the plans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Part of the covered linkway sits on top of a drain.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: No structure is supposed to be on top of my drain.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Shift your footpath out into the grass verge." And you know grass verge belongs to who, right?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: NParks said, "Nothing is supposedly to sit on my grass verge." So, I do not know what innovation solutions that PUB and NParks can think of.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Today, Palm Breeze residents have collected their keys, are shifting in, and the plans are still not approved.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Maybe I should seek our Coordinating Minister's help.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These are only small projects and we meet so many obstacles.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In bigger policy decisions, I am sure there are even bigger roadblocks.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can our civil servants not be more result-oriented and objective-driven instead of just guarding their own turf?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I note that some of the funds cut from agencies will be diverted to cross-agency projects.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope this will improve cross-agency cooperation and reduce such problems, instead of creating yet another layer of bureaucracy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope some of the funds will be used to examine innovation in the Government and in shoring up our ability to give innovative solutions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are many ways the Government can be more innovative, and I will suggest some below, especially with regard to the construction industry and the environment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The construction industry has been facing lots of pressures from the economic slowdown and Government requirements.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have heard that some smaller companies could not pay their staff on time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: More generally, while there are many efforts to assist small and medium enterprises (SMEs), I hope our Government can support the construction sector more to adopt more efficient work methods, so that they can raise their productivity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is there anyone in the Government to focus on such efforts, instead of only implementing rules?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Architects do the beam modelling just enough for submission.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Later on, contractors come aboard, they do their own beam model again because they cannot use what the architects have produced.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to speak on sports.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As the past President of the Singapore Table Tennis Association and Adviser for Singapore Swimming Association (SSA), I have witnessed how challenging it can be, from administration to the pressure of ensuring that our athletes perform at the highest level.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But I have to ask this very pertinent question.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are our national sports associations (NSAs) given enough support for the retention of staff?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The work which is done by the secretariat can be challenging and, what is worse, there is a lot of administrative processes which need to be completed before funding is released − all for good reasons.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, are our NSAs' secretariat staff being remunerated well enough at least up to market rate?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How will any, if at all, funding cuts affect the secretariat staff?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, are our NSAs getting enough support from the Singapore Sports Institute on sports science, nutritionists, biomechanics and so on?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But this sports science support system must be almost around the clock, 24/7, including weekends, because the swimmers are trained and also taking part in competitions during weekends.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Joseph Schooling's gold medal at the Rio Olympics has only further proven how sports is an important component for nation-building.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should try to find more ways to support our athletes and NSAs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This Budget introduced some bold moves to change habits, like the water price increase, carbon tax and diesel tax.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But there are more ways we can be more sustainable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One, I urge the Government to invest more in infrastructure for green energy, such as the use of natural gas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Two, we need to do more to promote reduction of consumption, that is use less, reduce waste and more recycling, that is, reduce, reuse, recycle.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to push the awareness of what will contaminate recyclables, so that nearly half of the recyclables collected do not have to be thrown away.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Every time I pass by the blue bin, I will peep into the blue bin.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I do not think our blue bins in our housing estates work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Besides the recycling bins, how can we make it easier for everyone to recycle?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: More recycling bins in public next to trash cans, perhaps?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources to think deeper about this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Three, in Singapore, electric cars are still expensive, around three times as expensive as regular cars.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What can we do to provide incentives to car buyers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some states also allow electric vehicles and vehicles carrying two or more people to use special lanes, to beat the jam.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: All these encourage consumption and production of electric vehicles.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Four, ensure that foreign cars coming into Singapore are subject to the same emission standards as local cars, if they want to drive on our roads.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our companies are competing in the global markets.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Malaysia, China and Taiwan, for example, the price of water is negligible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we increase it to 70%, like in Germany and Taiwan?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be any tax rebates or grants for the cost of adopting water recycling?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Speaking of water, let me briefly speak in Malay.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Malay):   Earlier, Minister Masagos explained why the price of water was raised.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But can the Minister provide an explanation, recently, in spite of the rainy season, if the reservoir in Johor can only reach one-third of its capacity, can we get a supply of water without any disruption when the dry season comes?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What steps will PUB take to help residents save water and reduce their bills?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These could be delivery operators in connection with the diesel tax, or food stall operators in connection with the water price hike.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The increase in their sale prices should not exceed the increase in cost.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Please allow me to summarise my speech in Mandarin.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   There are many bold measures in Budget 2017 which focus on Singapore's future.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, I hope that the Government can see how these measures will impact families and companies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is rainy season recently but the reservoir in Johor is only one-third full.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will we have enough water during the dry season?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How do we help our families to save water and reduce water cost?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government should also keep a close watch on businesses to make sure that they will not pass on the increase to consumers or even take the opportunity to raise prices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For the manufacturing industry, the water price increase, carbon tax and diesel tax will all lead to cost pressures.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To keep our manufacturing industry competitive, how can the Government incentivise them to save and recycle water?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government bring forward more projects and help the construction industry to adopt more efficient work processes?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, will the reduction in the budget for various Government agencies affect the services provided to Singaporeans?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is undeniable that a small number of civil servants insist on sticking to their agency's rules, making simple things complicated.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government has been rolling out incentives to support innovation and get businesses to increase productivity to counter cost increases.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, as innovation and the adoption of new technologies to increase productivity take time, the progress has been slow.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One main reason could be that businesses, while raising productivity, have to continue to provide jobs for our citizens.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the domestically oriented sectors which hire more workers than export-oriented sectors, productivity growth is understandably marginal.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The capital required for automation and productivity projects can be substantial, and Government grants and subsidies only offset a portion of these costs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While still coping with rising costs, in particular, labour costs, the impending increase in utilities cost due to the increase in water prices and the proposed carbon tax would be additional financial burdens.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The profit margins on these projects will be lower and companies that cannot reinvent themselves or keep up with productivity may find it difficult to stay afloat.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under such circumstances, would Singapore continue to be an attractive place for international companies to do business in?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will the Government continue to support SMEs to overcome these multiple challenges?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Any increase in cost of utilities, such as water, gas and electricity, has significant impacts on the economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It may be that water accounts for a small share of overall business costs and consumer expenses.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A small SME may not be a large consumer of water.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That would not stop their suppliers from raising the cost of supplies as a result of the water price increase.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Neither would it prevent the management corporation of the SMEs' office building from raising their maintenance fees.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The staff of the SMEs may need higher salaries to pay more to their respective Town Councils, children's service providers, and grocers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Eventually, the SMEs would have little choice but to pass on these added costs to end consumers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We do not question the need to increase water prices.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are very good bases to justify the increase.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is usual for price increases to coincide with the revenue recovery cycle of the economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Businesses are experiencing slow to negative revenue growth.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the drive to push productivity in a tight labour market, every added burden to business costs could hurt the viability of the business.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For individuals, Government credits and rebates lessen the direct impact of the water price increase to the households.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The indirect knock-on effects mentioned earlier are of bigger concern.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We expect hawkers to up their food prices.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What we are unsure of is the quantum of the increase.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While coffee merchants had said that the higher water costs would not affect the coffee prices, the hawkers themselves may be faced with more expensive supplies and higher cleaning fees, and they, in turn, have to pass on these costs to the consumers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government would have conducted an extensive study into the impact of the water price increase on all the economic and social sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Government consider releasing the details to the public so as to prepare them for all the likely consequences and scenarios?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government should also further reassure the public that they have mechanisms in place to prevent profiteering by businesses on the back of this increase.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Mandarin):   The increase in water price can be complemented by a push to change consumer habits in water usage.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this regard and to further assist the families, could the Government consider giving incentives or introducing a lower tier tariff for households that consume less water either on a household or on a per capita basis?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since water consumption depends on family size and not flat type, it might be more effective for rebates to be given based on the number of persons residing in the household.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A larger household would need more support from the Government than a smaller household staying in a similar flat type.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Let me now touch on boosting demand for our economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I applaud the strategies to bring forward or increase infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These projects will also create demand for services and products downstream − contractors, engineers, designers, information technology providers and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From locally produced fish and vegetables when catering for meals at events to engaging the services of a Singaporean infocomm technology company, as long as the specifications are met and fees are reasonable, we should support Singapore suppliers and vendors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure that some level of support is already occurring in our Government departments but a higher level of awareness and a stronger official mandate will go a long way to boost demand.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such a campaign will also send a signal to the market and individual consumers: if we do not support our own, who will?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Supporting our local companies and encouraging them to keep improving is the only way to help them grow big enough to spread their wings beyond our shores to increase their revenue sources which shall help mitigate the ever-increasing costs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should also ask ourselves if there are local industries that may potentially have an advantage in serving the domestic market that can be encouraged, supported or better funded to help them to grow.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is an important question which merits further and urgent study.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will incentivise our local companies to strive for higher quality.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These measures will no doubt increase Singaporeans' awareness of the importance of environmental sustainability.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, many customers now actively look for products that are not detrimental to the environment, with a lower carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, we can have more locally farmed produce, fashion or household items using materials that are preferably locally sourced.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not all companies will eventually grow into large multinational industries but they can play a part in fulfilling our collective environmental agenda.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Teachers of preschoolers use the "Preschool 3R Awareness Kit"; older children have the "Youth for the Environment Day" platform to showcase environmental activities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a father, I noticed that even composition and essay topics from primary school up to junior college use environmental issues as a recurring theme.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the Government and people work together to ensure environmentally sustainable practices, we will lay the foundation for an even more beautiful and liveable home for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With this, I conclude my support for the Budget.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In some quarters, it is viewed as underwhelming.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And there are some of us who question the timeliness of the imposition of tariffs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There are, of course, others who support the Budget and the Debate will just go on and on, even after the Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But to me, this is a Budget of hope because it is a Budget that tells us that despite the challenges and difficulties that have caused many a good man to stay awake and to worry, that this is an opportunity for us to move ahead for many years to come.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: With that, it also brings a caution that it requires us to understand what these challenges are, what the difficulties are, what they will morph into and what new ones will appear on the horizon, and how we may convert them into our strengths.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, we cannot live like we used to live.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Without discarding all that we have learnt and built in our individual and collective memories and achievements, we must, nonetheless, recognise that our success yesterday and today could be our failure tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, we must be prepared to say that something that has worked before may need to be changed before it is too late.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There is a saying, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In times like this, I think we do not have the luxury of waiting for some things to break.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But of course, unfortunately, something has already broken and this is something that bothers and troubles me a lot.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We hear a lot about the disconnect between the Government and the people.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And I have spoken with businesses, friends and associates and they complain about difficult times and I asked them, "Why not try and seek the Government grants?" They say, "It is no use.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They do not understand." And I wonder why.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Because if there is truly a disconnect, then whatever we are going to implement in our Budget is not really going to achieve what we want to achieve, because we are not going to be "one".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are not going to have that unity of vision and the unity of mind and the singleness of heart to move forward.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I hear so much and I am concerned.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that there are structural shifts that have caused unemployment and redundancies.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But I wonder, as some people have asked me, whether some redundancies could have been caused because the Government overlooked certain trends and certain sectors.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Was it because there were emerging sectors or fledging sectors that we did not, despite industries' feedback, nurture and grow?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know, I do not have the answers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But I hope it is something that we can look into to address this disconnect that we now perceive on the ground.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned because if we do not address the "disconnect", if we do not come across to our people as being willing to re-examine where we may have fallen short, that is very difficult to inspire confidence during difficult times.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And now, I come back to the main point of this message which I am sharing today.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have nothing to share, nothing to define the mindset with.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: All I know is that there is a fear that, over the years, the universal values of compassion, empathy, of the ethos of hard work, of caring for one another, of the duty to country, community, family, self, and the respect for one another may have eroded.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We may need the change in mindset in each individual citizen for us to come back to where we should be.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: To know that we owe a duty to ourselves and to our country for the Budget to work.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But we also need a change in the mindset of the Public Service and of the corporates.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I say this with some consideration, not that I do not believe in the quality of the Public Service, but rather that I think, someone has to say some hard things.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am very heartened that the Budget continues to talk about developing capabilities and employability of Singaporean workers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And I say the Government, employers and Singaporean workers must believe in that.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: You say, "Is it not odd?" The Government is the one that says we must develop the capabilities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And why do I say the Government must believe in that?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is because of that "disconnect" that I talked about earlier.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But I think that if people believe in what the Government wants, then the way they design their schemes will be very different.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But it will be with that knowledge and that consciousness that every decision we make in matching and in granting a grant to an organisation, we are making a difference to our country and to our companies.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And I want to talk about developing the capabilities and employability of Singaporean workers because I believe in it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And quite frequently, when I talked about the Singaporean Core, well-meaning people would remind me, "Be careful, you could be misunderstood as xenophobic or protectionist".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Let it be clear − I am neither.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But the Singaporean Core will remain connected to Singapore and we need to develop the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Just through schemes and measures, if the employers are not committed?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I want to say that we must not be embarrassed to tell investors that we would like them to invest in Singaporean workers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is because we also need to build our own industry movers and shakers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should not be happy with big companies setting up facilities here only to build foot soldiers for us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We want them here because we want to develop our own people, and we must not forget that.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As I said, I am not a protectionist, but I want to remind ourselves that companies will only stay in Singapore if there are benefits to them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We must ensure that when they leave Singapore, we continue to have the human capital that made them successful, and that the human capital will be our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I want to touch on another subject that is also very close to my heart.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: At the last Budget, I spent half of my speech on that and, that is, on innovation.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that since then, there have been some changes.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have filed some cuts, so I hope to hear more.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But I still hope that when our agencies are restructured, when our agencies reformulate the policies, we would be doing so in the context of what is good for our country.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that we would lift ourselves beyond our historical baggage within each agency and reach out to our community partners.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that when we negotiate licences and ownership and partnership agreements with industries and companies, we will be thinking about what is right and what is fair, and what will incentivise creativity and innovation.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And we will not try to win a greater share of the rights just for the sake of that.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that when we deal with people who are partnering the Government agencies, we will think about our country and not our KPIs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In the area of employment, where again we need mindset changes, we have worked very, very hard to reach to private employers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have also worked very hard to reach to the public sector.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And we are encouraged that the Government continues to affirm its commitment to assist persons with disabilities to be trained for and find employment.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There are many of us who have called on the Public Service, being the largest employer sector, to take the lead and to employ persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We do not ask for a compromise of the principle of meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We do not ask for an accommodation of our inability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I met with Mr Peter Ong, Head of Civil Service, and his team.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I was touched by Mr Ong's personal interest and commitment, as well as that of a couple of Permanent Secretaries whom I have interacted with over time, their commitment for the Civil Service to employ persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I do recognise, of course, that the final employment decisions rightly are left to the respective agencies.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I will await the replies to my COS cuts, but I think from my understanding, ground-up, this is another area where a mindset change is required.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to be afraid not to change, we need not be afraid to change.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I speak at the risk of offending my good and dear friends in the Public Service, of offending those in the Public Service who have earned my respect.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But I speak as a Singaporean, proud of our Public Service, and proud that our Public Service can be better.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And I share this both with a heavy heart and with hope, that as we look at how people are reacting to the policies that we have, we will think about how we can improve.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In the same vein, I also would like to urge my fellow Singaporeans to take responsibility for our lives and our future.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I think it is time for us to stop moaning that there is not enough assistance.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I think there is time now for us to take our own future into our hands, take what the Government has given to us, but shape it with our own hands.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Public Service is made up of imperfect human beings like ourselves.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And if we want them to be bold, to experiment, grow and lead, then we have to allow them to fail.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And when they fail, we must be ready to support them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: What I want to say is that this is a Budget that gives us hope, but only if we decide that we want to move forward on our own two feet, with the Government supporting us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we want to build a future for ourselves and our children, and we want to build a future for our Singaporeans and hold our heads high, then we must learn to stand on our own two feet, and we must learn to stand for one another.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And the mindset change should not just be about the Civil Service.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It should extend to all private sectors and all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If all Singaporeans have the mindset to do the best they can for themselves, the country, their families, I think Singapore will continue to be a shining red dot for many more centuries to come.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many Singaporeans had waited with much anticipation for this year's Budget because some feared that there would be austerity measures, while others were hopeful for goodies that can be given for this Budget.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I stared long and hard at this Budget after the Finance Minister delivered this Budget last week.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is about jobs, long-term viability and the growth of the economy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Of course, there is also much social support to help the needy to tide over, as they are the most vulnerable group during these difficult times.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But this is not the first time that this Government has been doing it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This Government has been doing it all along.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last of all, I am very happy to note that this Budget has much more for the environment this time round, compared to the last two years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These are important issues because environmental issues concern sustainability and our living standards in the long run.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, we should look at how, as we improve our environment, not to impose too much of a burden on our people.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Second is the future carbon tax which the Finance Minister mentioned.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Third is about globalisation of our students as well as our workers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: First, the inflationary impact of the water and diesel tax.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last week, as I was driving, I was listening to some of the talk shows talking about this water tax increase.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Of course, there was a lot of public unhappiness about this water increase.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Quite surprisingly, we heard one academic from one of the IHLs mentioning that the increase should be much more, that it should be more than 30%, that it should be 100%, to deliver a shock effect so that people will start to save water.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I hope that is not the intent of the Government to deliver a shock effect.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, I think the Members of both sides of the House have helped to deliver this shock to everybody.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And the Government is scrambling now trying to relieve this shock from everybody, to say that the impact is not that bad in the first place.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For domestic households, what percentage of their monthly utility bills does water consumption constitute on average?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And thanks to public education efforts, in fact, many domestic households, on the whole, are quite streetwise with their water usage.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, the water usage trend has been trending downwards in terms of water usage per capita.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, based on feedback from my residents, many are still concerned that water consumption cost will make up a significant portion of their monthly expenditure with this increase.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I hope the Government would dismiss that notion.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Water, like fuel, is something which has a very strong knock-on impact on the community as a whole.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We need water to drink, prepare food, cook and wash, sanitation, and it applies to all, including eateries and school canteen operators, not to mention hotels.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We need water to maintain a certain standard of cleanliness in public areas, homes, hospitals and buildings, and in keeping our public transport vehicles clean.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We need water for factory production processes and a whole gamut of various industrial activities that we see in our industrial parks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This was due to the higher cost of natural gas for electricity generation, which increased by 10.6% compared to the previous quarter.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Why was the water price not raised in between?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Why wait until 17 years later, especially now when Town Councils have already revised their service and conservancy charges on households?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, the rise in water price could have also pulled the rug from under the Town Council, as they would be facing higher operating cost now arising from the revision of the price of water.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The inflationary effect may well negate the various rebates and other schemes that were spelt out in the Budget.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I know it is a tough call for the Finance Minister but I hope at least there will be some explanation given to address the public concerns.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Or why not adopt an even more progressive water tariff to tax those with higher water consumption?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Major cities in many countries, such as the US, France, Australia and China, have adopted the use of multiple-tiered water pricing, alternatively known as progressive water tariffs, or increasing the block tariffs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Under such a pricing system, the first block with the lowest pricing usually corresponds with the amount of water that a typical household requires for basic needs, such as bathing, domestic cleaning and cooking.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Each subsequent tier then commands a higher charge on excessive water usage that applies to luxuries like maintaining large gardens or swimming pools.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: China is a country with a multiple-tiered water pricing system.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Like us, their price of water is state controlled.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Water prices are low by international standards, but there is a problem for them, because their water per capita availability is low.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: By raising water prices, the authorities feared would intensify the income inequality, as water consumption represents a higher share of income for low-income households.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, the concern with a tiered water pricing system may not be of much help to low-income households with many, many family members.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I hope the Government is continuously exploring ways to keep the cost of water affordable for low-income families, while discouraging excessive use of water.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They account for about 20% of the vehicle population in 2015.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Most are trucks, vans and commercial vehicles, rather than passenger cars.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Another round of price increases by transport operators, including school bus transport for school children?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many businesses use their vehicles to transport workers and equipment to and from worksites.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Not just that, but many of the diesel vehicles are used for transporting and delivering goods, from wholesalers to retailers, from retailers to consumers, especially for online purchases as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These are diesel vans that are used for various purposes, as handymen also use them for delivery for plumbing services, carpentry and electrical services, even delivery of liquified petroleum gas to homes and eateries.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am worried that we may see an uptick in their fees when they are called upon now to do minor repairs for our households.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is an additional cash rebate for operators for diesel buses ferrying school children.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We should reduce the road tax for diesel vehicles further to be on par with petrol vehicles.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What will the Government be doing to ensure that all these rebates will be filtered down to the consumers?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am deeply concerned about the impending carbon tax that has just been announced for 2019 which the Finance Minister mentioned.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Although the proposed tax will generally apply upstream on power stations and other large direct emitters, it will have a knock-on effect on all electric users, both domestic and commercial.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We signed the Paris Agreement on climate change at the United Nations last April and affirmed our support and commitment to the Agreement.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Singapore ranks 123rd in emissions intensity out of 142 countries worldwide, but promised that the country will "continue to do more", to quote the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' statement.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The introduction of a carbon tax in 2019 is a good move to stay in step with international standards on environmental conservation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We pledged to reduce emission intensity by 36% from 2005 levels by 2030 and stabilise emissions with the aim of peaking around 2030.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is still in the early days, but I would like to know what is the Government's take on how challenging it will be to meet this goal.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I note that to encourage car buyers to switch to cleaner and environmentally-friendly models, the current Carbon Emissions-based Vehicle Scheme (CEVS) will be replaced.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There will be a new Vehicular Emissions Scheme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The new scheme considers four other pollutants, on top of carbon dioxide, so as to account more holistically for the health and environmental impact of vehicular emissions.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Budget states that the new Vehicular Emissions Scheme will run for two years, starting from 1 January next year and will be reviewed before it expires.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the interim, CEVS will be extended till 31 December this year.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How bad are we performing or how good are we performing, in terms of the area of carbon emissions?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How much more carbon have we emitted over the past two decades?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Taking into account that we are a very small country with very limited potential to tap on renewable energy, what can we do to reduce our carbon emission?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is the Government considering the introduction of a Climate Bill in tackling this carbon tax?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think solar technology is something that we should tap on a larger scale.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We should also look at how to help homeowners to use solar energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And Town Councils should look at this as a source of energy for the future.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: My last point is learning from overseas globalisation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: One such measure is helping students in Singapore universities getting work experience in foreign startups.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is a region with huge cultural diversity.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They are also accomplished in many important sectors, including technology, finance, medicine, the arts and so on.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We should explore student exchange programmes with Grandes Écoles in France, and also many other design and engineering institutions in Germany and Scandinavian universities which are also known for their innovation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Currently, many university courses offer exchange programmes, but these programmes are often short term, with a focus on academics.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I hope partnerships can be developed with the aim of helping students establish a longer-term residence and also obtaining residency in terms of internship programmes and job opportunities in their host country.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With these measures to guide us, I am confident that we can look forward to a brighter, cleaner, greener and more sustainable future.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I support the key thrusts of the Budget, namely: first, to build capabilities among our businesses and people; second, to seek new opportunities in the changing and uncertain global market; and third, to build a caring and resilient community in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As proposed by the Finance Minister, there is a dire need for Singaporeans and our businesses to embrace digital technology so that we can seize opportunities to pursue a better quality of life in the future.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, the key challenge faced by SMEs lies in training staff to go digital or recruiting and retaining staff who already possess the skills to do so.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Due to the different learning abilities of workers, there is a need to adopt more standardised and industry-wide digital solutions.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will help to reduce the learning curve and ensure that the workers' new-found skills are applicable in various companies.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To further support a digital economy, we must also equip consumers to be digital savvy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many Singaporeans, especially the elderly, are still facing difficulties using e-services and smartphone applications.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thus, I would propose that we provide free e-services and smartphone applications training at every Community Club (CC) to build digital capabilities in our community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The construction industry is complex and comprises many stakeholders and trade associations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: At present, there is a general lack of initiatives from the ground up, as well as the necessary leadership to bring the industry into the future.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the last 30 years, limited progress has been made to enhance professionalism, productivity and quality in the construction industry.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To date, construction productivity is low, while its quality has struggled to meet clients' expectations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The industry's professional practices currently leave plenty of room for improvement as well.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Its main role is to provide feedback to the Government and be a think-tank to discuss strategies for industry development.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Based on the findings of the Auditor-General's Office, there are often lapses in the procurement and project management of Government projects.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is mainly attributed to a lack of expertise in inexperienced staff with regard to procurement and project management in the public sector.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As we move towards building a vibrant and connected city, we must ensure that the public sector has a core group of project managers and facilities managers to procure, implement and manage public sector projects.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The public sector can take the lead to develop a professionalism and quality assurance framework that incorporates industry best practices to upgrade the construction industry.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In line with the Government's push for environmental sustainability and the Public Sector Taking the Lead in Environmental Sustainability (PSTLES) programme, the North West Community Development Council launched its Eco CC@North West programme in October 2016, which focuses on two key areas of improvement for CCs, namely, first, the green "hardware", and second, the green "software".

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Green "hardware" refers to infrastructural works to enhance the environmental performance of CCs, which include aspects of energy and water efficiencies, while green "software" refers to the promotion of green consciousness and adoption of green practices among the users of CCs, such as using sustainable and environmentally-friendly products, reducing the use of energy and water, maintaining a healthy indoor environment, practising effective waste management and general education on the topic at large.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: A CC Green Committee was also set up to promote green living among residents.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, one barrier which currently prevents CCs from going green is the lack of funding to introduce green technologies and features into the CCs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thus, I would like to urge the Minister for Finance to consider providing a one-off Green CC grant to expedite the greening of all CCs in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As an alternative to further encourage the adoption of green technologies that will reduce greenhouse gas emissions, I would urge the Minister for Finance to also consider providing incentives or grants to companies or organisations which support such go-green initiatives.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The LED lighting programme will result in about 40% energy saving and, thus, a reduction of greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would once again urge the Minister for Finance to consider giving grants or incentives to further expedite the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is geopolitical turbulence in the international order.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: New technologies are disrupting the economies of many countries, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Protectionist sentiments in advanced economies threaten the sanctity of Singapore's central economic strategy, that is, free trade.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Government and our policymakers are very much aware of these macro, seismic global changes and are working tirelessly to ensure that Singapore continues to succeed and progress as a country.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, it is extremely important that we do not lose sight of the perspective of the individual Singaporean; the issues and difficulties that each Singaporean and their families face in their day-to-day lives.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Will an overall strategy aimed at the collective good result in unintended consequences for individuals?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, this is often the greatest complaint amongst Singaporeans, that the Government is too concerned with the big picture and often neglects the perspective of the individual.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is in this context that I rise to address two issues within the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As I am the Government Parliamentary Committee Chair for Transport, I will look at issues that relate to transport specifically.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They are (a) the Tiered Additional Registration Fees (ARF) for motorcycles; and (b) the restructuring of the diesel tax.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There have already been media reports that estimate that this will put prices of higher end motorcycles close to that of small cars.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Motorcycle enthusiasts say that they have been unfairly "targeted" by the revised ARF regime.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Some argue that super cars, such as Ferraris, Lamborghinis or Porsches, should have been at the receiving end of such an increased ARF regime, instead of higher end motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Motorcyclists who purchase higher end motorcycles come from all walks of life with varying financial means.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Owners of super cars, however, belong to the top 0.1% of income earners in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As such, why not increase the ARF regime on consumers who can better afford to pay?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: On its face, this is not an unreasonable perspective to take.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But a closer look at the Budget Statement suggests that the position is misunderstood.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Minister Heng alluded to two reasons in his Budget Statement for the revised ARF regime for motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: First, that there is a small but rising number of motorcyclists buying expensive motorcycles, and second, after the change in the ARF regime, more than half of motorcycle buyers will continue to pay the current ARF rate of 15%.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The rising number of motorcyclists buying expensive motorcycles is pushing up the overall costs of all motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The rising trend of Certificate of Entitlement (COE) prices for motorcycles bear this out.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Owners of smaller motorcycles, who often use their motorcycles as a low-cost mode of transport for work or essential travel, are being made to pay higher COEs because of the increased demand for expensive motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The revised ARF, therefore, serves this further purpose ‒ to reduce the demand for expensive motorcycles and, consequently, to lower motorcycle COE prices and lower cost for purchasers of smaller motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Reducing reliance on diesel fuel to reduce pollution is an admirable objective.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, this policy has drawn considerable concern from some quarters.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The loudest voice amongst them belongs to the class who consumes automotive diesel to make a living.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Taxi drivers make up a significant group in this class.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Taxi drivers consume a larger quantity of diesel fuel than all other diesel-run automotive because they travel around continuously to pick up customers.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A volume-based tax, therefore, implies that their overheads are likely to increase significantly.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If taxi companies pass this cost saving to taxi drivers, it will go some way to allay their concerns of an increase in overhead costs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, if one is to stop and examine the pressures faced by a modern-day taxi driver in Singapore, one can perhaps appreciate their frustrations better.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The entry of private hire cars in the point-to-point transport industry and the possible emergence of the automated self-driving cars in the not-too-distant future may give many taxi drivers in Singapore sleepless nights.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These new technologies have disrupted the transport industry considerably and it is important that the Government should manage the concerns of stakeholders affected by the disruption in order to assist in any transition that is necessary.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I shall address this further at the Committee of Supply Debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The world is filled with disruptions and the pace of change has quickened so much that nobody can be sure of what works and what does not in the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We cannot control what happens around us, yet we also cannot passively wait for things to happen before deciding on what to do.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What we can do right now is to ensure that we develop the agility to adapt and the willingness to learn.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I wholeheartedly agree that we need to focus our energy and precious resources on transforming the industries to create new opportunities and on building the capacity and capabilities of our people, so that we are ready to make full use of the opportunities available.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: All of these are long-term investments for the future, to make sure that we have the right skills and knowledge for a changing and competitive world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The key challenge for Singapore is to respond and change together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government is sincere in wanting to move all Singaporeans forward, but it cannot achieve it alone, no matter how strong it is.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To move forward together, we need greater support from the Government but also a concerted effort across the different sectors of our society and a willingness in each individual to give our best shot.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The fittest amongst us will survive and get ahead, but the more vulnerable amongst us will need help if we are to complete this journey together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our Government − the body that aggregates and redistributes resources − therefore, has an important role to play.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To be fair, our Government has done a lot.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But as opposed to giving out even more handouts, let us also look at other ways of giving the help to the more vulnerable ones amongst us and giving them the extra push.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are a few groups of Singaporeans who could do more with the Government's support, but I would like to highlight just two today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, families of unstable income or retrenched workers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Economic growth is expected to slow down and there are uncertainties ahead.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Unstable income workers, especially those in odd jobs or contracted without work guaranteed, will see their income fluctuating even more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given these circumstances, I worry about how their affected families would be able to cope with the rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Identifying distressed families early will allow the appropriate interventions to be made in a timely manner before the situation gets out of hand, when it would be even more challenging to resolve.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the years, I have seen families coming to seek help only after their arrears have compounded for many, many months.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By then, the interest would have compounded, late payment penalties would have been slapped on and, perhaps, some families would have even taken personal loans which would just only add on to the liabilities that the family faces.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of these families did not know that help was available, some simply panicked and went into denial when they saw their escalating arrears.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And some were struggling to juggle multiple jobs and did not even have time to seek help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, proactively seeking them out and offering timely interventions will help Singaporeans to focus on their jobs or studies, both of which are essential in ensuring their families' long-term independence and success.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We face a rapidly ageing society in the midst of a rapidly changing environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even as we transform and apply resources to transforming our economy and workforce, let us not forget to take steps to help elderly Singaporeans live well into their old age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That means continuing to advance innovations in the eldercare sector so that our seniors today and tomorrow can enjoy a good retirement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With our seniors taken care of, we can then better focus on the big picture and take comfort in the knowledge that no one gets left behind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We know that Singaporeans are living longer, but a longer life does not necessarily mean more years of healthy good life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This means one will have to spend more on healthcare as one ages.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is based on a household expenditure survey in 2012/2013.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The healthcare financial burden on an elderly is, therefore, heavier.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Not forgetting, infrastructural spending will also have to increase as we accommodate an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These translate into a greater cost burden on working Singaporeans in the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We cannot be building new nursing homes or hiring new people to do the caring on an indefinite basis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is unsustainable and neither is it the best solution.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the demand for institutional care for the elderly, including the elderly who can actually be independent with a little bit more support in the community, keeps rising, partly because of shrinking family sizes and partly because of changing family values.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, we need to change our thinking about eldercare, and there are several points that I would like to raise in this respect.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But looking ahead, as we need more healthcare workers with this projected increase of 30,000, I wonder if we can continue to maintain this 75% from now till 2020 and beyond.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With more Singaporeans leaving than entering the labour market, will we have enough to meet the rising demand for eldercare?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How many and for how long more can we top up with foreign manpower?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could we find ways to recruit more volunteers and organise ourselves in the community better so that the community can step in to supplement manpower demand and fulfil needs?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As it is, we know that there are technology solutions, such as sensors, assistive devices and telemedicine.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Leverage technology to enable independent living at home, even for those who have moderate disabilities and little or no family support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are already pilots being done with the deployment of the Elderly Monitoring System, for example.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But this is just one aspect of an elderly's daily living.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could we look into a more concerted, holistic concept of using digital technology to enable independent living for the elderly?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could we facilitate the integration of these solutions, so that the elderly can enjoy the services at home in an easy and seamless manner?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition to enabling a more independent living for the elderly at home and ageing in place, we should also consider providing and encouraging the provision of digital platforms to link freelance healthcare professionals and caregivers or those with spare capacity, to facilitate on-demand provision of home care or other related elder care services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the emerging gig economy, such platforms are the next new norm.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But some of these platforms are privately run and the elderly who wish to utilise them may be deterred for fear that the subsidies that they may be eligible for cannot be applied via these platforms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, we live in a world which is changing rapidly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is not possible to predict what tomorrow will be like.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, we cannot change the world based on our efforts alone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We can help equip companies and our people with the means and capability to keep up with the change.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This year's Budget, which will help companies continue their transformation and the people to upskill, is one that takes care of our long-term interests.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, as the Government is working very hard to build our economy for tomorrow, I hope that the Government will not forget to continue assisting Singaporeans who need help, so that they can also keep up with the economy and continue on this journey together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As our society ages rapidly, our needs on this front will increase dramatically.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Medical costs and infrastructure expenditure will inevitably rise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Rather than regarding these as costs that cannot be recouped, why do we not look at how we can help the elderly live more meaningfully?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, the Government can quicken the pace of building smart homes for the elderly and promote technologies that the elderly will find friendly to use.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will allow the elderly, even those who are not very mobile or in good health or live alone, to continue to live independently and age in place.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government should also expand programmes similar to that of the Pioneer Generation Ambassadors, to encourage more elderly to be volunteers as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As they become active in voluntary work, they will also keep their mind and body healthy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The elderly will not only live well but will also help ease the manpower shortages in the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will help ease our own worries and allow us to concentrate on working hard for our future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the saying goes, having an elderly person at home is like having a treasure in the house.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): The Government clearly can do much to address the challenges we face and the needs we have.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, relying on the Government alone is not enough.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even with new workforce entrants, there will always be a stiff competition for manpower.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is demand for people in industries that drive Singapore's economic development and there is also demand for people in sectors that provide care for people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The community has so far demonstrated how we can organise ourselves and achieve many things without over relying on the Government or, basically, paid workers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If manpower shortage is likely to be permanent and there are still needs to be addressed, perhaps we should look more to the community as a new resource pool − gig volunteers, perhaps?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have residents who have diverse sets of skills and knowledge and they may also have the capacity outside of work and family time to help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can physically fit residents form Citizens on Patrol to ensure the security, peace and quiet of the neighbourhood?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can neighbours step forth and be ready to respond to calls for help through the Elderly Monitoring System?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are not difficult things to do but impactful if done.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, these propositions are impositions on Singaporeans who may prefer spending more time on activities they enjoy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But if everyone could just set aside a little of their time for the community, we will have a wealthy bank of volunteer man-hours and, in turn, achieve much more than what we see in the community today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is much that we can do at the Government level and across the different sectors of our society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But ultimately, it is also the individual willingness of Singaporeans to do something, to give our best shot, that will keep the momentum going and make the difference.
