speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our economy, security and defence, all of these need each and every one of us to work together in order to succeed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And, most importantly, if we truly desire a caring and inclusive society, then let us show it through our actions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the course of our five decades since Independence, we had to reinvent ourselves many times, with the Government playing a proactive role in enabling the process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The CFE Report marks the plan for the next phase of our development.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The focus of CFE is rightly on economic growth, as this is the only way to meet the expectations of our future generations for better jobs and opportunities in an increasingly competitive and volatile global landscape.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: CFE includes a broad range of plans to ensure Singapore remains linked to the global economy, our people develop the deep skills needed to stay relevant and our enterprises develop the means to compete.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are roadmaps tailored for the different industries, too.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All these are welcome, and I look forward to the upcoming initiatives and changes to execute against the plans by CFE.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Equally important though is to ensure that our growth is equitable and sustainable and, on this, I would like to deal with a few matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this Budget, we already see some of the strains that will face us in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We, therefore, have to be very prudent in our spending.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many sectors, for example, SMEs were also expecting more support from the Government.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While I fully support the Government helping businesses to tide over difficult times, I am concerned about subsidies becoming entrenched.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In many other countries, subsidies to different sectors of the economy become entrenched, allowing them to continue operating inefficiently and preventing the redeployment of resources to sectors where they are more likely to produce more value.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In fact, I think the only principal justification for a subsidy to any segment is if greater welfare arises from that subsidy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, if giving a business a small subsidy to tide over a difficult cyclical setback prevents substantial numbers of jobs being lost, then it is probably defensible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In short, there should be what are called positive externalities arising from Government support to businesses and not just private profit for the business itself.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With the rising quality of healthcare, many of our workers are able to work even though they are older and, often, it is with some sadness that older employees tell me they have been "retired" by their companies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The unspoken reason for this is often higher costs associated with hiring older workers, particularly in relation to matters, such as workplace insurance, as well as the availability of younger and cheaper workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, there are numerous benefits with allowing older workers to continue working for as long as they wish.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For the individuals, it allows them to remain economically active and independent, and there many studies showing that there are mental and physical health benefits for seniors who remain active in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: From the country's perspective, this would ameliorate the strain on our fiscal base as economically active seniors will remain more able to take care of themselves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, I would go even further on this front and suggest that both the Government and the unions look into the specific concerns employers have to employing older workers so as to eliminate structural factors contributing to age discrimination as much as possible in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, it is my hope that older workers will be more able to stop work at a time of their choosing, rather than being forced into retirement that may be against their will.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second aspect of the Budget that I am heartened by is the manner in which it deals with environmental concerns.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In fact, this Budget specifically takes into account environmental consequences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the fundamental causes of environmental pollution and damage is that businesses, in their determination to maximise profits, do not adequately take into account the damage caused to the environment by their business practices.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The costs of environmental damage and pollution are often felt by the entire community, while the profit is enjoyed by the businesses themselves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a classic example of what economists call a "negative externality" where society pays the price that is higher than the benefit the company receives.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A carbon tax is one way to ensure that businesses pay a price for polluting as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will, hopefully, incentivise businesses to innovate or invest in green technologies to reduce their carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am also heartened that the revenues raised from these taxes will be used to support the growth of green businesses, as this is one way of reducing the private costs for socially useful innovation, and if these technologies are effective, they could also be something else Singapore could export to other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Following clarifications, I think most households have realised that the net impact on them will be manageable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, although this is an increase, most people I have spoken to believe that this is manageable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Everyone also agrees that water is a precious resource for Singapore and people should be encouraged to conserve as much water as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While nobody likes to pay more for water, I think everyone agrees in principle that water must be priced at a level that is sustainable for Singapore in the long term.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One suggestion I have in this regard is whether we can relook at water pricing to make it more flexible, so that, like energy prices, it, too, may go up or down depending on the costs of production.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This may mean that we have small gradual increases every year, rather than a one-off lump sum increase after 17 years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In fact, anecdotally, a few people I have spoken to were actually surprised that their water bill had not increased in 17 years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As many people received their water and power bills together, they had assumed that both prices were going up when, in fact, it was only the power component that was changing and the water component had remained the same in their bills for the last 17 years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, what I would suggest is, in order to prevent sticker shock or surprise every 17 or 20 years, as the case may be, that we find a way to make the water price more flexible as well so that people can adjust their consumption patterns along with the rising cost, and our usage of water will remain sustainable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One last area I wish to touch on is added support for parenthood.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I should declare my interest here as I recently joined the Club of Parents with my first child, and I have to say that it is a wonderful joy to be a parent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But the reality is that many young people hesitate in taking the step both towards marriage and towards becoming parents, and the demographic time bomb I mentioned is a very real one, and the best way to diffuse it or at least reduce some of the pressures on it is to encourage more people to take on the challenge of becoming parents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The other benefit, of course, apart from the personal joy of becoming a parent is that society as a whole benefits because, ultimately, the children are the ones who will take Singapore forward over the next 30 or 50 years, and they will be the ones to support the older generations, to support us when we are no longer able to work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And there are tremendous benefits to society for encouraging parenthood.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, with parenthood, the economic issues are a bit reversed because the cost of parenting is largely borne by the individuals themselves, whereas the benefits are not only to the individuals but also to society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is why I have always believed there are strong justifications for socialising the cost of parenthood more.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are many measures in place already assisting parents to defray the cost somewhat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But there is always more that can be done, in particular, childcare is one of the areas where there is a great deal of demand.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will help to take more of the strain off working families and working parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But as we go forward, my suspicion is that there will be a correlation between the more we socialise the cost of parenthood and the more willing people become to take this plunge.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think costs are often a consideration for people considering marriage and parenthood and, sometimes, there is misinformation about the costs as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But in countries like France, which is one of the few developed countries where they do not have a major issue with the population, we find the cost of parenthood being heavily socialised.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I think this is one area we can look more at in future Budgets as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Broadly speaking, Mr Deputy Speaker, I think this Budget will put Singapore on the right foundation for sustainable growth in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What I am most heartened is that the focus is not only on growth but on sustainability and the measures taken to ameliorate both the demographic and environmental challenges we face in the coming decades.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I had previously raised my concerns about the relatively lower participation in preschool by Indian families.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In particular, there appears to be a correlation in lack of preschool education and difficulties in primary school, where some of our students lag in areas, such as Science and Mathematics.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would strongly encourage all Indian families to enrol their children in preschool and take advantage of the subsidies available.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They should allow professionals to come in and assist.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our nation is at a critical transition point.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We must seize the opportunities brought about by the disruptive technologies erupting all around us or risk being irrelevant.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We must help our local companies, including our SMEs, survive and grow.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The plans outlined in the Budget will go some way, but companies must also help themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our schools, companies and people have to be ready for change.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Lifelong learning and training will be an integral part of our lives.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Over the last two days, my colleagues have touched on these topics, so I will not go there.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But I want to talk about something that is equally important from the medium to long term, something which bothers me and my residents and, that is, the issue of healthcare.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our healthcare services in the public and private sectors are lauded around the world as progressive, high quality yet cost-effective.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our unique MediSave, MediShield and MediFund (3M) system and Pioneer Generation (PG) Package have served us well.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many more have benefited as the enhanced MediShield Life now covers everyone, regardless of age and health status.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: During house visits, my residents would chat about many things and one recurring topic is their worries about becoming a burden to their loved ones, especially when it comes to medical bills.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He is very grateful to the Government and the system.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He and his siblings are all below 30 years old and starting out in their careers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It would have been difficult for them if they had to pay the full bill.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: His mother is now well and resting back at home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our 3M and PG Package have done well in helping families reduce their anxiety over medical bills.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, why are my residents so concerned about healthcare costs?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I believe there are several reasons why healthcare costs are escalating.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One is the moral hazard of health insurance.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My concern is whether more comprehensive insurance coverage might lead to over-consumption of healthcare.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Are patients tempted to use more resources than they otherwise would have, because they think someone else is paying the bill?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: MediShield Life, which currently covers all Singaporeans, has a deductible and co-insurance portion.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In recent years, more Singaporeans are enhancing their coverage with Integrated Shield Plans (IPs) for additional private insurance.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Riders are available to cover both the deductible and co-insurance portion.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Here comes a potential problem: are Singaporeans with better IP coverage more likely to spend substantially more and consume more healthcare than those who merely have basic MediShield coverage?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A resident in his 40s recently hurt his knee while playing soccer.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He was sent for a magnetic resonance imaging scan at a reputable private hospital.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The scan revealed a Grade 1 sprain of the anterior cruciate ligament.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He was given two options by the doctor.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Two, he could go for a relatively quick minor keyhole surgery with a night's stay in an A-class ward.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He went for the second option − surgery.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He paid nothing because he had an IP rider.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Another spoke of his father's cataract day surgery for one eye.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I verified with two other eye specialists and they commented that, from the bill, it looks like a standard cataract surgery.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am afraid some people might wonder if doctors are charging more because the insurance companies are footing the bill and not the patients.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: With IP riders and patients paying next to zero dollars, the patients are less likely to scrutinise their bills as thoroughly and this is not helpful.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I do not doubt that doctors are specialists in their field and do offer the best medical advice.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My point here is not to question their competence.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is also not a bad thing if wider and more comprehensive health insurance means patients could have more treatment options.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What worries me is that additional treatment options are sometimes made available to the patients not because they are essential but because the patients are now able to afford them, thanks to their insurance coverage.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If this happens on a large scale, will this over-burden our healthcare system and infrastructure and increase costs?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Another concern will be, will this result in a widening of disparity between private and public hospital bills?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If so, this disparity might cause more people to shift to public hospitals, leading to overcrowding and longer waits.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I understand there is no straightforward and easy solution.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Perhaps MOH and the Singapore Medical Council can study and regulate doctors' fees and hospital charges.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Two, educate patients on healthcare options so that they can be more discerning in their choices.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: During last year's Budget Debate, I spoke about coordinated care.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We should streamline some of this care from hospitals to primary care for more efficiency and effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have 27 specific recommendations for the Government and have filed 27 cuts, speaking about protecting the environment, curbing smoking and helping smokers quit, strengthening responsible financing, helping divorcees, single parents and their children, tackling animal cruelty and wildlife crime, improving our rehabilitation process for inmates, strengthening our humanitarian aid, helping domestic workers, helping neglected children, helping stay-at-home mothers, tackling oil spills, enhancing ElderShield, helping couples with difficulties conceiving, enhancing our ElderShield and helping our Institutions of a Public Character (IPCs) which internationalise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the key in our Budget, our policies and all the recommendations we will be making in this House will be in the implementation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A crucial player in the implementation is our Public Service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This year, I will focus my speech on how we can strengthen our Public Service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As fellow Member Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has mentioned, there is no doubt that we have an efficient and corrupt-free Public Service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our aim seems to be to process each case as fast as possible and to follow the book as strictly as possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Do not deviate, do not rock the boat and do not question.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, many people fall through the cracks when the system is so rigid, when we view things in black and white and where compassion is not exercised regularly enough.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are the famous four words "case-by-case basis" but, in reality and based on my experience on the ground, we have to fight with all our might to get that "case-by-case basis".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not long ago, one of my residents died in very unfortunate circumstances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her husband was remanded and she left behind two very young children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her sister was thrown into the deep water, while grieving the loss of her only sister and, still single, she suddenly becoming a mother of two.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke to HDB on her behalf urging them not to chase her for the mortgage, give her some time to grieve, compose herself for a very difficult next chapter of her life and, in any case, both owners of the flat are no longer there.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: HDB agreed, but later still sent a letter demanding payment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She came to see me in tears, worried that HDB will repossess the flat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I asked HDB why did they do that.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not long after, she received a letter from the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore demanding tax payment for her late sister.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that, on paper, we are right to demand payment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But, on compassionate grounds, should we do so, as our fellow Singaporean is trying hard to get back on her feet?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we not afford to show some compassion?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And this is just one out of the many cases I have encountered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are the exact things our Public Service needs to do as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need them to think out of the box.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have now developed a mindset where a solution, which has been used for years, becomes the right solution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We think that if we change, it means we have been wrong all these years and we do not like to be wrong.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke about chickens in Parliament last week, and now I will speak about monkeys.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our response to monkey issues is as "knee jerk" as it can get.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We receive a complaint, a trap is laid, a monkey is caught and killed, and we put a tick on the box that something has been done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And in a lot of the cases, that is "case closed".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was there when an Agri-Food and Veterinary Authority of Singapore (AVA) contractor was poaching monkeys from a protected area away from where he was supposed to be trapping monkeys.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But when a trapper returns to AVA with a monkey, how can we possibly verify that he trapped the correct monkey or even a monkey from the correct location?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I asked an officer on the ground why do we do this when science says it does not work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reply is that "This is what we have always done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do not think it works too, but my director told me to do it".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are other ways of managing this issue, we can choose to think out of the box, innovate and choose to address the root of the problem, rather than the symptoms of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps the easiest way to come up with new ideas is to listen to suggestions from others, engage the wider community, create partnerships.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have been to too many dialogue sessions where we talk so much rather than listen attentively, we defend our policies rather than listen to ideas on how we can make our policies better.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We still do sessions where we explain a decision rather than get feedback to make a decision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But will people feel more engaged, more empowered?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The answer, without a doubt, is also yes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are a rare breed who devote their lives towards serving Singapore, but I see issues that we need to resolve urgently so that we can continue to have an efficient, committed, yet compassionate Public Service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Moving forward, I have some suggestions to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For a start, we need to cut some slack for our ground officers, our frontline staff members who will be the first to detect people who have fallen through the cracks, who can alert us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many I have spoken to feel that when they bring such cases to their superiors, they are scolded for not following the books.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I suggest that Members of this House are also provided with a report on the suggestions made by members of the public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should list all suggestions provided, whether we agree with them or not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I suggest that senior public servants attend Parliament and listen to the debates so that they have a better understanding of the concerns we are raising.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like football, nothing beats watching a "live" performance than reading a report.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I listened to Senior Minister of State Indranee on the radio last week, and there were so many good suggestions on how we can improve the Budget.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But, of course, they were made after the Budget has been cast in stone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a wasted opportunity not to be able to implement some of the really good suggestions to improve Budget 2017.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a wasted opportunity to just have a one-way conversation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I suggest public servants who draft policies actually go down to the ground and experience different jobs related to their policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the past year, I have experienced what it is like to be a healthcare worker, a driver, a Town Council cleaner, a coffee shop cleaner, a Police Officer, a kindergarten teacher, a cardboard collector, a customer relations officer, a full-time father and, in December, a humanitarian worker.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I had shared on Facebook, it has been an enriching journey, to say the least.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And through these experiences, I have learnt a lot, seen the struggles they face and witnessed first-hand the sacrifices they have made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And through these experiences, I have seen how we can make the lives of our workers better and where we need to make changes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Committees made up of people who are on the ground and who perhaps might even have more experience on the issues than our public servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are committees which give the public servants a chance to listen and work with the community, to come up with new policies and even legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And as pointed out by Prof Tommy Koh last week, I quote, "When we appoint people to boards, we can also appoint challengers who are subversive and who have alternative points of view.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That's the kind of cultural change we want to see.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Engage them, do not be afraid of them, these are people who speak up because they care.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are people who put the welfare of others before theirs and we should embrace this spirit rather than fear it, we should support rather than penalise them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should work together rather than go our separate journeys when the end destination might be the same.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This fear of engaging them is very apparent when I speak to public servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I urge them to start the dialogue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have been and continue to be a civil society activist.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand that I look too fierce sometimes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, as the Prime Minister requested when he introduced me at the last General Elections, I am smiling a lot more now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I smile so much that it hurts, it really hurts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the words of Martin Luther King Jr: "Everybody can be great.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You don't have to have a college degree to serve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You don't have to make your subject and your verb agree to serve....

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You don't have to know the second theory of thermodynamics in physics to serve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You only need a heart full of grace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A soul generated by love." Sir, I hope that every public servant has a heart full of grace and a soul generated by love.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Finance Minister, it is very good to see you back.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I was encouraged by the kind support shown to you by many Singaporeans, especially across political divides.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Unity is one of the most precious assets any country can boast of.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I will always be grateful for every year that we still possess that in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is one of the richest parts of the inheritance we have received from our previous generations and I pray we will never squander it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2017 declares that our future lies in Moving Forward Together.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, Finance Minister, America's motto is "e pluribus unum" − "out of many, we are one".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is inscribed on every coin they have in circulation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It sat in the pockets of all their citizens as a daily reminder that unity was the very currency of their system.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And yet, this is the very same country which just recently voted to take a massive hatchet to a system they felt was no longer trustworthy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For a large swathe of the American people, the system was not even about Republicans versus Democrats anymore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many voters had lost all belief in the story the leaders of both sides had told them about Moving Forward Together.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Forty percent of voters were so disheartened that they simply stayed at home.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And many who did show up at the polls placed all their bets instead on an outsider who pitched an audacious story of "Let's just Move Only Some of Us Forward Together".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A flood of articles has been written since then trying to understand why people would seemingly vote against their interests.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And one common thread that was unearthed was this.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: To those feeling left behind, the story of prioritising Some over All was always the real story of the system anyway.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They had simply decided to play the game that they believed had been played on them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The true currency of any country is not in bills and coins.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The value of every country rises and falls according to the legacy of trust it still possesses and the level of trust it still inspires on the individual, institutional and international levels.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In a hyper networked world, trust is the most important currency.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many smart chief executive officers (CEOs) working in the new economy can tell you that.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But all that foreknowledge has apparently done little to arrest the huge crisis of trust that the world is now in.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Edelman Trust Barometer has been tracking trust in four key institutions − business, government, NGOs and media – since 2012.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And year on year, Edelman has seen public trust in these institutions decline across all 28 countries surveyed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The global rise of angry populism and pushback against elites that we see today are a result of unchecked erosion of trust from the past, coupled with present-day fears about the pace of change.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, Edelman reported the largest-ever drop in trust across all four institutions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Trust in media is at all-time lows in 17 countries.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Trust in government dropped in 14 markets and is now the least trusted institution in half of the 28 countries surveyed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The credibility of CEOs dropped globally to an all-time low in every country studied.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: People are now more likely to trust search engines over human editors, individuals over institutions, reformers more than preservers of the status quo.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Globally, 53% of respondents believe the current overall system has failed them and is unfair, offering them little hope for the future.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Only 15% believe it is working, the rest are just uncertain.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, how did we do on the Trust Barometer?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our high-trust climate is a rare thing which presents us opportunities we can leverage on.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, it is not just deep reserves of financial capital from our past that we must invest in, protect and multiply; it is our deep reserves of social and emotional capital as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Every country that hopes to ride out this global trust crisis must not only actively shore up trust in its system, it needs to also take a hard, honest look at where trust is being broken in its system and take noticeable, decisive steps to build it up again.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One of the insights in the report that struck me was the distinction between the responses from the informed public and responses from the mass population.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, if Edelman's findings are to be believed, we should not be surprised if the French elections see its own version of a Brexit or Trump shock result.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: You might be surprised to also hear that actually, in America, the level of trust the informed public had in their system was almost as high as the level of trust our informed public had in our system.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But it was the mass population respondents of America that ranked their system as deeply, deeply untrustworthy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That explains the genuine shock felt by Washington and the wealthier coastal cities at the election results.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is a small dip but still worth paying attention to.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: These respondents worried most about losing their jobs to immigrants and losing business opportunities to foreign competitors.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do see the year-on-year efforts by the Government to mitigate the costs of that pace of change.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Silver Support Scheme, Workfare − these are all good, progressive moves towards strengthening our social safety nets.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But what I also see is that those schemes still have much further to go to help Singaporeans who are feeling left behind.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Goods and Services Tax, U-Save Vouchers, conservancy rebates, education subsidies, weekly food donations − these are all good things, and these are all greatly, greatly appreciated things.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But for some of our struggling families, all these good and helpful gestures still feel like drops in a constantly leaking bucket.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am speaking especially for our working poor.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The ones who feel left out and left behind by our yearly calls to "upskill", "internationalise" and "innovate".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But because they are just busy trying not to drown under wave after wave of new demands, new costs and new changes to their world.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: To those who are drowning, even the calmest, most reasonable technocratic explanation about why a rise in water and motorcycle prices is justifiable will feel like salt on a wound.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because when you are drowning, all you want is for somebody to just stop talking, dive in and grab you before you sink.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: You do not care about the facts of the policies.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Debates over what makes sense or does not make sense are all Greek to you.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What is most real and relevant to you is simply how those facts are making you feel: I do not have enough.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When you are in that claustrophobic space of anxiety and scarcity, you do not have enough mental bandwidth to deal with anything more than each day's demands.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And having the breathing space to consider alternative choices or plan for the future, that is a luxury the working poor do not have.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That is why compassionate communication of available solutions rather than a "don't know, go talk to your MP" approach by frontline officers matters so much.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That is why finding a way to provide universal support for childcare, eldercare, faster access to affordable housing, caregiver respite across all classes of people matters so much.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because all of these interventions go a long way to create bandwidth, a space for the drowning to feel like they can breathe again.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are missing a big point if we say, "Well, people must deal with the facts as they are.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Not where they feel they should be." But honestly, nobody understands their life just according to facts.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is an intellectual's fantasy to believe we are perfectly rational, fact-driven beings.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Most people make their choices according to their feelings about the facts.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we care about making sure people hear us out on the hard facts about our country's situation, we must start all our communications with connecting with people where they are: which is how they feel, even if that feeling is disagreeable or irrational to us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If not, let us just accept that your words may never impact anyone outside your echo chamber.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot effectively uplift our working poor if we do not connect our solutions more effectively to the deep narratives and emotional realities that they live in.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We love the idea of being a Smart City that uses Big Data to solve our wicked problems.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But I sincerely hope we will also fall in love with the idea of being a Wise City that looks at Deep Data as well, to make sure the policies we come up with are not just technical solutions but empathetic, human solutions that resonate with the communities they were meant to serve.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know enough numbers to put up an elegant fight to justify a request for $X increase in Workfare and $Y increase in Silver Support.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: All I want us to just consider is this: knowing what they know now, seeing what they see now, what would Washington's elites have done different for their poorest states if they could time-travel just four years, two years or even just one year back?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If Downing Street could time-travel, what would they have done different for their most depressed regions to prevent Brexit?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some decisions that looked too high-risk, too ridiculous back then, I am sure, suddenly look well worth investing in now because they finally see the high-stake consequences at last.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Their time for intervention has passed them by.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What must we do to stave off a future shock scenario of our own?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget Speech declared, "We can aim for quality growth of 2% to 3%…if we work hard to help everyone who wishes to work find a place in the labour force".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It also said, "On the social front, Budget 2017 supports families who wish to buy a home, experience the joys of parenthood and help their children towards post-secondary education." So, what can we do for our working poor, especially those in single parent or sandwich class families, so that they may feel included in those statements as well?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Consider just one kind of life story, a composite based on real stories familiar to our local social workers: a woman gets divorced, she gains custody of her three kids but no promise of maintenance.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But she does not quit her job because she loves her work, she needs her work.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Giving up her salary even for a month is not an option.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She cannot afford the downpayment for a flat.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: None of her relatives or friends has room to spare her little family.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She rents on the open market but rents are high and leases are short.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When her boss offers her a higher paying job opportunity, she has to turn it down because she cannot work far away from her child's preschool.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She knows she can never pick up her child on time.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Not by bus, which is all she can afford.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Plus they need her to work nights when she has zero childcare options.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And then that damn electrical fuse box has to blow up, forcing her to choose between paying for the lights to come back on or buying better food for her kids.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And some nights, at the end of some very, very, very bad days, she considers just giving it up.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Taking up a lower paying job to at least get a rental flat of her own where her kids can study in peace, suddenly feels like the smartest and safest decision in the world.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Are you tired even just listening to that story?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because she sure the heck is tired living it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And you have to appreciate that for many of the poor, they believe that they will never not feel tired.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: All she wants is to move her life forward again, together, with everyone else she sees around her, but there are all these structural hurdles that keep coming up her way.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What is the Singapore we want her to experience?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What is the Singapore story we hope she will pass down to her children?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Does this user experience of the Singapore system matter to us enough to form a strategic team and warrant a complete overhaul of her customer journey?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Is her trust, and her children's trust, equally worthy of winning as the trust of a university graduate or a corporate high-flyer?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If she still stays resilient all the way through, and if she still maintains her high trust in our system despite every trouble she has endured, is that not more of a testament of strength on her part, rather than ours?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And should she lose trust in our system, whose job will it be to help her find it again?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not believe the answer is the Government alone.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The hardest answer is that it is all of us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It always has been, and it always will be.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They say you become an adult the first time you realise that nothing is truly free and everything worthy comes at a price.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We just seldom want to be the one footing the bill.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In every request for a right, there is always a correlated offer of responsibility.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is easier to say moving words about the equal rights we want every Singaporean to have, than to say the challenging words about the equal responsibilities those rights do require every Singaporean to take on.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But if we who request for those rights are not prepared to take on some measure of the correlated responsibilities demanded of us − through taxes, donations or volunteering − then our request feels that much less honest and much less powerful.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, just as much as I wish for the state to stay open to radical solutions, I also see we the people have to stay equally open to the radical responsibilities that those solutions may place on us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We need more open and honest conversations on that front.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: American author Ursula Le Guin wrote a provocative little parable called "The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In that story, an unnamed narrator guides us through the fantastical city of Omelas, taking us on a dizzying tour of the city's amazing technology and wonderful people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But the journey takes a dark turn when we are led down into a basement tucked beneath this beautiful city.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Imprisoned in that basement is a weak and wretched child.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And the narrator tells us to accept that, in some mysterious way, should this child ever be set free, the whole city's success will be utterly compromised.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are asked to accept that all the freedoms the many enjoy above is wholly and inarguably dependent on the oppression of the one beneath.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And the most disturbing part about Omelas' secret is that it is not a secret.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are told that every citizen there who comes of age has been ushered into this very room to see the truth for themselves.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Though all get upset, most eventually accept that life is just about terrible trade-offs.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The tale ends on a mixed note, talking about a small handful of citizens who choose to walk silently away from the city, towards an unknown destination that the narrator warns may not even exist.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The story is disturbing because everyone who reads it knows instinctively how true to life that story is for every city in the world.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Every city has a child in the basement and a nagging feeling that they all share in the complicity of keeping that child there.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have always wondered whether the narrator of the story was meant to be an unreliable narrator, pushing out a narrative that deserves to be challenged.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When I think about the parallels to Singapore, I see narratives that need to be constantly questioned, rather than casually accepted as sacrosanct.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We do not know without engaging in honest conversation with everyone, especially the ones who respectfully but deeply disagree with us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They are done with trusting, done with trying and done with the heartbreak of putting up with those who passively accept the unfairness.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They may still be here in body but, in spirit, they are already walking away from their Omelas.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know how and, certainly, I know I sound naive, but I will always hope that we can be that country where more of us are able to say to the ones who walk away: "Stay.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And permit me to share what I see as well".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because in a world threatening to grow apart, our small city needs more ones who walk towards than ones who walk away, more than ever.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The ones who dare to go where few want to go − towards one another, towards the conflicts, towards the problems, towards the solutions and, most profoundly, towards the children in the basement who still long to be free.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such prudence in our fiscal management has served us well and will ensure that we will have sufficient resources to tide us over future downturns.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The most notable feature of this Budget is the line-up of initiatives to transform our economy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These measures are expected, coming on the heels of the recommendations by CFE.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am heartened that we are taking bold and swift steps to prepare for the changes new technologies will bring.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fortunately, numerous clarifications since the announcement have helped to reduce public anxiety.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The feedback I have received from many residents has been quite encouraging.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They do accept that a 30% increase after 17 years is not unreasonable.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They support our efforts to be self-sufficient in water.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are also aware of how expensive water processing technology and infrastructure can be.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What they did not like is that there were no prior public consultations about the increase.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such discussions would have provided the opportunity for the people to share ideas about water conservation and sources of funding for water infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While price increases are never welcomed, periodic increments with justifications shared in advance would be preferable to a sudden jump.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This incident highlights the importance of good public communication.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need a better approach for communication between the Government and the public.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How well we communicate new policies and measures will affect the level of support and cooperation we receive from the public, especially for those which affect our daily lives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent years, our Ministries have held many public consultation exercises on a wide range of issues with success.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Valuable inputs from stakeholders and the public help shape our policies and legislation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such dialogues also build trust and goodwill, which the Government will need to draw upon for unpalatable but necessary policies in the future.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A similar exercise for water would have been useful.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their profit margins are low and any assistance will be very much appreciated.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Rental rebates also mean that they will not have to pass on as much of the cost increases to their customers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the new model of having social enterprises like NTUC Foodfare manage our hawker centres has made some progress in keeping the prices of certain food affordable, this remains limited to some basic dishes in these hawker centres and I believe more can be done to reduce overhead costs for the hawkers through some form of rental rebates.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to speak on behalf of a group close to my heart − the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we set about restructuring our economy, we must bear in mind that whatever changes we make, we must continue to make an effort to consider the impact on our senior citizens and ensure that they are accommodated in our plans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Coming back to the topic of better communication between the Government and the people, seniors used to joke that the answers to their queries at Government departments always start with "www" − the website addresses which the staff shared helpfully, or so they thought.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have learnt since then that we need to reach out to our elderly through more interactive ways.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Making adjustments to accommodate our seniors is a signature of a caring society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another example of an area where improvements can be made to be more elderly friendly would be our Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last week, I witnessed a horrific incident when a senior, who had difficulty walking, was going through the door of a train car.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It closed on her hands while she was holding onto her trolley.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Her trolley was out on the platform while her hands were stuck in between the doors inside the train.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Luckily, the doors opened and she rushed out, very pale and very frightened.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How about designating a train car for the elderly, disabled and commuters with children in prams?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Able-bodied passengers will be allowed to use it but priority will be reserved for the less ambulant.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The train car should be the one nearest to the platform lift when it stops and have seats in a loud and contrasting colour, for example, ang pow red, to signal its function.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This car will be an additional service to our current priority seats.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If possible, a staff can be stationed on the platform nearest to this car so that he or she can provide assistance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This staff can also provide instructions to other passengers when necessary and help enforce order and security on the platform.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, we should try to build flexible, adaptable structures which can accommodate the elderly since this is a rapidly growing group.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The speed at which we are developing today can be intimidating for our elderly, particularly older women who are considering rejoining the workforce.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is typical behaviour for many homemakers who are used to putting the needs and wants of their family members above their own.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since they have already embraced personal responsibility in picking up new skills, let us help them by lowering the barriers to learning as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am now on a personal quest to persuade more of the elderly in my constituency to pick up courses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not all of them see the need to.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not easy to convince some of them that learning is good for their mental and emotional health and would enhance their quality of life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the process, they may find their calling in certain areas of the care sector and want to develop further in these areas, carving out a new career in the process.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These personnel will help to fill up the manpower shortage in the sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Both companies have been viewed as disruptors in their sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would be good if they would consider giving back to the community through volunteer services, such as driving vulnerable seniors to and back from hospitals or dialysis centres.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is already done by taxi companies, such as ComfortDelgro, that have programmes in place to provide ferrying services for the elderly and the disabled.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: He also said that, "It is critical that we take decisive action to reposition ourselves for the future.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The title of my speech is "SAFEcare" which stands for Smart Ageing and Future Enabling care, through technology and preventive medicine.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: As the Finance Minister said: "Our needs are growing.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Our population is ageing, families are smaller and our social needs are more complex." There is thus an urgent need to consider an innovative way, with the help of technology, for preventive healthcare to keep disability away for as long as possible.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will ensure seniors improve their lives with graceful living, especially at the later stages, when their needs are at a peak.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: He also said that the healthcare spending will continue to rise as our population ages.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is according to a report by Marsh and McLennan.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This estimate also assumes that there will be continued ready access to cheap foreign labour, which may not be the case in the future.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: So, going forward, how do we care for our seniors better and at the same time reduce this steep cost curve?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The concept I am suggesting is based on the tenet of prevention is better than cure.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In this instance, it means it is better to prevent mobility difficulty and maintain independence, rather than treating the disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, it is better to prevent fall and getting fractures, or having uncontrolled hypertension and getting strokes, rather than curing the fractures and strokes to gain back independence.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The purpose is to facilitate independent living for the seniors, till ripe old age, in their usual dwelling places, without having to be admitted to nursing homes, community or acute hospitals.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Presently, this is the only option available for many, although not all of them require the intensive nursing care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a pity, as it is not making wise use of our limited resources, which are increasingly expensive.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many older adults express the desire to age-in-place for as long as possible.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, the aim is to enable seniors to age gracefully in their own homes despite their frailty or medical conditions by preventing disability and to better manage disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: How do we prevent disability among our seniors?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The most common causes of disability among older adults are chronic diseases, injuries, mental impairment and visual impairment.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Physical activities and keeping active can make our seniors stronger and lower their chances of falling, reducing fractures and injuries that result in disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is never too late to exercise even for seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The good control of chronic diseases, such as hypertension and diabetes, can prevent disability, such as stroke, and regular eye check-ups for seniors can diagnose cataracts and other visual impairments for early treatment.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Facilitating social wellness to seniors helps prevent mental illness, such as depression, that can cause disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: All the above should be practised as early as possible before disability sets in.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The use of medical technology is the way forward.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Technology-assisted centralised-control health monitoring can be deployed to check on the well-being of seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These monitors can screen many seniors for hypertension, pulse rate or heart rate, temperature and so on from seniors wearing medical technology wristbands.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Monitoring devices using advanced sound event technology and long-range passive infrared motion sensors to detect abnormal sounds and motions inside the house are useful for detecting falls at home.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Remote monitoring systems allow the care required by seniors to be significantly reduced, alerting caregivers to intervene early when necessary.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The ideal scenario is to have one central monitor overseeing hundreds if not thousands of residents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The main aim is to have good preventive medicine in detecting emergency health conditions and preventing disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Information technology can ensure a realtime flow of data between care recipients and providers and make administration, record keeping and reporting of data more efficient.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: More collaborative partnerships with Institutes of Higher Learning can be forged to develop new technology, while researching and developing cost-effective systems that promote age-friendly living environment in homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In embracing technology, over time, it will be increasingly beneficial and affordable, when more advanced technology is launched with more competition in the market.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: A living environment that embraces accessible design and fosters independent living can make a difference in terms of a good quality of life for seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The suggestion is to help seniors overcome their intrinsic disability through either the removal of environmental barriers or the provision of environmental modifications.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The environmental hazards at home are situated about 60% in the bathrooms and 40% in the other rooms.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Common hazards are the absence of grab bars in the bathrooms, dim lighting, slippery tiles, and absence of kitchen work surface at a height suitable for sitting and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The use of smart technology is useful for a safe kitchen that will help seniors to function with automatic turn-off for stoves and other electrical appliances.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, modifications and adaptations of the home environment or elderly-smart home for those with disability, according to the individual's need, will improve functional ability-related outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Environmental modifications are particularly important for those living alone.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, those living alone with no family members to depend on are the ones who usually require nursing homes when they face disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Living alone per se may not be such a bad thing.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: According to one study, of the seniors aged 85 and older who were found to be in excellent health, one in five or 20% lived by themselves.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: What is the best avenue to practise "SAFEcare" through smart technology and preventive medicine?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The main aim is to enable seniors to continue living on their own with graduated daily living assistance according to their frailty and keeping residents independent for as long as possible with the prevention of long-term disability by preventing the causes as mentioned earlier.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In these instances, the daily service delivery accessibility is important, as this will provide better management of service delivery and resources, such as helpers, nurses and doctors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For this, accessibility to as many seniors as possible will be ideal.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Cluster housing concept where many seniors live in the same block of flats is one example.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Seniors live on their own in 1- or 2-room flats in such clusters.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will be better for planning and prompt delivery of services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will also facilitate companionship for residents with their neighbours.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: A team of several helpers will be able to provide daily living assistance, where necessary, such as food delivery, cleaning of the homes or bathing for the very frail seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Some may only need such daily assistance during short-term illnesses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Nurses can assist in monitoring the well-being of the residents in such blocks of flats.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The nurses can help to monitor the seniors' medical conditions and to refer them for early treatment when necessary before disability sets in.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These conditions may include uncontrolled hypertension and diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We can build new HDB flats with the above concept or we can also modify and convert more HDB rental homes or the present 14 senior group homes, or some of the studio apartments with the above concept as and when the need increases.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead of using the whole high-rise blocks, using the lower half of the blocks will suffice for ease of service delivery.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The upper floors of flats can still be used for younger families and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The ground floors of such flats should cater for community services, for example, senior activity centres to enable those well seniors to come down daily for physical, social and mental wellness to prevent disability and to monitor their chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This venue also serves as a coordinating centre, enabling concept partners like the grassroots organisations, voluntary welfare organisations and various corporations to volunteer their services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is the concept of the many-helping-hands approach in the community.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Since we are starting the PAP Community Foundation (PCF) Sparkle Care centres to cater to the more dependent seniors, it will be good to plan such concept homes hand in hand with Sparkle Care in the same vicinity.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides focusing on building more nursing homes, perhaps MOH will consider my above proposal of smart cluster homes through technology and preventive medicine as a cost-effective alternative but, more importantly, to enable our seniors to remain in their own homes and to have better living.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: How do we cushion the dependence cost curve impact?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is through preventive medicine to keep our seniors as healthy for as long as possible, and the use of technology to mitigate the manpower needs to enable independent living as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The Finance Minister provided Enabling Masterplan 3 to support persons with disabilities and their caregivers in this Budget.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In view of the urgency of our ageing population, will the Finance Minister provide another Enabling Masterplan to provide for seniors with disability next?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope the Finance Minister would consider my "SAFEcare" or Smart Ageing and Future Enabling care favourably and to improve the lives of our seniors and helping them to age gracefully.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, let me deliver my speech in English and later in Malay.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, let me express my appreciation to the Finance Minister for the delivery of Budget 2017.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is a Budget that I consider as targeted at ensuring continued employment and employability for our citizens by helping to keep our SMEs afloat and sustainable in this choppy and uncertain economic trend and yet, preparing the nation for the long-term challenges as recommended by CFE.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While I applaud the various measures and "goodies" that have been suggested, I would also like to highlight the worrying trend on the rate of job redundancies that has occurred in 2016.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While this can be considered as small in percentage, it also means that the same number would have lost their income stream, which also means that the same number of families is now being impacted.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What would this mean if we are to relate it socially?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What does it mean to those families who have school-going children?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: How will this impact us in the next 10 years, or will this, at all, have any impact?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The biggest question is: what does it mean when someone loses a job today and, 10 years later, what will that be?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Before I proceed further, please allow me to share and relate the experiences which I gained whilst I was serving as a Board Member of the Association of Muslim Professionals (AMP) on many of the community activities there.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Many social issues which the Malay/Muslim community faced then and now, can be traced back to dysfunctional families as one of the several main root causes.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Be it issues related to drugs, underperformance in academic studies, juvenile delinquency or even teenage pregnancy, and many more, one of the main root causes will often, more than not, stem from dysfunctional families.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The more unstable the financial position of the family is, the higher the correlation to dysfunctional family will be.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The difficult part with regard to this phenomenon is time.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The whole process leading to the social problems is usually a long one.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: When a family becomes financially unstable which can lead to social problems may take many years.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The impact can only be seen much later in time.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: When this process starts and ends with a social problem, then a new vicious social problem cycle exists and even starts, unless we intervene.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Simply said, a family with a sound and stable financial position will have a better chance to be not dysfunctional, hence will also mean a higher chance to stay out of the social problems, hence lower social issues.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As such, being employed and staying employed are the best assurances to keep our social problems at bay.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I guess you do not have to be a rocket scientist to understand this.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, in our quest to eradicate, if not, minimise problems, it is best to ensure high employment as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And I am sure this sentiment is also strongly shared by Minister Lim Swee Say, I believe.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The less social problem we have, the healthier we are as a nation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Of particular concern are the middle- and low-income segments, which the Malay/Muslim community is a big part of.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While I appreciate the slew of schemes and programmes that MOF and MOM have taken and embarked on, this may not be sufficient to circumvent the problems that it may entail.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, anecdotally, it is said that there are not many Malay/Muslim clients who have come forward to MOM, after being retrenched, to seek help in finding new jobs, or even for advice to take up the various schemes and programmes that MOM has to offer.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It could be due to many factors which led to this phenomenon.
