speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Understandably, this is logical as it is quite normal that a person's self-esteem is negatively affected after such an experience, which may make him to react as such.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, I believe that the affected worker may be open to engagement to his or her own community organisation like AMP, Majlis Pendidikan Anak-Anak Islam (MENDAKI), Persatuan Pemudi Islam Singapura (PPIS) or Jamiyah.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I guess they may be more comfortable to relate and be advised on the available options which MOM has to offer.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I would like to suggest the following idea.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The chosen or appointed MMOs can play an important role in trying to ensure that the affected workers can be counselled and engaged so as to try to have them back in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This work must be done in conjunction with MOM.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As such, MOM will have a kind of mini-MOM at the various VWOs and SHGs.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, we can expect a better outreach to the affected workers or PMETs, with the objective of placing them back in the workforce as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to express my concern on the uncertain and worrying economic outlook in the coming years in 2017 and 2018.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is very important to look at the impact on families when a person had the misfortune of losing his job.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is very likely that this will affect the family's finances and stability and, hence, will result in a situation that is both significant and worrying.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The bigger impact is the likelihood that this will result in social problems, for instance, dysfunctional families, drugs, youth issues, children borne out of wedlock and so on.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This phenomenon was observed in a short research conducted by AMP in 2015.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This process will take place over a relatively long period of time.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the impact of job loss is very serious and can haunt us in the long run.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In order to eradicate the possible social problems that may arise, it is imperative for us to ensure that every individual who lost their jobs is helped and be able to rejoin the workforce as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This will ensure that their financial situation will remain stable.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We can, therefore, avoid the undesirable social problems that may appear in the future.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: These Malay/Muslim bodies can play a role as agents of MOM and help those who are affected.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, the involvement of the self-help groups or VWOs and MMOs is a very important step in dealing with our social problems.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support Budget 2017.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Azmoon, I just want to assure you that the Senior Minister State for Finance Ms Indranee Rajah takes cognisance of the points made in your speech as well.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First of all, I would like to say that I am very happy to see Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat back in the Chamber delivering his Budget Speech.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The past year must have been difficult for him and his family and I wish him good health for many years ahead.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we have to accept that as a developed economy with labour force constraints, our target long-term growth of between 2% and 3% will be slower than what we have experienced in the past.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Against a backdrop of slower growth and thus flat Government revenue, our spending on infrastructure, health and social support has increased and will continue to increase significantly, especially as the Baby Boomer generation is reaching their 60s and 70s.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over the past few years, we have also introduced and strengthened various social support schemes, all of which are necessary and welcomed by residents.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The truth is that our overall expenditures will continue to grow with an ageing population and we have to prepare for it.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a responsible and prudent Government, we must maintain a balanced Budget and ensure that the Government's revenue can match the increasing social and health spending as our population ages.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Minister Heng mentioned in his speech, we may have to raise revenues through new taxes or raise tax rates in future to meet the rising domestic expenditure needs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On this front, I would like to talk about our stamp duties related to residential properties, which I believe there is room for us to be more progressive.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Buyers of residential properties are required to pay Buyer's Stamp Duty.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is also Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD), which was introduced in December 2011 and revised upwards in January 2013 to cool the residential market.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, I would like to suggest replacing ABSD with a tiered Buyer's Stamp Duty.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that the objective of ABSD is to moderate demand for residential properties and to promote a stable and sustainable property market.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because the ABSD scheme is seen as a cooling measure, it is viewed as a temporary measure which will be removed when the market has indeed softened.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But we always run the risk that the property market may spike up when ABSD is removed.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: ABSD for non-citizens should remain but be adjusted to take into account the revised tiering of Buyer's Stamp Duty.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As it stands, the rates for Buyer's Stamp Duty are computed on the purchase price or market value of the property, whichever is higher.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Stamp duty payable for amounts above $360,000 is 3%.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the higher threshold of $1 million, I believe this will not significantly affect most middle-income families and HDB upgraders.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would also be similar to having ABSD of 7% on top of the current Buyer's Stamp Duty of 3%.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This change would also be seen as a permanent change to the stamp duty structure rather than the current ABSD scheme which is seen as a temporary scheme.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, if a residential property is held under a special purpose vehicle (SPV), and if the SPV is transferred from seller to buyer, normal residential stamp duty is not payable.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because the registered owner of the residential property still remains as the SPV and does not change.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think this is an anomaly which needs to be addressed since, for all intents and purposes, the beneficial interest of the property has changed hands.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this type of situation, not only does the buyer of the SPV avoid paying Buyer's Stamp Duty and Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty, he also avoids paying Seller's Stamp Duty, which would have been payable if the new buyer then flips out the underlying residential properties within the four-year period.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most of the time, transactions of such nature are carried out by property developers and property investment companies, and this change is unlikely to affect individual buyers and sellers of residential properties.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, the nature of such stamp duties is that they are discretionary in nature, as buyers and sellers already know the stamp duties payable beforehand and would have a choice of whether to enter into the property transaction.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that with these additional revenue sources, we will not need to increase other taxes which may impact low- to middle-income families.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I think I speak for everyone in this House when I say that perhaps the best thing about this year's Budget Speech was to see it being delivered by Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans want to be the best at whatever we do and strive hard to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is that drive that has brought us this far and will take us further.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But I wonder if this almost instinctive need to compete, to be the best, has come at the expense of graciousness, compassion and kindness.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It seems to me that the more achievements and accolades we collect as a country, the harder we drive ourselves.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is a relentless drive for excellence that, in my view, has some Singaporeans climbing up the scale of increasing ungraciousness.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: How else can we even begin to understand ungracious behaviour that has become everyday experiences?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There are people who now drive against the flow of traffic on Singapore roads, block your way out of a lift or MRT train and complain about everything – from the noise that kids make playing football to harmless neighbourhood chickens that remind us of our kampongs.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And we must surely be one of the few countries in the world where a car indicator signal to change lanes almost always results in other drivers who speed up to prevent you from making that switch.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We are not short on daily anecdotes of ungracious behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We just seem to be short on patience, courtesy and kindness.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I am not quite sure that we are succeeding.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have made tremendous achievements as a country along the political and economic fronts in those two decades.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Can we say the same for our social development as a gracious society?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Graciousness is a building block of a strong community and is as important as productivity, resilience and all those other qualities that define us as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Research has shown, many times, that attention to the social development of a community results in deeper bonds, improved health and a culture of paying it forward.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Key social values, such as graciousness, compassion and kindness will help address issues, such as the unity of our society, our attitudes toward the elderly and the development of our youth − all crucial factors in achieving the goals set out in Budget 2017.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Some in this House may find it surprising that I have never felt like a minority in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, it is true, and it is not because I am delusional as I am fully aware that the Indians are a minority in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But the reason I have never felt like a minority is because of a life lesson I learned in an HDB lift when I was about five years old.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: My mother had been walking me home from kindergarten to our 1-room rented flat in Margaret Drive.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We lived on the seventh floor and had entered the lift to go up.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The two middle-aged Chinese women in the lift immediately pinched their noses as soon as my mother and I entered the lift.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I tugged at my mum's saree and wanted to know what was going on.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: She gave me a look that said "Keep quiet and behave", so I stayed silent.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When we got out of the lift, I asked my mother why the women had pinched their noses.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Someone had spilt something in the lift and it was very smelly." I insisted that there had been no such smell in the lift, to which she replied that it was probably because I had been hiding under her saree.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: That incident took place about 45 years ago and her graciousness in the face of deliberate prejudice taught me a life lesson I will never forget.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It shaped my deep appreciation for diversity and understanding in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Consequently, my childhood was spent running in and out of my neighbours' flats along the common corridor.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I grew up thinking we were all the same − it did not matter whether we were Malay, Indian, Chinese or Eurasian.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And I suspect that a lot of us from that generation grew up in similar communities.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, when the Government introduced the Elected Presidency Bill late last year, I had thought that most Singaporeans would, like me, share similar views.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The ethnicity of the President does not matter to me as long as he or she is qualified for the role and deserved to be there.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, I soon realised after attending a few community dialogue sessions that the Singapore of today is very different from the one that I grew up in.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I was shocked that the community that I belonged to had some serious and deep prejudices about sub-communities within the group, perceived divisions carved along the different dialects spoken.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has made great progress in fostering unity in the community and continues to take the lead.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But surely, the rest of the unity-building must be undertaken by members of the community.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Parents must still be the main role models for children to learn about graciousness and understanding.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Our young learn from us and it is vital now, more than ever, that we step up and behave in a manner befitting citizens of a proudly multi-racial society.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We live in an age where the world is becoming more polarised, and communities and countries are becoming more inward-looking.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's strength and resilience as a nation has always centred on our multi-racial unity.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This foundation will be crucial as the nation moves into the next phase of rapid development.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We will welcome more and more new Singaporeans and friends of Singapore who will join us in our transition to the economy of the future.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We will need to give them time to adapt and understand our norms and the values we hold dear.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We will need to be gracious, compassionate and kind, as was my mother all those years ago.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We are an ageing population and we stand on the shoulders of those who came before us.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The logic behind this thinking is that, for a fraction of the cost, a young worker can actually take on a lot more than an older worker leading to a perception of increased productivity.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: A few years ago when a local telco launched its digital television service, as with any new service, there were teething problems.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: On two separate occasions, rather young and inexperienced technicians were sent to my home.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: On both occasions, after several hours, the technicians could not resolve the problem.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: On the third try, I asked the telco to send someone a little more senior, someone with experience, to help resolve the matter.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They sent me a senior gentleman in his early 60s.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He sorted out the issue in less than 15 minutes and even gave me his personal handphone number so that I could call him if I encountered any further issues.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This senior technician had about six months to go before retirement and wanted to continue working.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: These attitudes are prevalent in other industries, too.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In the local media industry, we see a diminishing representation of experienced anchors and veteran journalists.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: On international cable networks, we watch Christiane Amanpour, Wolf Blitzer, Richard Quest and natural historian Sir David Attenborough − who is in his 90s now, many of us have followed them for decades.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They have paid their dues and earned their credibility.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When they give an opinion, it is backed by decades of experience and stories.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we seem to be losing experienced talent, both in front and behind the camera, as well as in print newsrooms.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The common comment I get from international media colleagues is that the newsrooms in Singapore are very "young".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While there is need for a balance in the composition of the newsrooms, I do wonder, as do many older Singaporeans, if we might have a better representation of experienced news anchors and journalists.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We may have an ageing population, but that does not mean that we should hide them away from public view.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Earlier this year, Minister for Education (Schools) Mr Ng Chee Meng spoke to The Straits Times about his journey in his life from fighter pilot to Cabinet Minister.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There was one particular phrase the Minister used which caught my attention − and the attention of many others, too.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He used the colloquial term "chiong", and urged students to "dare to 'chiong'".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Loosely translated, what this means is to go after opportunities and to make the most of opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, the Minister explained at length that "chionging", and I quote, "was about breaking boundaries, creating value and having that x-factor".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Sadly though, we seem to have created a system of "chiong kings" − people who "chiong" at all costs − at the expense of important values like empathy, graciousness and compassion.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: For a lot of parents, "chionging" means winning at all costs.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This is not a bad trait if children are also taught how to moderate the amount of "chionging" because what we want to hire in industry are people who are both independent workers and team players.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The key to tempering this over-enthusiastic drive to be the best is for parents and schools to ensure an equal emphasis on graciousness and compassion.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The signal must be sent that gracious and compassionate behaviour are as important as good grades and impressive CCAs, for it is these values that will ultimately guide them through their adulthood and careers.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There is much that Singaporeans have to be thankful for.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, these days, thanks to social media, as a society, all we seem to be doing is to complain and criticise.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Social media has created a community of self-styled "experts" in crisis management − individuals who seem to be waiting in the wings to freely offer their opinions on everything from politics to PR, from sports to poultry.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While some of the commentary has been constructive, much has been conjecture and assumptions that are not necessarily based on facts.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: These opinions and comments are shared and repeated often enough on social media that they become the "truth" in the eyes of many.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Social media, of course, was rife with criticisms and even comparisons to governments of a bygone era, completely ignorant of the current state of geopolitics in the world.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Much of the vitriol might have been predicated on an arrogance stemming from a history of accelerated development and success.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, what we needed from social media was balance, a sense of gratitude and support for the way in which the Government dealt with the issue.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It has become almost unfashionable to credit the Government on a job well done.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It would be a shame if this self-defeating sentiment continues.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Remember that the person you are criticising and abusing is someone's father, mother, son, daughter, brother or sister.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Put yourself in their shoes − how would you or your family feel if it were you who was being abused online, or your photo shared without reservation?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans have much to be thankful for and even more to look forward to the in future if we can embrace these virtues.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yesterday, the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources gave various reasons for the water hike.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The justifications, such as increased cost of production, the need to build more desalination plants and so on, did not come up suddenly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the last 17 years that the water price was unchanged, did it not cross the Government's mind before this year that it would want to raise the price of water?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This lead time is welcome, as it will enable businesses and consumers to prepare, such as by strategising and investing in energy-efficient measures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to water, why was it not possible to prepare Singaporeans for the increase to take effect in July this year, with an announcement similarly two years ahead of time − in July 2015?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, July 2015 was not a good time to make such as announcement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Few people would quarrel with the need to invest more in healthcare and infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our healthcare system is still facing capacity shortages, as seen from the 20-hour waiting times for beds at certain public hospitals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I understand that the waiting time at some hospitals providing Long-Term Acute Care are indefinite.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for infrastructure, Singaporeans will benefit from a more comprehensive rail network, which will hopefully ease traffic congestion and provide more efficient connectivity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One legitimate question to ask, however, is whether there is an effective mechanism to assess whether expenditure that has been incurred has been effective in achieving desired outcomes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Take, for example, the Productivity and Innovation Credit Scheme (PIC) introduced in 2010.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe the Government's intention was to design an inclusive scheme, with less red tape, which would be easy for businesses to access.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that businesses are supportive of the PIC scheme, but for various reasons, not necessarily related to productivity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But now that the scheme has run for some years, how effective has the PIC scheme been in achieving its aim of boosting productivity?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The PIC is a huge scheme, with the Government putting in billions of public funds.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Do we know whether the results were worth the huge cost?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As it turned out, millions of dollars were also sucked out of the system through fraudulent or dubious PIC claims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We now read that the SkillsFuture Scheme launched just last year, has also been subject to a potential fraud of $2.2 million, already paid out.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I understand that designing a scheme is not a simple process, what lessons have we learnt in order to minimise such wastages of public funds?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This year, the Committee for the Future Economy (CFE) has come up with seven broad strategies to tackle the challenges ahead.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Minister Iswaran took us on a tour on some of the key thrusts on Monday.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have also had such committees to review our economic strategies in the past.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Have we had any review of what had worked in the past and what had not?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in 2010, we had the Economic Strategies Committee (ESC).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The ESC had made recommendations to improve productivity which the Government accepted and implemented.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, after seven years, productivity improvements are way off target and weak in domestically oriented sectors like retail and food & beverage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And can these lessons be applied to the CFE's strategies?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They called for greater accountability on the outcomes of public spending, which they thought was necessary before the need for additional revenues and new and higher taxes should be called for.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the roundtable organised by the Economic Society of Singapore, SIM University economist, Dr Walter Theseira, made the following observation, "Every few years, we have a big transformation package.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We spend a few hundred million dollars here, a billion dollars there on different kinds of programmes, but we never really found out years later whether those programmes were any good or not." Since the Government looks to the people to raise funds for such expenditures, public accounting of the outcomes of spending is warranted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I raised this matter during the Budget debate 10 years ago and I am glad that other Members also see the pertinence of raising this question in this year's Budget debate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Economists have recently also revived this question in their current discussions on Singapore's fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the time I made my speech 10 years ago, the revenue from land sales was in the region of $4 billion to $5 billion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Tapping on land sales to fund annual Budgets is internationally accepted and practised by other governments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As our expenditures are expected to rise in the coming years, is it not reasonable to seriously think about utilising land sales revenue to fund the Budget?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will reduce the need to tax the people further.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, I would like to touch on four topics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, the need to maintain a strong defence budget in light of the growing tide of nationalism in countries around the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, the need to support workers to transition from one type of career to an altogether different type of job scope on account of changing growth sectors in the economy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is heartening that, despite the challenging economic outlook, we are maintaining a strong defence budget.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just a few weeks ago, Singapore was remembering the 75th Anniversary of the fall of Singapore into the hands of the Japanese.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The pain that the Japanese Occupation brought to many is still fresh in the memories of our pioneer Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since the birth of Singapore as a sovereign nation, spending on defence has always been one of our top priorities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Defence planning continues to be important as the very existence of Singapore's sovereignty as a nation depends on it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thus far, Singapore has enjoyed exceptional defence relations with many countries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, Singapore's forces have been able to train overseas in countries, such as Brunei, France, United States, India, South Africa, Indonesia, Canada, Australia, Germany and in other skies and fields.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This allows Singapore's forces to test their mettle and manoeuvres in a wider area − something that is difficult with Singapore's space constraints.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not only does this stand as testament to Singapore and Australia's close defence ties, but it also allows Singapore to have yet another terrain to train in.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must regard the defence of Singapore as a priority.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This means allocating a strong and healthy fiscal budget for defence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The recent growing tide of nationalism around the world provides a clear signal that Singapore and the Government must continue investing in the protection of our sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, in Parliament, we should continue to press for and secure a strong defence budget.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Europe, there has been a rise in nationalism and anti-globalism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In France, Ms Marine Le Pen's nationalistic party is gaining popularity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Germany, the Alternative for Germany party has increased in popularity in recent times and is reported to have attracted voters who are "anti-establishment, anti-liberalisation, anti-European, anti-everything that has come to be regarded as the norm".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not an isolated movement, but one that has pockets of trends around the globe.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Growing tides of nationalism across the globe must prompt Singapore to muscle up its defence capabilities to ensure our sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Singapore, there have been plans to enhance Lim Chu Kang for military training purposes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The plans for the new urban training facility include featuring high-rise buildings, complex road networks, an MRT station and a bus interchange.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Simulation technology is also increasingly used in training.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With such political climates around the world, such initiatives are timely and necessary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important that we maintain a strong defence budget, and I am heartened that we are doing so.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should maintain this even if we enter lean economic times.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is necessary to support workers to transition from one type of career to an altogether different type of job scope on account of changing growth sectors in the economy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lucrative industries in the past no longer pay as much today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, the oil, gas and marine industries in Singapore went through − and continue to go through − a very competitively tough environment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When industries slow down, ripple effects are felt across the economy, including the finance and banking sector.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have met with residents in the constituency I serve, who have, unfortunately, lost good paying jobs in the marine industry.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Freelance or temporary contract work becomes options for them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unfortunately, as a result, they face a large pay reduction and no CPF employer's contribution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a tough position to be in.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, the drive to assist these workers − from presently vulnerable industries, such as oil, gas and marine − to reskill and get employed in permanent jobs is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will allow the laid-off worker to chart his employment path in a more permanent second career instead of relying on temporary contract jobs to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To reduce the hindrances to reskilling, the focus will be on providing short, modular, e-learning opportunities to upskill and retrain.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This increases the flexibility so that learning and upskilling becomes easier and more a part of life.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Eventual consequence is more potential job openings for reskilled and resilient workers who seek to move from vulnerable industries to enterprises where the sun is rising.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I move to my third and penultimate point, Madam, that of social mobility.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ensuring social mobility of Singaporeans is a precious ideal and a worthy aim − it is a constant work in progress.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important for Singaporeans, and critical for a cohesive society, that all Singaporeans are presented with a wide menu of opportunities to excel.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When in the constituency, I am so happy when I meet residents who decide to purchase a 2- or 3-room HDB flat instead of continuing to rent their flats at subsidised rentals from HDB.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is a classic example of social mobility − from non-ownership to home ownership.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a considerably larger financial commitment but it is always good to see that with a steady income, CPF contributions and a HDB loan, residents decide to own their first major asset − a home.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is the Singapore way and we must preserve it, nurture it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Education plays an important role in catalysing and fuelling social mobility.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to continue to provide Singaporeans with opportunities, especially at an early stage of their lives.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is good that we start early with pre-school, providing affordable, accessible pre-school for children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This year, we are investing into increasing the infrastructure of our pre-school sector at an even earlier stage − infant care.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This accommodates an increased demand for centre-based infant care.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This helps ensure that Singaporeans, even at an early stage, are given a wholesome menu of opportunities allowing the potential for social mobility to commence early.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To provide a wide a range of learning opportunities throughout a child's schooling life, MOE could help ensure the fair distribution of very good teachers across all schools.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is an excellent move and one that is important to young couples who are planning to get married or wanting to start a family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For young couples commencing working life, a private property purchase can be very financially daunting.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This new HDB resale grant provides young couples with the real possibility of owning a more affordable first property more quickly and quite possibly near their parents.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would mean that when the parents happily become grandparents, the precious and necessary support will be close by.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, there are many merits to these new resale grants.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Before I close, Madam, I would just like to share that I was in the House and had the opportunity to listen to the hon Ms Sylvia Lim's speech just moments ago.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: She seems to be supporting the Workers' Party position that it is good to not have carbon tax introduced so quickly, yet it is not good to introduce the tax on water quickly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I respect that she is entitled to her views but I am afraid, Madam, I cannot agree with those views.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For carbon tax, the history was that once we ratify the Paris Agreement, we have to reaffirm commitment to address climate change and reduce emissions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is actually quite a long runway in order to implement what we need to implement to honour the ratification.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The issue of carbon tax affects all countries, not just Singapore, or not just Singapore and our immediate neighbours.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, a long runway and we can be cautious in how we move ahead, and we have the freedom of time to decide these things.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think water, the Workers' Party's position is why is it so fast, why not take a little bit more time as you have done for carbon tax?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Water is completely in a different pool, if I may say.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There has been an increase in price as demand for water that cost more to produce increases.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to value water, and technology has already been deployed for water and has already been invested in.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think we have heard from both Minister Chan Chun Sing and also Minister Masagos that the Linggiu Dam is twice the size of Singapore, and we need many years to build the water level up again.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also need to take into account climate change.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Budget 2017 advances these ideals and, therefore, merits our support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But I think if he had listened to my speech carefully, the point I was making was that the reasons used by the Government to justify the water price increase have been there for quite some time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Unless he is trying to suggest that these factors only dawned on the Government recently and that is why they had no time to give Singaporeans more warning of the increase.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That is not my understanding of what Ms Sylvia Lim said.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think Ms Sylvia Lim said, "Look, on the one hand, you have a two-year runway or an X number of year runway for carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Why do we not just take a little bit more time for water?" I have explained that they are completely different subjects.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Carbon tax, we have got to look at how our commitment is corralled within an overarching Paris Agreement, and how it impacts all the members who have ratified that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Versus a situation where we have had to deal with a situation where water is precious, it is a commodity, it is scarce and we have to act promptly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We are doing all we can in terms of the 17 reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Again, I go back to Ms Sylvia Lim's point.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Ms Sylvia Lim's point was to compare carbon tax versus water.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think people in this House and people reviewing this debate will say that it is chalk and cheese.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Budget has many good and targeted initiatives to support businesses, in response to the report by the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as we had just experienced our weakest economic growth rate since 2009 and the growth outlook is weak, many are waiting for the Government to share more details about how the economy will achieve the target growth of 2% to 3%.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Where are the growth sectors in the immediate future?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding, I must thank Minister Iswaran for his assurance to the House the day before.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Some residents told me that they could not understand the relevance of the CFE Report.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not everyone can be in the fields of engineering, information technology (IT) or artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, quite a number of residents feel stressed by the advance of disruptive technologies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are totally at a loss about how to stay in the competition, never mind about staying ahead.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They cannot keep up and cannot fill in the gaps in knowledge and skills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are fearful, feel down and left out.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government can step up their efforts to share relatable success stories to motivate them, show them how others have adapted so that they do not have to worry or be fearful, share information about how people have managed transitions and, very importantly, how changes can benefit them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans must recognise that these changes are not threats but opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The fundamentals do not change – for example, robots assist, not replace humans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are concrete developments they can relate to.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, the Government should share more news about how it will pump up the economy and attract more investments.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, the Government can highlight updates about how many more direct and indirect jobs will be generated by Changi Airport Terminal 4 and the other projects in progress.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): We have to make a greater effort to focus on the tangible benefits for workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Success stories about jobseekers benefiting from matches at our National Jobs Bank, our Career Support Programme, Professional Conversions Programme and the Work Trial Programme will also boost the morale of the unemployed and encourage them to enrol and persist in their training.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Periodic updates about the new Attach and Train initiative should be shared in the media to raise awareness of its benefits.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must strive for "a great Singapore: Singaporean is the most preferred choice" for all employers, not only locally but internationally and wherever Singaporeans are.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Singapore Government must continue to invest in all Singaporeans and make every Singaporean the best and most preferred person to employ and work with wherever Singaporeans are in the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Internet has removed many geographical barriers to enable a global market.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, more local companies should think about tapping the bigger global market overseas through e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The number of people making purchases online is increasing exponentially and they do not care where the e-commerce websites are based.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is it possible to compete with Amazon, or Tmall or Taobao?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even though these sites seem to sell almost everything, there are many niche sites out there which are able to build their brands online and secure loyal customer bases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, even as we encourage our companies to venture overseas, the fact is that they are based here in Singapore and our high business cost structure is a problem.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some sectors, like construction, are heavily reliant on foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are limits to how much innovation in construction can help assist to reduce costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As HDB is a major developer, it can consider taking the lead in construction innovation as it is in a position to enjoy economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government share what innovative practices it will be engaging in and what would be the expected savings in terms of costs, manpower and time?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recall meeting a foreign contractor recently and checking with him how the contractor competed in the market.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was particularly struck by the fact that the company was not reliant on the relatively cheaper unskilled labour for their competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A good, experienced, skilled and productive plasterer could produce four times more than an unskilled labourer even though he may be one and a half times more expensive than the unskilled labourer.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, the company could save on unnecessary hidden and unforeseen costs, such as wastage and material costs ,if the job needs to be reworked or improved.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He shared that, in conclusion, cheap is not necessary good, and increased productivity is relatively important in ensuring the competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do share the concern of Singaporeans over the price hike and worry about the impact on the cost of living and business costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even until today, people do still laugh at us for drinking "long kang" water.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Putting aside such remarks, businesses that I spoke to shared that the consequences of not having reliable and sustainable water solutions are far-reaching.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If not solved, it might be worse, and we might lose businesses and investors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Imagine, if we do not have such alternatives, what would be the price Singaporeans would have to pay in the future?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A 60 ml bottle of drinking water usually retails for about 50 cents to about $1 in the supermarket.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It made me puzzled and I could not reconcile it.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I certainly support our move to become even more self-reliant in our water supply through the use of the latest technology.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the cost increase cannot be avoided due to the huge investments required, more efforts should be made to continue to increase the sources of water supply and the use of technology that can help reduce the cost of water production.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should continually remind Singaporeans of the importance of conserving water.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should have more dialogues and discussions about how to motivate Singaporeans to save water.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In short, I believe in incentivising rather than having penalties in promoting water conservation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, in Hong Kong, every household is served by two water pipes − one for potable water and one for non-potable water.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In some areas in Japan, it is common for the toilets to be designed in such a way that used water from wash basins are fed to the flush tanks.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also heartened to note that the Singapore Government has increased the grants for Singaporeans to buy resale flats so that they can live near their parents or working area.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we need to be mindful and remain cautious, and monitor whether such additional grants may end up pushing up the prices of resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, with these grants, resale flats are becoming more attractive.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry share if the prices between BTO and resale flats are narrowing?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened by the announcement that more flats may be built to shorten the waiting time for BTO flat applicants.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My residents have given me positive feedback on this.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will HDB consider increasing the allocation for new BTO flat upgraders or second-timers slightly, cautiously, moderately?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These owners will, in turn, release more resale flats into the market for young couples looking for this option.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are not small amounts, totalling $900 million.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I also appreciate the diversity of opinions from economists and journalists; and heartfelt feedback from Singaporeans and business owners.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The more specific issues that Members have raised will be taken up by my Ministerial colleagues during the Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Mr Liang Eng Hwa observed, the Budget is not an occasion where there will always be many "tasty goodies".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Rather, it is an opportunity for the Government to set out our plans and priorities to work with our people and businesses to bring Singapore forward.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is within the range of 2% to 3% as set out in the CFE report, and is comparable to the performance of many other high income economies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the US, Switzerland and Germany for example, their economies have been growing at about 1% to 2% yearly on average in the last five years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We also remain an attractive investment destination globally.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I think it is a good vote of confidence for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our labour force growth is slowing down because of smaller cohorts entering the workforce and a slowdown in foreign worker inflow.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To counter this, future growth has to come from sustained productivity growth.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We need to help every worker maximise his potential, and support our businesses in innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This will put us in good company among high-income, productive economies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Winds of change are also sweeping across the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many of the favourable conditions that buoyed our growth over the past few decades are now under threat.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: New technology arrives in waves, sometimes with disruptive consequences.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Unlike the 2009 Global Financial Crisis or the 1985 recession, we are not in a crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Nevertheless, the changes we are facing have far-reaching implications.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The best way to address them is to meet them head-on.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many Members, including Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Saktiandi Supaat, have spoken about the pressures on our businesses, especially SMEs, in a time of restructuring.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Notwithstanding the 2% growth in 2016, we recognise that the economy and labour market exhibited uneven performances across different sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some sectors did well and could not fill vacancies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Yet others had to relook their business models due to more fundamental changes in their sector.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We recognise that some businesses are facing cost pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we must also recognise that in a functioning economy, cost pressures serve as price signals, so that resources can be channelled into the most productive use.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must be careful not to hamper this process.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: An across-the-board stimulus would not be effective as it may further push up cost pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, we monitor the situation closely and calibrate the fiscal stance accordingly.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Budget this year strikes a careful balance between reinforcing restructuring efforts and providing support to businesses and households.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Against the current macroeconomic backdrop, the slightly expansionary fiscal stance is appropriate.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There are many Government schemes, as Minister Iswaran pointed out, that benefit businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These are on top of the substantial stimulus measures introduced in the last three to four years, of which their cumulative effects are still working through the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, the Government is providing support, and Minister Iswaran has given a very comprehensive explanation of the range of support from the Government for businesses, especially SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, different firms and different sectors face varying challenges and opportunities and will require different solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are thus giving more targeted and customised help.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For firms that are ready to internationalise, we are providing more help to scale up and go abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For firms that are ready to upgrade their capabilities, they can tap on the Capability Development Grant in a wide range of areas, from raising service standards to adopting technology and staff training.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There are also firms in sectors, such as retail, which are facing structural challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs)are the platform for individual companies to work together with agencies, unions, trade associations and others to restructure, to stay competitive in the new environment.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are also accelerating public sector infrastructure projects to support the construction sector.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is what in Chinese is called "对症下药", or giving the right medicine to cure the ailment.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A painkiller may work for a while to dull the pain, but it masks the underlying problem and delays needed action, or, in Chinese, "治标不治本".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are providing near-term relief, but we do not want to provide only temporary relief.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We want to help our businesses build deep capabilities that will enable them to adapt to a fast-changing world and seize new opportunities where they arise.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And this is the key to continued success.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In Mandarin):   I thank various Members for their suggestions on how to help businesses overcome challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We understand that many companies have been affected by the slowing economy and are hoping for the Government to come up with some near-term measures to give them a helping hand.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In reality, different companies and industries face varying challenges and opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We urge leaders of trade associations and chambers to continue to work closely with the Government and to take the lead in bringing about transformation and innovation amongst their member companies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Only then will companies be able to maintain their competitive edge, seize new business opportunities and succeed in the ever-changing environment.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In English): Let me now touch on building our future economy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When the Prime Minister announced that we will form the CFE, he said, and I quote, "With an ageing population and uncertain global conditions, growth will be harder to come by.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Yet, our economy must grow to create opportunities for Singaporeans and to improve our lives." And, indeed, this is what guides us in the CFE work − to create opportunities for Singaporeans and to improve our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We live in a world undergoing major and rapid structural changes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Shifts in global trade and production patterns are opening up new markets, even as parts of the world appear to be moving towards greater protectionism.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Advances in technology, in particular, digital technology, give us new ways to improve productivity, efficiency and service delivery.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These trends may throw up potential disruptions, but they also bring many new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To seize these opportunities, our businesses and our people need to build deep capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Only with deep capabilities can we thrive in an unpredictable and fast-changing world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our businesses need to digitalise, innovate and internationalise, to create value and bring it to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our people need to continuously learn and re-learn skills, to be entrepreneurial and flexible in adapting to varying circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: All these are brought together in the CFE's recommendations.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is not about different people pulling in different directions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Instead, we need a sense of partnership and collaboration, to work together for economic development and in all areas.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Taken together, the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The way in which the CFE strategies can be brought to life is through two critical elements.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, we need a spirit of enterprise, a willingness to try new things, to seek creative solutions to problems, to venture where few others have gone; an attitude of continually striving, of persevering, of drawing out the best ideas from every individual.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, effective partnerships with one another − between the Government, the community, businesses and individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Together, we will refine our ideas and put them into action.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: By working together and making the most of everyone's abilities, we can achieve more than we will on our own.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To those who are looking for a new blueprint and a plan to follow, let me say that what we need is not a change in strategy, but a strategy for change.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must recognise that we are in a different world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The world is changing, but we do not know for certain the pace and direction of change.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many Members, such as Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Muhamad Faisal, have also noted this uncertainty.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: What we need is not a cast-in-stone roadmap, but a spirit to constantly forge forward and to find a new way forward.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This strategy for change requires a significant shift in mindset.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is a Budget to position us for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Ms Chia Yong Yong has shared, it is time for us to take our own future into our hands.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Structurally, we have always faced constraints as a small nation-state.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But our strength, our enduring strength, has been to break through all of these constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have proven to the world that we can do this time and time again.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are on a journey of transformation together, where success is not an endpoint but an ongoing process of change, as Assoc Prof Randolph Tan put it.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am confident that we will succeed, as one people, on this journey of change.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am confident because I see many positive examples of people, of firms, that have embraced the spirit of enterprise and partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, let me first talk about our people.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our people must be willing to go beyond the familiar and explore new prospects.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, as Mr Ong Teng Koon, Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Kok Heng Leun noted, with rapid changes in technology and business models, job roles will be redefined more often, and new skills will frequently be required.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Chandra used to be a network engineer in a bank.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In 2008, he was retrenched but he persevered and found a network engineer job in a telco.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It was in his new job that Chandra got exposed to a very interesting and growing new field of work with good opportunities: cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Now, he has taken up a new job in cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Yvonne has done different things in her career, including working in the financial sector and helping with her family business.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Through this programme, she is currently taking the WSQ Professional Diploma in Early Childhood Care and Education and working as an assistant teacher in a childcare centre.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Upon completion of the PCP this April, she will take on the role of a pre-school teacher.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, one way we can explore new opportunities is by going beyond our current job roles.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Another is to go beyond our geographical borders and venture into different markets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Amirul was the first Singaporean Malay student to participate in the NUS Overseas College in Beijing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He did an internship there with Traintracks.io, a data analytics startup.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Despite not knowing much Chinese, Amirul had such a positive experience in Beijing that when he returned to Singapore, he joined the local startup scene, working full time at F&B tech startup Oddle after graduation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He is currently the company's Digital Marketing Lead, introducing the company's solutions to the Southeast Asian and US markets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, I share Mr Gan Thiam Poh's objective of helping Singaporeans to be great in what they do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Chandra, Yvonne and Amirul exemplify the spirit of enterprise we need to flourish in today's economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I urge all Singaporeans to be bold and proactive like them, to go beyond the immediate confines of what we are used to and find new prospects in different places.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Global Innovation Alliance will also give our young people more overseas exposure, especially to exciting startups with good ideas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the same time, in supporting our people to try new areas and learn new skills, we will also pay careful attention to those who may be more vulnerable: As Mr Zainal Sapari has noted, it is important to take care of the needs of lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This tops up their wages as they upgrade themselves with new skills.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Wage Credit Scheme has also supported businesses in sharing productivity gains with workers through wage increases.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In addition, we share Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Ang Hin Kee and Mr Ong Teng Koon's concerns for freelance workers, and are looking into how we can work with our tripartite partners to support them better.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Minister for Manpower will say more on this at the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having spoken about our people, let me now talk about our businesses.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Like our people, our businesses must have the courage to adapt and try new ideas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Often, we can tap on the expertise we already have to create new value for others.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am encouraged by the progress that many of our local firms have made.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many of us use radio frequency identification (RFID) tags every day − when we check out library books or tap our EZ-Link cards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Tunity Technologies, in collaboration with A*STAR's SIMTech, applied this technology to something unexpected − food trays.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Customers make a $1 deposit to borrow a tray and they get their deposit back when they return their tray to an automated system, which detects the returned tray using RFID technology.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This encourages customers to return their trays after use and allows the cleaning staff at a food centre to concentrate on other more productive tasks.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Matex International Ltd is a specialty chemicals company that has adapted to enter a new area of business.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Subsequently, Matex combined this technology with its own in-house knowledge to create customised ways to remove particles from waste water more efficiently.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This allowed Matex to move beyond being a specialty chemical manufacturer to also offer industrial waste water treatment solutions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It could have stopped with solving its own problem, but Matex took its solution, asked themselves who else would find it useful and opened up new business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In addition, our businesses stand to gain when they bring these ideas into new markets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To do this, we should develop stronger in-market presence to gain insights about consumers' needs and preferences in foreign markets, so that we can tailor our products and services accordingly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Lee Yi Shyan put it, we need to develop a "deep awareness of the world".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We should also be willing to explore new destinations, especially those places where few others have gone.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is about improving our businesses, as much as it is about contributing to the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, businesses on the Ninja Cloud platform can make use of spare capacity on other fleets in real time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our businesses need to develop a strong spirit of enterprise by innovating to create new value and internationalising to bring this value to new markets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They can tap on a range of support measures for these efforts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, businesses that wish to innovate can tap on measures like A*STAR's Operation and Technology Road-mapping, Headstart and Tech Access initiatives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even as our people and our businesses adopt a greater spirit of enterprise, we must all work together in close partnership, as Mr Darryl David and Dr Tan Wu Meng pointed out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many Members, including Ms Jessica Tan and Ms Foo Mee Har, have expressed support for the ITMs and I thank them for their support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Heng Chee How pointed out, these ITMs must be dynamic plans, which will be updated even as they are carried out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And as Mr Henry Kwek noted, the key is in getting things done − how the different partners can work together to drive industry development.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: After the Budget, one economist asked me, "Is the Government really the right party to drive the ITMs?" It was an indirect way of saying: does the Government really have the business experience to say what should be done to restructure each sector?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Government cannot, on its own, design plans for the tens of thousands of firms across different industries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is just not possible, nor is it what we want to do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What the Government can do is to catalyse and bring stakeholders together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is what we seek to do with the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The ITMs are a joint effort among all partners in an industry.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What the Government will do is to catalyse action through ITMs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We can provide a platform for different partners to share ideas; we can help to facilitate change, for example, by reviewing regulations where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But, ultimately, the ITMs need to be driven by the industry with strong participation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The quality of the ITMs will depend on the quality of inputs from industries and partners and how well we work together for the larger good.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope that entrepreneurs, businesses and trade associations will take the lead in developing and implementing the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We need everyone to contribute actively, to work together to get things done, in order for the ITMs to succeed.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am glad to hear Mr Thomas Chua's call for companies and TACs to play a more proactive role in industry development.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, our TACs must play a leadership role to galvanise companies to seize opportunities and embark on the challenging but fulfilling journey of transformation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this environment of rapid change, when individual companies may be uncertain about how to proceed or how best to tap on available Government support, this is a great service that TACs can perform for their members.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Unless we have strong leadership among our partners in the ITMs, the ITMs cannot take off.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
