text: I am also encouraged to learn that even before all 23 ITMs have been launched, we are already seeing good collaborative work among different industry partners.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Companies involved include both ground handlers at Changi, as well as Singapore Airlines Cargo and four freight forwarders.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These companies from across the air cargo supply chain will undergo training and have their processes and facilities accredited by IATA.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will help to attract global demand for these services, thus boosting the growth of the airfreight, logistics and pharmaceutical industries in Singapore ‒ a good example of cross-industry collaboration.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Another example of partnership involves local firm, V-Key Pte Ltd.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: V-Key has developed a patented virtual secure element which makes mobile phone applications and transactions secure, and serves more than 30 million banking and e-commerce users across Southeast Asia, India and China.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To develop more digital talent and nurture future digital leaders, V-Key has partnered our Institutes of Higher Learning and local banks, to enable selected students in infocomm to complete multiple structured internships with V-Key over the course of their studies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Students can gain valuable industry experience, and those who perform well are offered a permanent job at V-Key.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Such programmes benefit both the student and the employer.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The TechSkills Accelerator (TeSA), which was launched last year to develop talents for the infocomm sector, brings together trade associations like the Singapore Infocomm Technology Federation (SiTF), NTUC representatives and Government agencies like the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On our part, the Government will support the needs of our people and businesses, so that they can achieve their full potential.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, we will create a regulatory environment that both supports innovation and manages risks.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We need not regulate everything down to the last detail for fear that we will expose our society to risks.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Instead, we should stretch our thinking and come up with ways to encourage enterprise growth, while still mitigating risks to an acceptable level.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I mentioned in the Budget Speech, agencies like MAS, LTA and HSA are already moving in this direction.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The seven strategies of the CFE are mutually reinforcing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is important that we pursue this with a spirit of enterprise and partnership.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Only then can we come together to transform our economy and succeed in a more unpredictable and fast-changing world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Rather than following a blueprint, this is a journey of doing, learning and adapting.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am excited for what we will achieve together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have had a lively debate in this House on this Budget's measures for protecting the environment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many who spoke expressed support even as others pointed out the impact on households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In particular, Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Mr Pritam Singh, Ms K Thanaletchimi, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Png Eng Huat raised concerns about costs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There will be some costs, but also assistance measures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These should be debated, but at the end of the day, as Minister Chan Chun Sing said, the Government needs to be responsible in taking care of not only the short-term needs but also address future challenges.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must also change our mindsets and habits, as Er Dr Lee Bee Wah pointed out when she suggested the need to reduce consumption and to be more conscious about recycling.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And indeed, everyone has a part to play − from parents teaching our children conservation, to volunteers picking up litter in our waterways and parks, and firms adopting green technology.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources addressed Members' questions yesterday.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I shall reiterate a few key principles and say more about the Government's additional investments in the water system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Water sufficiency is a matter of national survival.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Members are well aware of how Mr Lee Kuan Yew, our Founding Prime Minister, obsessed over water since the Separation Agreement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Securing a sustainable water supply for Singapore has been an all-consuming pursuit of the Government since Independence.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We lodged our water agreements with the United Nations, invested in a strong defence force and developed strong capabilities in water technologies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Singaporeans have enjoyed uninterrupted and high-quality drinking water through rainy weather and droughts alike.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is not mere good fortune or our birth-right.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Rather, it is the result of long-term planning, a can-do attitude, innovation and sound policy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources explained, the cornerstone of our water policy is the pricing of water on sound economic principles to reflect its long-run marginal cost (LRMC).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This reflects the cost of supplying the next available drop of water, which is likely to come from NEWater and desalination plants.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This ensures that users will conserve water and we can make timely investments in the water system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked why raise the water price now and carbon tax later.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The carbon tax is new and the details will have to be carefully studied.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I think a more fundamental point is whether Ms Lim agrees that water is of strategic significance and we should each do our part.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng highlighted yesterday that the Government spends more than it collects on the water system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The revenue which PUB collects from users is only enough to cover operations and the depreciation of waterworks, pipelines and water reclamation plants.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The annual surpluses that PUB records are transferred to its capital reserves to finance these property, plant and equipment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is clearly stated in PUB's annual reports.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These expenditures exceed the amount of revenue from the water conservation tax which is expected to be about $1.6 billion over the same period.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In other words, the Government pays for part of the total cost of securing a safe and clean supply of water for our people and businesses.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Dr Teo Ho Pin shared their views, among others.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Introducing a carbon tax is the economically efficient way of reducing greenhouse gases.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A carbon tax places a price signal to incentivise emitters to lower emissions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Singapore will join dozens of other countries in pricing carbon to address climate change.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many jurisdictions that have put a price on carbon, such as Sweden, are reducing their emissions while maintaining economic growth, promoting green growth and reaping environmental benefits.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have restructured diesel taxes to introduce a volume-based component.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will incentivise reduced usage and lower pollutive emissions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Nonetheless, as a number of Members have noted, the restructuring of diesel taxes will impact some businesses.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is an important measure to help improve the health of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the longer run, we hope users will switch to cleaner fuels and technology.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the short run, we have put in place significant offsets to help businesses manage the transition.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The reduction of the annual Special Tax on diesel cars and taxis will also help to cushion the impact on these drivers, as Mr Sitoh Yih Pin has noted.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the Budget speech, I had urged taxi companies to pass on the Special Tax reduction to drivers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am glad that taxi companies will be doing so in various forms.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have earlier spoken about the spirit of partnerships which will help drive our economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Similarly, everyone has a part to play in securing a better living environment for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are taking decisive steps in this area because we want a cleaner and healthier environment for ourselves and our children.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We want businesses, visitors and Singaporeans from all backgrounds to enjoy a lush city scape to work, live and play in.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We invest in keeping our living environment in good shape because we care for our future and our children.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is the home that we have been building and will continue to build.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Home comes alive because of our people, because of our relationships.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the last decade, we have steadily increased our social investments.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We introduced major schemes to open up multiple pathways to success for all, provide assurance in key areas of need, and strengthen social safety nets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In education, we significantly enhanced the quality, affordability and accessibility for all, across all levels from pre-school to tertiary.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In housing, we increased housing supply and housing subsidies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In healthcare, we enhanced Government subsidies across all care settings, like CHAS, and introduced MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Pioneers receive additional subsidies and benefits from the Pioneer Generation Package.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For the lower income, we enhanced Workfare, introduced Silver Support and made GST Vouchers permanent.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue to refine our social policies and study new ideas and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, MOH is doing a major review of ElderShield.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the years, we have built up a strong social security system that serves Singaporeans well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In Budget 2017, we are focusing our efforts on continuing to empower the community and forge partnerships.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a movement towards the future, where we nurture a culture of caring for one another, of many helping hands, to meet a significant increase in societal needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have a rapidly ageing population and our families are getting smaller.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We can expect social needs to increase, for example, in healthcare.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the same time, Singaporeans are living longer, healthier lives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our seniors can contribute meaningfully to the community as they age gracefully and actively.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, many Singaporeans, both young and old, want to make a difference and give back to society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We want to empower all to try new ideas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Hence, our social compact must be one of partnership, where each of us gives our best.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Louis Ng pointed out, we need to strengthen community bonds.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And as Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin pointed out, it is up to, and I quote, "all of us".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, everyone − the Government, the community and individuals − all of us have a unique role to play.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are functions that the Government is best placed to perform − such as legislation and the provision of public goods and services.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And there are areas where we can achieve more, much more, when we all work together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When it comes to customising assistance to the specific needs of certain communities, or providing last-mile social service delivery, community action is critical.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even the strongest social safety nets are no substitute for the caring hearts and helpful hands of neighbours.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we want a close partnership among individuals, communities and the Government, because this is an end in itself.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a society that we aspire to for Singapore − a caring, resilient and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A society where Singaporeans help fellow citizens in each way we can and where individuals and community organisations work together to make Singapore a better home for all.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is not new to us, but we can do more to foster stronger partnerships and bring collaboration to the next level.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Government will do more by helping to create the right supportive environment to encourage community efforts, where everyone plays the part that we are best placed to perform.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are placing greater emphasis on bringing together community efforts for key areas of need.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Last year, we piloted the Community Network for Seniors to better support seniors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It has brought the Government and the community together to build "communities of care" right within our heartlands.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is a small start but, at the same time, it is rewarding to see how community and the Government are working together to touch lives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is nice to see her energetic and happy, exercising outdoors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But it was not like this for her just six months ago.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You see, at 70, Mdm Lee has weak knees and a history of falls.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Until the Community Networks learnt about her, Mdm Lee was keeping to herself at home, afraid to go out for fear of falling.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A Pioneer Generation Ambassador visited Mdm Lee and saw that she was at risk of social isolation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All the parts of the Community Networks sprang into action.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They worked with HDB to install grab bars in her home under the EASE programme.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: REACH Community Services Society introduced befrienders to Mdm Lee.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Her new friends visit her regularly and bring her down to the fitness corner near her house for simple exercises.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is the story of how the Community Network for Seniors, by bringing the different parts of the community together, helped to bring Mdm Lee out of isolation and lead a more active lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Community Network for Seniors pilot shows us the power of partnership.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Ms Tin Pei Ling and Dr Lily Neo raised interesting ideas on how we can better support the elderly to age gracefully.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These are useful suggestions that we will study further.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this Budget, we introduced the Community Mental Health efforts and the Third Enabling Masterplan.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I also take heart to see a growing spirit of enterprise in the social sector.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope that, over time, there will be more enterprising Singaporeans and community organisations that start ground-up initiatives and make significant social impact.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It was started by AMKFSC Community Services Ltd to help prepare unemployed women from low-income families to enter the workforce by equipping them with baking and other skills, while providing them opportunities to supplement their household income.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The project grew with support from community resources and is able to touch the lives of many more families.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We continue to encourage more of such ground-up projects, as well as philanthropy and volunteerism.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Azmoon Ahmad suggested VWOs and self-help groups can play a greater role to support communities in various areas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Members would know of the Alzheimer's Disease Association, which provides a range of services for people with dementia and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Tapping on the VCF, it is upgrading its IT system to centrally manage client and caregiver records and enhance data analysis capabilities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This allows its staff to increase productivity and better serve their clients.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope many other community organisations will likewise build their capabilities to do even better work for those they serve.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: By building many overlapping networks of community self-help and Government support, we build a more caring and inclusive society, and one that is resilient to weather change, in whatever form it takes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Just as we seek to protect our home and environment for our future generations, we must ensure that our finances are sustainable for the long term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Government had, in fact, anticipated this and prepared early, by raising revenues ahead of our spending needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, this is the approach this Government has always taken.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We had, therefore, raised the GST in 2007 and introduced the NIR framework in 2008.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the last term of Government, we had also undertaken measures, such as making our property tax rates more progressive and increasing the duties for betting, liquor and tobacco over time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In Budget 2015, we announced increases in top marginal rates for personal income tax and revisions to the NIR framework.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These measures now serve us well to meet our spending needs through to the end of this decade.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But beyond this decade, we can expect the fiscal situation to become more challenging as expenditures exceed revenues in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: With slowing economic growth, our revenues will also grow more slowly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, our population is ageing rapidly and we can expect rising expenditure needs, especially for healthcare.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Third, our infrastructure needs are rising, as we seek to build new infrastructure and renew old ones to enhance our quality of life and Singapore's economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Going forward, we must continue to prepare for our greater needs in the long term by working on two fronts: spending prudently and effectively; and growing our revenues fairly and sustainably.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: With higher spending needs, it is ever more critical to ensure that we spend within our means to get the outcomes we want, as Mr Vikram Nair noted.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the Ministry level, we have designed our funding policies to drive agencies to operate efficiently and effectively.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, we budget for on-going functions using a Block Budget Framework, where Ministries are provided with budget caps for a medium term period.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Within the cap, each Ministry decides how best to allocate its budget.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will free up resources that MOF can re-deploy towards higher priority requirements and projects that deliver value to citizens and businesses, such as initiatives by the Municipal Services Office.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Within their adjusted budget caps, agencies will decide how to prioritise their programmes and projects, and review how they can achieve greater efficiency.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Fundamentally, we want to imbue these values of prudence and innovation in all officers in the Public Service: to always seek value for money and constantly strive to improve and innovate, so that we can do more, and do better, with less.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This process taps on a panel of senior public officers and industry practitioners, those with deep technical expertise and experience in major infrastructure developments, with the aim of optimising the project's overall design, use of space and cost-effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the programme level, we are designing our schemes so that subsidies are targeted at the right groups.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As a general principle, we price services to recover full cost and discourage over-consumption.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We then target subsidies appropriately at those in need, such as through GST Vouchers, S&CC rebates and Public Transport Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is more progressive than under-pricing services, which implicitly subsidises all groups, including the rich.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether we evaluate programmes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On economic programmes, Minister Iswaran gave a detailed explanation about how agencies evaluate those programmes and have to adapt and change when necessary.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Then, she raised the issue of the PIC.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The PIC, in fact, has largely achieved its objective.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But she raised examples of abuses to make her case.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, the fact that those abuses are uncovered is because of extensive audits that are done by the agencies, and we should commend the officers for the seriousness in which they undertake this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In many other countries, those abuses would not even be known.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The schemes were done in a way that is broad-based and reaches the right groups of people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The alternative, of course, is to have every detail scrutinised and approved before the businesses can use it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And, in fact, in many of the Budget dialogues we had with businesses, their concern was if you have too many schemes that are just based on approval, things will not move.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, it is a delicate balance and a good balance which the agencies should be commended for.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This challenge of raising revenues for growing needs is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you look at many other countries, the need for more revenue to meet spending needs is a common theme that cuts across different systems.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, Hong Kong had announced at its recent Budget that it would be setting up a tax policy unit to comprehensively review its tax system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: One of its objectives would be, and I quote, to "explore broadening the tax base and increasing revenue, so as to ensure that adequate resources are available" to support sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Yee Chia Hsing had asked how we intend to review our own tax system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What this means is that those who are better off must contribute more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In recent Budgets, we have continued to make our personal income tax and property tax rates more progressive, even as we introduced or enhanced permanent schemes, such as Silver Support and Workfare, to provide more support to lower-income groups.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, a sustainable tax system is fundamentally one that rewards efforts by individuals and enterprise by our companies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har pointed out, the only way to sustain a healthy revenue stream is to have a healthy and growing economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In more recent years, more countries have lowered or announced their intention to lower corporate income tax rates.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The new administration in the US has also indicated plans to cut corporate tax rates.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must ensure that Singapore continues to be an attractive place to work and do business, so that we have a thriving and vibrant economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Third, sustainability is also about striking the right balance between current and future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have spent prudently, built up our reserves and tapped on their returns judiciously.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is the right and responsible way, rather than leaving problems to be dealt with by future governments when Singapore comes under fiscal strain.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Planning for the issue now will allow us to better ease in the needed measures, to give our people and businesses some time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must plan for the long term, not five years, not 10 years, but big ambitious plans for decades ahead.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Like the new airport, new towns each with distinctive features to attract families, new MRT lines.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are in a good position today, because we have planned early and invested in the long term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This Budget sets the strategies for building a better Singapore in a sustainable way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We can move forward confidently on these strategies, as we are starting from a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a cumulative effort from previous Budgets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have a well-functioning economy where most Singaporeans have good jobs; we have a good social security system that serves the majority of Singaporeans well; we have spent prudently so we have the necessary resources.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this fast-changing world, we cannot predict how the journey ahead will pan out, but we can expect that it will not be always smooth-sailing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There is no step-by-step guide for how to venture into the volatile, unpredictable future that lies ahead for the whole world, not only Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But for Singapore, we have our compass, a compass of our shared values and our common hope.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this Budget, we set our minds to seize opportunities to succeed; to be part of, to play a part in, a caring and inclusive community; and to build, protect and pass on a truly special home to future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Let us develop the deep capabilities, strengthen the spirit of enterprise to adapt and try out new things, work together in partnership, and care for and support one another.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Each time, despite the naysayers, we emerged stronger and more adaptive, as we held strong together as one people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yesterday evening, those of us who were in this Chamber were very moved by Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin's speech, a heartfelt one about how much heart we need to put in to help people in need.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As I reflected through the night, I thought I would like to clarify with her, in respect of the divorcee she mentioned with two children earning $1,600 seeking rental housing and other forms of social support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The first clarification is: is this an individual whom she could put us in touch with so that we can look at what happened and see how best we can assist her?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Even as cases do fall through the cracks, it is important for us, as a Public Service, to make sure we pick up on all these cases and assist them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The second clarification is: some people may take away from the speech the impression − perhaps wrongly − that the Public Service has lost heart.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I am asking for this clarification on behalf of the officers who work at the rental department, the Social Support Offices, the Family Service Centres and the many other social service agencies across the Public Service who are Singaporeans and who care.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I want to thank the Senior Minister of State for his care.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: First, I want to affirm what I said yesterday.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I actually do not believe that it is all on the Government and that everyone has to work together to solve all these issues.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I want to affirm that I actually do not believe that the Public Service has lost heart, as some reports have said.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I personally know of many deeply compassionate civil servants, especially those who work for people in rental housing, who actually go out on a limb to make things work out for the needy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to take the opportunity to state that I am also aware that, for some, they do not actually look for help because they believe mistakenly that nobody cares about them in the civil service and I think that is a mistake because that stops them from actually getting their needs met.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On behalf of all the officers who work in social agencies, we will continue to work hard.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And for those cases, we will follow up on them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Earlier, he referred to my raising of the PIC scheme.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The point I was making was whether, as an example, the PIC scheme, but, in general, whether there are any mechanisms to assess the effectiveness of expenditure in terms of the outcomes that are intended to be achieved?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: He mentioned that the PIC scheme was largely effective.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We have seen productivity data that seems to be very mixed and also weak in the domestic sectors for the last couple of years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And I am wondering whether he could elaborate further on whether there is any publicly published Government report that shows the effect of the PIC scheme on productivity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Because I may have missed something that his Ministry or MTI has published.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is within the range of what the ESC has set out to do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, these measures, in terms of the productivity numbers − yes, it has achieved that sort of outcome.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I think, more importantly, the PIC scheme was also intended to create a greater awareness amongst our SMEs of the need to take productivity seriously, to upgrade.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The fact that so many businesses have actually taken up the scheme and improved their performance is a sign that the objective of raising awareness of getting businesses much more involved in it has achieved its purpose.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why, last year, I spoke about why we need to move on to more targeted measures in the next phase.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I just have three points of clarifications for the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before I start, I just want to wish the Minister many more years of good health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My first point is regarding the presentation of the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister for Finance consider presenting one or two pages in future Budget Statements which presents the Budget according to IMF guidelines, reflecting the total net amounts of money leaving the economy to the state, and money that the state is pumping back into the economy?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is so that Singaporeans can make a well-informed assessment of whether future Budgets are expansionary enough to facilitate genuine, democratic consensus formation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because I highlighted that net birth of companies has been plunging in 2016.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The last time we saw such a figure was in 2009.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if we push the data series even further back, the last time we saw a below-10,000 net birth figure was —

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Your point has already been made in your speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The last point is that I just wanted to ask the Finance Minister again about the timing of the price hikes that we have seen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And given that the Government has shared that the reasons behind these are not political − and I believe that was shared yesterday − can the Minister help Singaporeans understand a little better?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What are the non-political reasons behind timing the price hikes in this way?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The reason why the Budget Book is presented the way it is, is that this meets our specific needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We need to know, for particular Ministries, how much spending is available, what is the development spending, what is the operating spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Whereas the IMF is for a macroeconomic evaluation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As to whether a particular Budget is expansionary or not expansionary, in fact, it is not just by looking at those numbers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you consult the economists, you will know that they actually take great pains to model the effects of the monetary and fiscal policies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And, in the case of fiscal policy, how much of a fiscal impulse a particular Budget provides to the economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Here, we are fortunate that MAS would do some of these simulations to give us a sense of whether it is appropriate or not appropriate, because we also have the important objective of keeping inflation in check.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These are not numbers that are not available, or numbers that you can just read off and conclude that it is expansionary or not expansionary.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It takes a general equilibrium model for us to look at some of these impacts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The next question on the net birth of companies, whether it is an indication that companies are not doing well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, there are many reasons behind the birth rates and exit rates of companies, and we must expect that it will fluctuate over cycles, depending on the economic conditions and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I think Minister Iswaran has explained that if we are looking at the health of SMEs, there is a broad range of factors that one has to look into.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If the Member's specific question is, are SMEs doing okay, I have indicated in both my Budget Speech and in the round-up speech that the performances across sectors, across industries and across firms differ.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And that is why we need a targeted approach.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why I used the Chinese phrase, 对 症 下 药, which means to have the right remedy for the right ailment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not a case of having broad-based measures, that every firm is doing badly and therefore, we need a big rescue operation, as we had during the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, those things will have to be carefully studied and we cannot just draw a simplistic conclusion, just a number of firms are formed this year, that year and, therefore, the situation is better or worse.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Member's final question was on the timing of the increases.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The fact is, first and foremost, do we agree that the price signal is important so that consumers know what the actual cost of the resource is and, therefore, can then take action to mitigate the use?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because I do not think any Finance Minister finds it a popular thing to come here and say, "Oh, I am going to increase this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I do not take great joy out of announcing all these increases.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But the fact is, we have to do the right and responsible thing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The right and responsible thing is to make sure that the price signal and the correct price feeds through with the economy early enough.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a fundamental point that we got to make sure that we do things correctly, we have the right price signal, and that every one of us factors this into our decision-making and do our part.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There has been quite a lot of calls on that, so I would like to hear the Minister's response.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Second, Mdm Speaker, is whether the Minister will also consider suspending income tax payment when someone is unemployed, as well as more flexible use of the CPF in order to tide them over to pay mortgage.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, on state land, whether it can be used by SMEs and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The amount of land that is used, whether it is commercial, industrial or residential, is planned very carefully by the various agencies, and also together with the economic agencies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Where there is a need, more land can be released, but where some temporary uses can be made, in many cases, the Singapore Land Authority has allowed for some of them to be used.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we should not take that as a matter of course, because, if we do, then a lot of that planning will have problems later on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If the business is a startup, perhaps, it requires a lower cost, but if it is going to operate permanently in a particular way, we cannot just permanently subsidise rental because that would eventually make it harder for businesses to adapt.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, if you do know of particular cases, you can advise them to apply to IRAS.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The first is to the Minister for Finance in relation to the diesel tax − whether he would consider ameliorating the impact for vehicles that are serving the needs of VWOs, in order to also help the organisations save some costing.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: My second clarification is for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources − whether the Government will consider water rationing across the board for individual households as well as commercial entities, as also previously suggested by a former Nominated Member, Prof Tan Tai Yong.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I would ask the Ministry to have a look at it in greater detail.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But let me say that for the VWOs, there are also many other schemes to help with the transport-related matters.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I thought it is odd for me to respond during the clarification of my Ministry's COS.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For rationing, we have been asked by many Members, as well as the public, to try and put this rationing regime into a yearly exercise for everybody.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This year, more schools – 11 schools – are participating and preschools are also participating.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hopefully, we will never have to go into rationing when we are ready with our desalination plants and our NEWater plants.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I think to press the point about how precious water is by making it difficult through rationing may not always be productive.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a recent article on Bloomberg, Norway Central Bank Chief warned of how the risk of a 50% decline in 10 years of the sovereign wealth fund increases five times if government withdrawals from the fund increases from 3%-4%.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given our reliance on NIRC to fund our Budget, what are the inherent risks we face?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should there be huge changes in global outlooks of capital markets, how does that change our expected long-term rates of returns and our ability to use NIRC to fund our Budget?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First of all, let me put it in perspective that, indeed, we are drawing about 20-odd percent of our Budget from the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The fact is that we still have 80% that is based on current revenue.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is important that we keep a vibrant economy and that we keep our tax rates in such a way that allows us to do this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Is there a risk that the returns will not be adequate in the future?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When the former Finance Minister, Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam, revised the NIR framework, there were a number of careful safeguards that were put into the spending rules.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our spending, first of all, does not depend on the fluctuations in the market from year to year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, it is the expected long-term rate of return.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That means that in a very good year when markets are very vibrant, we do not just take very vibrant returns but, rather, the agencies give us an expected long-term rate of return, and we look at that number.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you look at the numbers, it has been conservative, compared to many of the endowment funds.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As long as the return is positive, we add to the reserves, not only through new revenue sources, new surpluses but we add to it through the returns not spent.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is something that we take very seriously.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The third thing that we do is to make sure that if the returns are very good in one particular year, asset value tends to be very high, the rate that we apply, the long-term return that we apply, is not to the very high base, because we know that the markets will go up and down.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you apply to a very high base, you may overspend.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For that reason, it is based on a smoothed asset base, so that in good years, we do not overdo it, and, in bad years, we will still have adequate resources.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All these returns are real returns, net of inflation; it is not just some big nominal numbers that are used.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, the Member's point is a very important one; that we have to be very, very careful in guarding the use of these reserves and in making sure that we spend on a sustainable basis.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I apologise I did not make myself very clear just now.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I was not referring to vehicles owned by VWOs but, rather, to the commercial operators because many VWOs are not able to or, for some reason, do not own their own vehicles.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The general response from the businesses to this year's Budget has not been positive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From the media reports, we have read strong statements from the Singapore Business Federation, Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCCI), Association of Small and Medium Enterprises and the other trade associations and chambers (TACs) expressing disappointments with the Budget for not doing enough to help businesses cope with the immediate challenges.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is understandable and natural for businesses to always seek an even better business environment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It happens in all countries to varying degrees and for as long as we can remember.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I did some quick homework to satisfy myself as to whether this barrage of criticisms by the businesses are fair and justifiable, or whether the Finance Minister is, indeed, doing the right thing from an economic management and, of course, from a prudential standpoint.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, let us start with the most recent economic numbers to see if the economy is, indeed, in a dismal state.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Granted that the key driver from the surge in growth came mainly from two manufacturing sectors, namely, the semiconductor and pharmaceutical sectors, but we can expect spillover effects to other sectors supporting these two sectors, such as precision engineering, transport, warehousing, financial and other supporting services.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, we have also seen credible growth from the services sector which accounts for about two-thirds of the economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, clearly, from a data standpoint, we are not seeing the sort of sharp contraction similar to what we saw in recent downturns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, it may not warrant the Government to roll out a massive rescue package to save the economy but rather to continue with and enhance existing schemes to assist businesses, which include the cash schemes, like the Wage Credit and the additional Special Employment Credit (SEC).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are in addition to the other assistance measures in the Budget, some of which were recommended by the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, in my view, the Finance Minister has struck the appropriate balance here.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, it is worth noting that we are seeing the new realities of our economy setting in.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This probably explains why some businesses are feeling downbeat.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, businesses are beginning to feel the effects of life under a slower 2% growth environment, compared to what used to be a 3% to 5% growth a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is showing up in their order books in the form of fewer orders and, as a result, more competition and compressed margins while, at the same time, seeing business costs continuously creeping up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we further overlay the picture with the employment situation, then we are beginning to see troubling signs that we ought to be concerned about.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could be due to a combination of cyclical downturns in some sectors and structural shifts taking place within the economy which lead to higher job mismatches.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we intensify digitisation, we can expect possible job losses but there will also be new jobs created for those who can adapt.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under such circumstances, giving out broad-based short-term cash grants to businesses will not reverse these trends.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It requires a whole-of-system approach to deal with the challenge.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The CFE and Budget 2017 do have a host of recommendations and measures to address this development, including the Adapt and Grow initiatives and specific industry transformation support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For businesses, the perennial concerns are still about the costs of doing business in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do agree that the increase in water prices and diesel duty do not help the situation, even as the businesses can understand the reason for the hikes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, I read last Thursday in Lianhe Wanbao about how the food industry and food manufacturers are most concerned with the hikes as both water and diesel are their major inputs in the food production chain and there are no direct rebates in the Budget to help them.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We do know that there is no turning back on having less air pollutive fuel and to have better air quality, as that is what we want.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also know that the cost of an additional drop of water will cost more as we tap more of the expensive sources of water going forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather than look for short-term painkillers, let us tackle the problem head-on and collectively work on longer-term alternative solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, in the case of water, perhaps the food industry's Industry Transformation Map (ITM) can be the platform where industry players and all stakeholders come together to seek longer-term solutions and working with the Public Utilities Board (PUB) and the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) for both research and development (R&D) and resource support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, necessarily, Budget 2017 would be more heavily weighted in the areas of economic transformation and setting our sights on the medium- to long-term horizon.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We noted that a number of the suggestions put up by the GPC, primarily on the supply-side areas, were also in the report.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some have critiqued that the CFE report offers no new ground-breaking ideas and that it was lacking in detailed execution plans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, we are in uncharted territory in this new fast-paced ever-changing landscape, having a well thought out strategy and clear directions as to where we should go will put us in pole position.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the important next step is to develop quick response capabilities that can react swiftly and seize opportunities whenever they present themselves and these opportunities are likely to come in shorter cycles with greater injects of newer unknowns in play.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many of the key ideas of CFE were well-shared and ventilated during the one year of public engagement and, hence, most of the recommendations come as no surprises, though they are not any less impactful.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We know that this is the to-do list on hand and what is more crucial is to get as many done as soon as possible and to do them well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since not everything is cast in stone and more plans are being hatched on the move, I hope the Government can still take new ideas on board to transform the economy, and I have some of my thoughts and suggestions here today.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Building strong digital capabilities is among the foremost priorities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must quickly capitalise on our competitive edge to stay way ahead of the curve, so that we can exploit the powerful multiplying effect that digitisation can bring.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Jack Ma recently said that Alibaba aims to be the fifth largest economy in the world with its e-commerce platform and digital connectivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is no other more enterprise-centric way to carry this out than to go one-on-one with enterprises, offering step-by-step advice on the technologies to use at each stage of the growth, roping in resources from the Infocomm media Development Authority (IMDA), the Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING) and other lead agencies, giving some funding to those that are ready to pilot emerging infocomm technology (ICT) solutions and starting with sectors that are in greatest need to improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the national level, the Government should also see building nation-wide digital capabilities and infrastructure as a public good and to go beyond just playing the enabling role.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often, decisive actions are needed to fast-track or build such capabilities ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The private sector may not always be commercially aligned to the ultimate national objectives and may have other nuances or take longer to mobilise, for example.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A case in point is the setting up of the national digital payments system, which was suggested by the GPC for Finance, Trade and Industry to CFE, where leaving it to the private sector may take ages to happen, given the multiple commercial stakeholders involved.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government should also hasten the proliferation of sharing economy platforms, enabling trade and e-commerce connectivity across and up and down the economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the area of innovations, the GPC believes that enterprises should leverage on R&D as a key competitive driver.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through the ITM platforms, more R&D support, such as Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2020, can be made available to promising local enterprises to develop breakthrough and trendsetting products and services.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, most of our R&D resources are being utilised by very large companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to "bite-sized" this R&D funding support so that it is within the scope of smaller enterprises and, through ITMs, to cluster businesses together to seek joint solutions to common challenges, such as water and carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the new landscape, superior global connectivity will be the key success factor.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It can expand Singapore's economic spaces and add excitement and vibrancy, notwithstanding a slower 2% to 3% home-based growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On internationalisations, given recent global political developments and the anti-free trade sentiments in Europe and the United States (US), we clearly need to further expand and diversify beyond traditional markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is scope to pursue more opportunities within the ASEAN markets, riding on the growing middle class and its expanding infrastructural needs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We would need to further expand consular and International Enterprise (IE) Singapore's presence in these locations, expand air links and develop closer multifaceted ties, including setting up more location-based business councils with the local jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Amidst all these initiatives, the oxygen for businesses to scale up, innovate and venture overseas is funding and capital, which was also addressed in the CFE report.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, this is one of the bold ideas of CFE.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also gives the Government a greater handle in keeping the company's headquarter and core operations rooted in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And should the company's owner decide to cash out and sell their stakes, the Government's equity stake in the company would be better able to help retain the value in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These requirements should be clearly stated in the investment mandate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have seen that in some countries, for example, in Sweden, there is this Wallenburg Foundation which will invest in companies to pursue their own Swedish national interest.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should expand the availability of low-cost spaces.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, France opened Europe's biggest accelerators with space for 1,000 startups in a refurbished Paris train station.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are many more such newly set up accelerators in Europe today, very much like our Block 71.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, from overseas experience, precincts near the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) tend to be good fertile ground for like-minded innovators to gravitate towards and a community of innovators to spontaneously form.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope the Ministry of National Development can consider making available unused buildings or spaces in locations near IHLs, such as Clementi and West Coast, which are near to the National University of Singapore, Dover Road, near Singapore Polytechnic, to foster closer social networking and economy shaping between IHLs and the innovators.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On skills, Mdm Speaker, the key word in CFE and Budget 2017 is to go deep.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, while I can appreciate the need to make training more accessible via e-learning platforms, I am not sure that a modularised and technology-enabled training programme can achieve the right depth and rigour to meet the needs of the market place.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I fully agree we need to strengthen on-the-job skills utilisation and to urge employers and TACs to take the lead in the design and structuring of skills upgrade.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The nexus between skills acquisition and utilisation will be better aligned if employers and TACs take ownership.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, I hope that the Government will also consider three other suggestions related to skills and jobs that the GPC has earlier put up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mature students, with their rich life and workplace experience can bring useful perspectives to the classroom, even as they learn new skills there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I like a particular line in the CFE report, which said "we need to go beyond the pursuit of the highest possible academic qualifications early in life to focus on acquiring and using knowledge and skills throughout our lives." I hope the Ministry of Education and the IHLs can start making changes in this area and turn these words into action.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, I hope companies can be incentivised to provide sabbatical leave to long-serving employees who may wish to take stock of their accumulated skills and experience, take learning breaks to reskill and re-energise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is consistent with enhancing long-term employability in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many of the Fortune 500 companies already have such practices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should also review the curriculum of junior colleges and to consider placing a greater emphasis on applied learning, beyond just pre-university education.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also timely to study and weigh the long-term benefits of national A-level exams in the new future landscape.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, these are real observable data on why we could not find Singaporeans to fill those jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the deeper understanding, we can map out the right skills development programme to reduce mismatches.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Information gaps are among the reasons why there are mismatches between employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am glad that CFE and Budget 2017 have undertaken to step up the functionality and user experience of the national Jobs Bank.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to harness the value of the whole-of-economy data to do a better job in matching jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The transition to a more entrepreneurial, international and innovative economy will obviously come with risks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And the best way to mitigate these new risks is to always maintain a strong financial position, ready to act with effective measures when the situation warrants and have the internal resilience to weather external shocks that will definitely come time and again.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Amidst all these, we must maintain social cohesion, alongside capable political leadership.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must avoid the discontentment and divisions that we recently saw happening in Europe and the US to globalisation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the last 10 years of Budgets which I have debated as a Member of this House, I can only remember one year where the Budget was almost entirely short term.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That was in 2009 when the economy contracted by 17% the quarter preceding and a negative growth of 2% to 5% was forecasted for that year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Everyone would love to have a Budget package with tasty, immediate goodies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, we would find our fruits tastier, if they were harvested through hard work and prudence from plans put in place many Budgets ago.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That has been the spirit of Singapore Budgets since our Independence and has been core to our values.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should continue to do it this way, even in the future economy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The intensity of the pace, scope and scale of this change is what is different.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The rapid changes are driven by the combination of globalisation and technology that are removing the constraints of geographic boundaries and limitations and blurring the lines between the physical and our digital world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This "learning and adaptive approach" may be uncomfortable, and I think the feedback we received has indicated that it is uncomfortable for many of us, as we are used to certainty and clear plans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But given the pace, scale and impact of these changes we are seeing, none of us, not even the Government, can predict the future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Rather, we must take some bets directionally, and that enables us to be ready but be prepared to adjust and adapt to the changes that will unfold.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is no longer simply about picking the right bets, having the right skills and then just executing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the uncertainties that unfold, nurturing a culture of learning and having the mindset and flexibility to adjust and adapt will be key.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The measures in this Budget focus on the quality of growth in a future economy that is anchored on building the capabilities of enterprises, deep skills in our people and enabling innovation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that, together with the ITMs, these are the right strategies to enable businesses and our people to stay relevant and thrive in the future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But to achieve deep capabilities, skills and innovation is not easy, because it will require structural changes and partnerships between large and small enterprises, local and foreign, educational and research institutions, trade associations, unions and the Government.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One is the strategy for economic growth and innovation, and the other around ensuring a caring society and inclusive growth in helping those impacted by the transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To build enterprise capability, the Budget outlined the need for enterprises to use digital technology, embrace innovation and scale up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is evident that enterprises, both large and small, cannot ignore leveraging digital technology to transform their businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many are already facing the impact of the disruption brought about by technology.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although many SMEs today do see the benefits of leveraging digital technology to transform their businesses and address the changing business environment, many do not have the skills or resources to do so and have not done so or do not even have the plans to do so.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Klaus Schwab, and I thought he shared this very well and I wanted to share the thoughts that he shared about the Fourth Industrial Revolution, because he talked about the demand and supply side impact on businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On the supply side, what he shared was that new technologies in many industries are creating entirely new ways of serving existing needs, enabling new ways of working and significantly disrupting existing industry value chains.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Access to global digital platforms for research, development, marketing, sales and distribution has enabled new entrants to compete and thrive by improving the quality, speed or price of what they deliver.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On the demand side, technology has also enabled a change in how products and services are being consumed and new services and business models are emerging to address demands and creating new markets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Obvious examples that many of us are familiar with, are online shopping, from Grab to Uber, Deliveroo and Airbnb, just to mention a few.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These are giving competition to established incumbents, both large and small, from all industries, whether it is retail, transportation, F&B, hospitality, learning.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The barriers to entry have been lowered and new entrants are driving new demands and addressing new demand areas as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Going digital is important but I do want to stress the point that we must be cognizant that it is not about going digital.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Rather, becoming a digital business is a means to an end.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is key that our enterprises, both large and small, as they embark on their digital transformation, keep the consumer at the centre of their strategy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The importance of using data as a key business currency to understand and get insights of both the demand and supply side opportunities and challenges, will be key for businesses, and being able to stay relevant.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As our businesses leverage digital platforms as well, they need to continue to build credibility and trust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Keeping data secure and ensuring that their digital platforms stay secure will be critical.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Building cyber security skills is an area that all businesses will require.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But for SMEs, this is going to be an extremely challenging area, given the challenges they are already facing in the adoption of digital technology.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Another area I would like to touch on is that driving transformation and growth need strong leadership.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we know, successful reinvention, business change and innovation require strong leadership.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In order for our businesses to expand and scale up, they need strong leaders to make decisions, transform and grow the businesses locally.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are good examples of multinational corporations (MNCs) already doing this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are those examples today, but we need more.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because with the pace of change, this needs to be done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are real fears amongst our workforce that these changes will not only disrupt jobs but displace jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The measures announced in the Budget and the ongoing measures to help our people access, acquire and deepen skills are needed and welcomed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not going to speak about the specific measures but I would like to touch on one segment of the workforce, that is, the middle-income and middle-aged.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While there are other segments of the workforce impacted by the disruption, this is a talent base that is significantly impacted by the transformation of businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Across several economies, we are already seeing a growing discontent amongst those in the middle-income group.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must ensure that the measures are effective in enabling this segment to deepen their skills and adapt and grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I want to also share a point that we need to ensure that this group continues to see that the opportunities that they have are not about transitioning and not just about finding employment, but that they can find fulfilling jobs and see an opportunity to improve their lives and those of their families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The then US Vice-President Joe Biden, in a keynote address at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting 2016, told participants "the middle class is about possibilities − the possibilities for anyone willing to work hard to achieve a decent life".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He said that a thriving and growing middle class has been the main reason for social stability in the world's democracies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is our own responsibility to make sure that this group continues to be able to thrive, because they are impacted by the changes that we are seeing in businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I strongly believe that if we strengthen the Singapore Core and give our people confidence and hope in the future, we will have a culture of growth and learning, but we must continue to remain open.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because it is only when we are able to stay open can Singapore benefit from strong partnerships and learn from foreign companies, both large and small.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On the point of definition of who needs help and how the help is extended, when distributing rebates and subsidies given, we all understand the finite resources and budgets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I agree that there must be criteria for qualification.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The criterion is also not based on ownership, but on the type of housing you live in.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While logical, this may no longer be as valid or accurate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are some living in Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats who may not be worse off than someone living in a private property.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is not a straightforward matter and it will need further study what needs to be addressed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I feel that we need to relook our approach.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not asking that we grow the size of the number of people getting help, as it will not be fiscally sustainable to do so.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What I am requesting is that we relook at the distribution to ensure that those who need help do receive it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On social inclusion, as we build a society that is moving on and moving on fast, it is important, another aspect of inclusion is about helping people feel that their contributions matter.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We already have many platforms of recognising people from all walks of life and professions and we must continue to do so.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I recall NS50 is a recent example of a platform to recognise the efforts of National Servicemen, past and present, including bringing them together and sharing their experiences.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because it is through the experiences, having the platforms that we can feel part of, that would make people feel included and bring us forward together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have spoken on many occasions in this House of ensuring that Singaporeans continue to have "hope" and see Singapore as the home and place for each and every one of us to aspire and build a better life for ourselves and our families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have seen in recent times how many economies are driven by fear and anxiety and facing pressures to become more protectionist.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To this point, it is apt that the theme for this year's Budget is "Moving Forward Together".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The journey we are embarking on is not going to be easy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the past, lies an economy driven by foreign direct investments, state initiatives and capital and labour inputs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the future, lies the dream of an economy driven more by productivity and innovation, local enterprises and private initiatives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How do we move from A to B?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some have criticised these for being too broad, but I do acknowledge that there are details contained in the ITMs and other Governmental statements outside the CFE report.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There was also not a great deal that was new in the CFE report.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A few new ideas, like the Global Innovation Alliance, for example, but not many.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the most part, CFE referred to and affirmed existing initiatives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I acknowledge, however, that we should not value novelty for novelty's sake.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
