text: If indeed, what we are doing now has little room for improvement because it is delivering results, then so be it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But is what we are doing now delivering the results that we need?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to one city-level study cited by the Prime Minister in 2012, our per capita GDP is not even among the top 20 cities worldwide.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That refers to the formation minus cessation of companies, companies, generally being larger and more economically-weighty entities than proprietorships.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the last three months of 2016, the net births of companies have plunged.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since December 2015, this indicator has registered negative net births of companies four times − in four months out of 13.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The total net births figure for 2016 was about 6,000.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the previous four years, it ranged between 12,000 and 21,000.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, in the last 10 years, this figure has fallen below 10,000 only twice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2009, the year of the financial crisis, and last year, 2016.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SME sector situation is seriously challenged at the present moment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But how can we make sure that the Red Dot does not dim for our children and our grandchildren?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What was lacking in the CFE report was a deep self-examination about why we are producing these kinds of results.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From deep self-examination, and even self-criticism, could come fresh thinking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our drive towards high productivity is not new.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The US, Korea, Hong Kong and Australia have better real productivity growth compounded on an annual basis from 2004 to 2014, according to one analysis published in The Straits Times on 24 April 2016.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet other developed countries have reversed their TFR decline, such as Japan, France and some Scandinavian countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To take a micro example of what I am referring to here, Budget 2017 announced a new SkillsFuture Leadership Development Initiative (LDI) to groom corporate leaders, which is good.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet an initiative to groom Singaporeans to become leaders in global companies had already been announced several years back.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Turning now to Budget 2017, is it a Budget that deals with the economic situation we are in?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what if we properly reflect the cash going out of the economy to the state in the form of land sales, projected to be $8.2 billion in 2017, net of other elements that may not be reflected, such as the actual cash spending of endowments and funds?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once all of these items are accounted for, is the Budget as expansionary as the basic deficit of $8.2 billion would suggest?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such transparency is important to enable Singaporeans to make up their own minds as to whether future Budgets are, indeed, an effective response to current economic realities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So much so that some economists now openly predict the Budgets in certain years will be election year Budgets that spend off the accumulated surplus from the preceding term of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the Government held back on fiscal stimulus in 2017, so as to keep ammunition in reserve for closer to the elections?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Seven hundred million dollars in construction projects have been brought forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the Government considered bringing forward projects in other areas of expenditure than construction − ICT projects, for example?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will provide a greater and more sectorally-balanced stimulus.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleagues will comment and discuss in detail on the water price hike and other price hikes and taxes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But let me make a few observations now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The timing of these price hikes seems more synchronised to the political cycle than to the economic cycle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The economy is facing numerous problems and net births of companies are plunging.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this the right time to raise the electricity tariff, gas price, parking fees and, last but not least, the water price, all within the space of a few months?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hitting the economy with these multiple price hikes within the space of a few months may make good political sense, because people have three years to forget them, before the next General Election.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why introduce all these price hikes now at a time of relative economic fragility, when they could tip some SMEs at the margins over the edge, when they increase the hardships faced by Singaporeans beset with job market insecurities?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not introduce some of them later when there is an up-swing in external demand?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are some initiatives to address SME funding, and there are some new measures announced at this Budget, for example, tweaks to IFS and the new Globalisation Fund.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are welcomed moves to be sure, but is this enough to uncage our local firms?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When this was debated in the COS in 2016, the reply was that we do not need more measures, because the retail and industrial space market was already softening due to market forces.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the Government should understand that for entrepreneurs, it is not all about the costs today, but what will be the costs tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An entrepreneur will not invest blood, sweat and tears to build the business, only to see commercial rentals surge due to market forces and wipe out his/her commercial viability in five or 10 years' time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A larger share of JTC in commercial and industrial space and a smaller share held by real estate investment trusts, as was the case in the past, or another similar suite of policies, would help to underscore that long-term assurance to entrepreneurs and would-be entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Time does not permit me to delve too deeply on this subject, but we can and should do more to enable our students to understand how entrepreneurship is both a viable and a socially meaningful calling.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, I fear that most of our aspiring students dream of becoming civil servants or working in an MNC.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On funding, in New Zealand, for example, an SME can obtain a bank loan for a merger and acquisition project overseas based on a certain price-earnings ratio.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In countries like Switzerland, Germany and Japan, local banks have close ties to local companies in particular states or prefectures, and both parties see a commonality of long-term interests.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is such funding easy to obtain in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, I fully recognise that not all ideas and companies are fundable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is this kind of tough-minded results-driven approach which enabled Japan and Korea to groom world-leading companies in the 1960s and 1970s, companies that, to this day, employ many people in their home countries, both directly and indirectly, in the form of complex chains of suppliers and sub-contractors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is no coincidence that the countries with the most innovative companies and disruptors are also the countries which have a larger role for social safety nets and risk-pooling.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One is managing the risks of redundancies from ever shortening product lifecycles and continuous disruption.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Here, Ms Sylvia Lim has proposed the redundancy insurance scheme during the Budget Debate 2016.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is due to high property prices depleting the CPF Ordinary Account.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Managing these risks are important if a globalised open economy and society is to thrive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must create enough security and confidence for Singaporeans to become the disruptors, and not the disrupted.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There have been some measures announced to address these issues over the past few years, but the basic structural impediments remain.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most households are exposed to cyclical economic risks without robust safety nets and risk-pooling, reinforcing a tendency to focus on short-term cash flow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This makes it less likely that they will set up companies, take risks to innovate, take time off work for education, reskilling or training, because they cannot afford to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, Madam, our education system excels at training literacy and numeracy to a high standard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government takes pride in our Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) scores.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But equally important to competitive success in the 21st century are "skills" like lateral thinking, creative problem-solving, leadership, communication and self-confidence, as I spoke about during COS 2016.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we sustain the current high academic content workload and add the cultivation of these softer attributes on top, like the icing on a cake?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will our students be able to cope with these demands?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some recent research suggests that there is generally an inverse correlation between a country's PISA score and that country's Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) score which measures entrepreneurial qualities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not arguing that we should reduce our PISA scores in the hope that our GEM score will go up, nor am I saying that having both a high PISA and GEM score is impossible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague Mr Png Eng Huat has spoken about the need to study the reasons behind the vast tuition industry in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are we helping our children compete in the world of disruption that they will live in when they grow up?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, Members of Parliament, good afternoon!

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Today, my topic is, "Successfully transforming the Singapore economy amidst adversity".

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: After the Budget Statement, as President of SCCCI, I have heard many feedback from businesses.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: After the Government announced the increase of water tariff and diesel tax, some related industries immediately felt the impact.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Water cost affects millions of users and would have an impact on every industry.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: But businesses feel that infrastructure is part of public service and the Government should not compute this on a commercial basis.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The major concern of businesses is operating costs, while the Government's concern is the nation's mid- to long-term competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: How to strike a balance can be challenging.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Countries which were previously more advanced than we were, are now becoming less expensive; countries which were less expensive than us, have become more advanced.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Our Singapore companies have to innovate in order to adapt to this new business environment.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Government encourages companies to innovate and internationalise.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, businesses also hope that the Government could apply a new mindset to plan its expenditures.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, there are still many areas that need expenditure, such as social development, healthcare, environmental protection, defence and foreign affairs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In order to increase revenue, the Government is likely to continue to adjust other taxes.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Government revenue comes from two sources, one is taxes and fees, and the other is the Government's investment returns.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The economic outlook will not be rosy in the days ahead.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If businesses cannot raise their competitiveness and increase their profits, tax revenues will not increase.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, the Government's investments are inextricably linked to the economic situation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If the economy is weak, there would be no magical formula to turn stone into gold.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: One is "broaden the sources of income and cut costs" and the other is "live within our means".

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The meaning of the first idiom is to increase income and save on spending; the second idiom means to spend based on one's income.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As the saying goes, "If a man has nothing to worry about in the long-term, he will definitely have something in the short-term to worry about." We have domestic and external factors to consider.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The domestic factor is that for many years now, we keep increasing the budget on certain areas, but the results cannot be seen.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Now, should we not begin to review if this is the right way of spending?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Just because it was correct before does not mean it is correct now.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Our thinking should not be based on what we are used to.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I am quoting Minister Chan Chun Sing.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Externally, there is a protectionist wave emerging globally, and the wave is becoming increasingly stronger.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, we should prepare ourselves to address this adversity.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Compared to more than 50 years ago, Singapore is, overall, much stronger.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We have advanced infrastructure, top-class port and airport, and an extensive network of undersea cables and a comprehensive financial, legal and education system.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Many MNCs have set up their regional headquarters in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Our own companies should also use Singapore as their regional headquarters and venture overseas boldly.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government would do its best to reduce business costs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, businesses should also review the internal factors which could contribute to their operational problems to see whether it is their product quality and service standards that are not up to the mark, or it is their business model that is outdated.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: During this economic transformation period, companies, especially chambers and trade associations, should play a more proactive role.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They should work closely with the Government, based on their industry's specific circumstances.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone should come together to think of ways to revive and promote the Singapore spirit, a spirit which has steered Singapore into success in the nation-building days, to overcome adversity and head towards success!

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are many things that I like about this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I like the fact that the Government is trying to prepare Singapore for the future economy and to sustain employment for the seniors.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I like the budgetary provisions to help all of us build an inclusive society and to strengthen our economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The CFE's recommendations are important and relevant proposals.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If well executed, they will help Singaporeans prepare ourselves for the future economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also believe that the young couples hoping to start a family would appreciate the generous increase in housing grants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is a clear indication that the Government cares for our younger generation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope that younger Singaporeans hoping to start a new family will consider the option of buying a resale flat with the increased housing grant.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also want to say that I appreciate the increase in Goods and Services Tax (GST) Voucher, U-save rebates, the cash special payment and the increase in service and conservancy charges (S&CC) rebates.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: All these would provide much needed relief for the average Singaporeans who face higher cost of living expenses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, Madam, allow me to express the concerns of many smaller businesses which are facing serious struggles to survive in an unpredictable economy and which are also facing declining sales.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The reality is that not every business is doing well over the past few years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of these businessmen were hoping that Budget 2017 would provide them with some form of financial relief or reduced costs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, it seems that their hopes may not materialise.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The feedback which I have received is that many of the budgetary measures in this year's Budget would only help a specific segment of the business community.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The focus of the Government is to strengthen capabilities for the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, for some of the smaller businesses, this year's Budget may not be a major event.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Instead, some of the measures taken to protect the environment and the water price increases may hurt them more.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I do not believe that businesses are hoping for a handout from the Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What they are appealing for is a business climate which is less costly and friendlier to businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Although there is an SME working capital loan, the feedback is that not many SMEs are aware of the loan or how it works.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There is also the perception that it is not easy to get such loans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How can the Government do more to reach out to the many SMEs which are looking for a lifeline for their businesses?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Government elaborate on its plans to conduct more outreach to the SMEs on all the available help?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, allow me to express my concern for the middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have a large number of such middle-income residents in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of them are PMETs who are living in condos or five-room flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also have a number of retirees living in private homes which they had bought many years ago after saving for many years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For this category of residents, they feel that they have been left out in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They feel penalised simply because they were trying their best to live their aspirations in the past.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For the retirees, they have no income and are relying on their savings, pension or their children to provide for them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For the PMETs, their income is unlikely to rise due to wage freeze in many companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Yet, these retirees and the middle-income PMETs will face increases in water pricing, car park and S&CC charges.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of the PMETs may also face job insecurity.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This group will not benefit from many of the support measures of Budget 2017.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If they stay in HDB flats, they may receive a smaller S&CC rebate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And the retirees also do not benefit from the tax rebate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I urge the Government to consider ways in which we can allow the retirees and middle-income Singaporeans to share or enjoy the growth of the country and to move forward together as a nation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We should find other more equitable ways to share and redistribute the country's wealth rather than rely on home type as a proxy for measurement of their wealth.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Let us do more for the middle income so that they too can find the theme for this year's Budget, "Moving Forward Together", a meaningful theme for them as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There is never a good time to raise prices for utilities.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, it seems to have distracted many of us from the much important message that all Singaporeans need to focus on, which is how to plan our future, how to develop stronger capabilities in a fast changing world.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: That is the main message of the Budget but, seemingly, when I go for feedback sessions, everybody's first question is about the water price increase.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And I felt that it is really an unnecessary distraction for all of us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I thought a lot about it in the next few days.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Was I disappointed because this Budget contained relatively few goodies for SMEs, workers and consumers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was the first question that crossed my mind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many businesses and Singaporeans expressed the same sentiment, as reported in the papers and as can be read online on social media.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This time round, the support given by the Government is targeted rather than broad-based.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have gotten too used to spectacular Budgets with goodies for everybody and the fireworks of snazzy phrases, pictures and presentations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, there is nothing positively spectacular in this Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is why Minister Heng opened the Budget Statement signalling a time of VUCA − the volatility of populist politics, the uncertainty of economic protectionism, the complexity of technological disruptions, the ambiguities of the changing global order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In such a context, it is prudent to wait and see before committing national resources to a set path with a clear destination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When everything is up in the air, we need to wait and see, to keenly observe the trajectories of the things being thrown up to decide which gems to catch and how to catch them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Wait and see does not mean to do nothing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I read an article in the Harvard Business Review that helped me see the pattern and logic of the "Budget in Brief" I was staring at.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was an article written by two US Marine Corps officers who switched careers to become business consultants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They wrote, and I quote: "As Marine officers, we always ate last, ensuring others had food on their plates before ours were filled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During down-time, we kept our teams busy with training opportunities so they could broaden their skills, which also curtailed complacency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When it was dark and cold in the field, we made a point of being present on the lines, not hiding out in a warm tent, to show our teams we were right there with them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Through our actions, we demonstrated that we were willing to go without food, free time and comfort to ensure our people knew they were supported.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our teams felt cared for and valued, and they demonstrated their loyalty through their initiative and engagement." Waiting means to keep ourselves busy with training and development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, many of the Budget initiatives are focused on the long-term development of business capabilities and enhancing the affordability and accessibility of training for our workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Seeing means to be vigilant and being prepared to respond quickly to opportunities and exigencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, many of the Budget initiatives have to do with road-mapping and transformation-mapping, and prototyping, testing and experimenting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the Marine officers related, waiting and seeing also means cultivating strong bonds of trust through shared engagements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, many of the Budget initiatives emphasise partnership, alliances and integrated spaces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Despite my initial disappointment and dissatisfaction, I believe this Budget is making the right moves of waiting and seeing in these three thrusts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I do not think we should dismiss the negative sentiments of disappointments and dissatisfaction with this Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are also signals to possible deficiencies and gaps in the Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe they point to one defect that the Government can do a lot better to address.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the psychological effect of insecurity induced by the VUCA environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is getting very dark and cold in the field and ordinary Singaporeans are feeling unsettled by the uncertainty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to understand and alleviate this psychological insecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are three ways to improve the psychological security and mental well-being of ordinary Singaporeans, even as they are exhorted to train and develop themselves as they wait and see.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, we should maximise the availability and accessibility of the training programmes as far as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, we should transform the current management culture of top-down leadership to one of service-based leadership, which is more conducive to fostering real partnerships of trust.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first way to improve psychological security is to maximise the availability and accessibility of training and development for workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not under-estimate the sense of security that comes with knowing that there are many options available to us for deepening our skills or changing tracks to pursue new dreams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have three substantive points to make in this respect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Adapt and Grow programmes are excellent for promoting functional skills and the practical placement of jobseekers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we should not forget the psychological impact of the various conditions and restrictions that the programmes place on workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The new Attach and Train initiative is interesting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Notwithstanding the details to be elaborated later by the Minister for Manpower, I ask that the Government pay close attention to the psychological aspects of attached participants, as there is a risk that the attachments could backfire if participants find themselves treated as mere interns and not as valued would-be employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regarding the Global Innovation Alliance, going forward, it would be good to open up the Innovators Academy to mid-career workers who would like to explore opportunities and build up experiences in innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many entrepreneurs are not born straight from the universities, but become enterprising innovators after accumulating years of experience in the marketplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand our six universities have been launching various types of work-study programmes with SkillsFuture support and in partnership with industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But many of these programmes are understandably starting out slow and small, and targeted at young adults heading to university and not adult learners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope this would accelerate to cater to adult learners who defer their university education to later and even to mid-career switchers, especially since the size of cohorts heading to university would start to shrink due to plunging birth rates two decades ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second way to improve psychological security is to strengthen the safety nets for middle income households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Middle-income households do not have the benefit of the enhanced financial transfers to low-income households to soften the impact of the water price increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Compared to low-income and high-income households, middle-income Singaporeans will feel the head-on impact of the increase in costs of living most strongly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the flip side, high-income earners will be receiving the full $500 tax rebate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This effectively means that the Government will be subsidising the expenses of high-income earners many times more than the middle income workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Middle-income workers need the rebates a lot more in order to soften the impact of the water price increases and the knock-on increases in costs of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Middle-income workers are also facing higher risks of retrenchment and under-employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the Adapt and Grow programmes help to mitigate the fallout from retrenchment and encourage retrenched workers to reskill and return to employment, the Budget could do better to provide for short-term relief to allow workers to find their feet and not be mired in temporary cash-flow problems that could distract them from training and job-seeking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Short-term tax deferments would also help retrenched workers to manage their cash flows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third way to improve psychological security is to promote service-based leadership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Management thinker Robert Greenleaf introduced the concept in 1970 in his famous essay, "The Servant as Leader".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In contrast to traditional leadership involving the top-down exercise of power and the taking of individual credit from the team's work, the service-based leader focuses on the growth of the people they are leading and the well-being of the communities they serve in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SkillsFuture Leadership Development Initiative announced by Minister Heng is an excellent initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a belated recognition that we need to consciously cultivate Singaporean leaders in all our industries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have focused on talents who could follow through the logic of development and faithfully execute the plans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we need now are thought leaders and visionaries who could inspire teams of talents and workers to collectively chart and create new pathways of growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, to maximise the return of investment in leadership to ordinary Singaporeans, we should focus on cultivating service-based leaders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Traditional leaders who are focused on their own power and achievement may well achieve the same level of growth as service-based leaders, but the benefits will not be equitably distributed to workers and the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, because service-based leaders are committed to the personal and professional growth of their workers, growth will benefit everyone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In turn, this will foster committed and engaged workers who will use their initiative and give their best and all to the team's efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The two Marine officers I quoted at the beginning of my speech, consciously applied this concept of service-based leadership to build up a cohesive team of well-trained and deeply committed warriors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of producing an elitist group of leaders commanding regular troops, they forged an elite fighting unit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is down-time and the Government is encouraging Singaporeans to get busy with training and development, mapping and testing, partnering and team building.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are preparing for the fight to come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it is also getting dark and cold in the field.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The price hikes and the looming tax increases do not help.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other than the three ways to improve psychological security even as we train and prepare, I have highlighted above, there are two things that the Government, the political leaders, can do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, we are still not getting a sense of the big picture of the changes in the global order and how Singapore features in this big picture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to have a shared understanding of what we are fighting and what we are fighting for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not my place to lecture the Government leaders on what they should be doing to be present on the lines with the workers and small businesses, but it is my duty to register that there is a need for it.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, you have a clarification?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I just have a couple of clarifications that I would like to ask about the evolving corpus of the Workers' Party economic model.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I understand that the previous speaker Mr Perera had mentioned land sales could be lost revenue.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I was wondering if Assoc Prof Goh might elaborate on what he views as an appropriate level of land sales to front our current Budget.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, what percentage of land to sell in this term of Government and what percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) the sales should be?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Should be it more, less, or the same amount as we have today?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, I am not sure what I am supposed to clarify.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Dr Tan, do you want to respond to that?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: The point was raised by Assoc Prof Goh's colleague earlier, and there is a thread about standing with our people and our SMEs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: So, I was wondering whether these points might be clarified at some point.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Perera or Assoc Prof Goh, would you like to respond?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Leon Perera, do you want to make any clarification?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: On the second point, this is something that we did not touch on in our speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think for SME development, we did give a number of ideas and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I do not think we brought up our proposals on manpower per se in the speeches that we made.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Businesses had expected more help in this Budget to ride out the challenging operating environment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Support is promised, but in a targeted manner, instead of being as broad-based as in the past − I support that this is a more efficient approach.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: When studying the Budget financials, we should all be concerned about our weakening fiscal position.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Additional funds that were afforded by the inclusion of Temasek in the NIRC starting year 2016, not too long ago, appears to have been exhausted quickly − this is worrying.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Finance Minister spoke about the implications of rising long-term expenditures, particularly in healthcare and infrastructure, and the need to prepare options to strengthen the revenue base.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This has rekindled fears of new and higher taxes, including GST hikes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There are those who would advocate tapping our reserves further and others like myself who would call for a cap on how much we should take from NIRC to fund our expenses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Clearly, Singapore must find a sustainable fiscal footing for our future generations and we need a thorough review of both expenditure and revenue.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am encouraged by the efforts of the CFE.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The seven strategies put forward by CFE form a comprehensive plan to capture the opportunities of the future economic landscape.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But it is one thing to strategise, but quite another to execute.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The 22 sets, I counted, of recommendations spelt out in the CFE report all seem to be the right things to do.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But, taken together, I cannot help but felt a little overwhelm with the long list of tasks ahead to reposition Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: From deepening our knowledge of markets, acquiring better skills, strengthening innovation ecosystems, to developing and implementing 23 Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These lofty objectives demand significant change and adaptation involving Government agencies, companies and people, working in unison.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How Singapore executes as a team, with each pulling its own weight, will make the difference.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A common theme in the CFE's recommendations is for the Government to create enabling environments, within which companies become nimbler and more innovative, to cope with the rapid pace of innovation and increasing competition around the world.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In this context, I commend the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) for leading the way.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To meet their ambition of building a Smart Financial Centre, MAS instituted the concept of "regulatory sandboxes" to enable fintech experiments and trials of promising innovations, to be tested in the market with appropriate safeguards.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The sweeping reforms announced recently by MAS have made it easier for smaller firms and budding entrepreneurs to secure financing for their businesses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: MAS intends to simplify the venture capital regime, introduce dual-class share structures, strengthen the role of finance companies and develop private market platforms.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is also actively laying down technology infrastructure to drive innovation, including an electronic trade finance platform, infrastructure to enable the pervasive use of e-payments and an industry know-your-customer utility, the first of its kind that I know of, that will greatly improve productivity of banks when on-boarding clients and managing money laundering risks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These wide-ranging policy measures set a great example of forward-looking regulations which creates a dynamic ecosystem that enables growth and innovation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If more sectors adopt a similar approach, it will go a long way towards enhancing Singapore's vibrancy and competitiveness, and accelerate our pivot towards the future economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The high cost of rentals is often quoted as prohibiting the setting up of new businesses and the survival of businesses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Is there a way for entrepreneurs to be offered affordable premises to kick-start their businesses, in the same way that the Government actively intervenes to keep housing affordable with HDB flats, and food prices affordable using hawker centres?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: JTC Launch Pads is a great initiative, but we need more platforms where businesses can operate in low-rent spaces acting as public offices located across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: State lands that have been earmarked for medium-to-long-term use could also be leased out on short leases with temporary built-up structures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Making some of these premises accessible as public offices, at nominal rent for a limited period of time, will help businesses bootstrap their operations and develop the critical mass needed before they transition to private market rentals.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In this year's Budget, there are many initiatives to help businesses scale their operations, go international, go digital and innovate.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the development of ITMs for 23 sectors, covering 80% of our economy, the Government has offered support to all sectors, not just selected ones, to seize growth opportunities and make the necessary transition.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Through ITMs, industries with good growth prospects can take advantage of global opportunities and technology whilst domestically-focused industries, such as food services, will get support to increase productivity and upgrade jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, regardless of which sector it is in, every business has a fighting chance of realising their fullest potential and reposition themselves for a brighter future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is heart-breaking to encounter stories of families impacted by retrenchments, and my sense is that increasing numbers of PMEs, especially older ones, are being displaced.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Economist magazine published a special report in January on the need for lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is apparent that if 21st century economies are not to create a massive underclass, policymakers need to urgently work out how to help their citizens learn while they earn.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The need for new and constantly updated skills in the new economy is universal, and many countries are ill-equipped to do so.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Unfortunately, lifelong learning in most societies is undertaken by those who are already doing well, and is therefore likely to widen the gap of inequality rather than narrow it.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: My worry is that not enough of us accept this as a personal risk and do not proactively seek to future-proof ourselves.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With longer life expectancy and unending shifts in the jobs market, the ability to learn will be the key skill to nurture, along with the willingness to do so.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The path ahead will not be easy, there are mountains to climb and rivers to cross, whilst the weather changes constantly.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our firms and our people must be the agents of change, taking greater charge of our own destinies, learning and improving, whilst the Government fosters enabling environments in which to grow and thrive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whether we succeed in reaching our destination depends on how we prepare together, support each other and keep pace with one another as we stay the path.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am very concerned with some of the measures announced in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not only was the increase of water tariffs sudden, the scale of increase is also higher than expected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, the Government has also decided to impose a water consumption tax, which will increase the burden of the people during this water tariff hike.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Companies and industries that uses a lot of water, such as the food and beverage (F&B) industries, will be affected the most.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned that this large increase in water prices will have adverse knock-on effects, leading to price hikes of other daily necessities and increasing the cost of living, which will in turn, increase the burden of the people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can the Government ensure that the rise in water tariffs will not lead to price increases at hawker centres, coffee shops and other products?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many industrial and commercial activities require the use of water.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This rise in water tariffs mean that operating costs and living expenses will increase.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With uncertainties in our economic prospects and growth, the hike in water tariffs will make the situation worse.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would like to know if the Government will offer assistance to industries that will be adversely affected by the increase in water tariffs, especially those that require a lot of water.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What puzzles me, is that the Finance Minister has mentioned in his Budget Statement that water is essential to our survival, so the pricing of water must reflect the higher production cost of desalinated water and NEWater.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My question is, we have had desalination and NEWater plants for some time now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, water reservoirs, desalination plant and water supply from Malaysia and other water issues have been better resolved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We already have more choices when it comes to water supply.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then, why the sudden mention of higher cost of water?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why was this not mentioned in recent years?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reasons given for the increase in diesel tax are, firstly, diesel is a source of pollution; and secondly, to encourage users to reduce consumption by imposing diesel taxes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I can understand and agree with the problem of pollution, but I do question the timing and scale of increasing diesel tax.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that it is not the right time to increase diesel tax under the current difficult economic situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The tax increase will cause diesel prices to go up and this will directly affect transport costs, such as those of taxis and buses, as well as school buses and buses ferrying workers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Government assure the people that our transport cost will not increase?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the short-term road tax rebates ensure that transport costs will not increase?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Finance Minister has also announced a cut in Special Tax for diesel cars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is calculated based on the distance of 250 kilometres to 500 kilometres that a taxi needs to travel every day, assuming they will need to consume 25 litres to 50 litres of diesel a day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Diesel is the general fuel for delivery trucks, vans, lorries and other heavy vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the 10-cent increase for every litre, transport and delivery costs will also increase, and this will also affect the operating costs of businesses that depend directly or indirectly on transport services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The increase of diesel tax at this point will only add on to their operating cost.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In view of the economic uncertainties and anxieties over job prospects, it is regrettable that the measures announced by the Government in this budget have not given the people a stronger sense of security.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, they have increased the cost of living of the people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The world today is quite different from the one that many of us are used to.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many countries that were once champions of globalisation and trade are experiencing fundamental shifts in their political orientation and attitudes towards globalisation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Economically, the VUCA environment that businesses are operating in has led to the shortening of business cycles and the increasing occurrence of creative destruction.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The biggest causalities of these changes are jobs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Employees in every sector and industry are at risk of experiencing structural unemployment that resulted from skill obsolesce.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The danger of being replaced by automations or algorithms is real.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we are living in the VUCA environment, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, earlier on our colleague Assoc Prof Daniel Goh mentioned this image of us living in darkness and in fear.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think, perhaps, that may be exaggerating the image somewhat.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do not believe that we are living in a wait-and-see mode, but rather using the analogy of military exercises, it is more of a mode that we are anticipating what will happen, we are preparing for what could come up next.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is something that I feel very strongly about.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is easy to take a big broad brush and try to solve a situation by bombarding with artillery, for example.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What you end up with is you have very much collateral destruction.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think the Prime Minister is aware of the impact of too much artillery in a situation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I prefer to see us not so much as Marines but a Seal Team Six, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, whereby we work fast, we work sharp, we are small, we are nimble, we are strategic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And we are far from a people cowering in fear and darkness.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It also reflects a paradigmatic change in how the Government views our economy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to take a mid- to long-term view of our economy and implement a Budget that will continue to meet our long-term objectives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yes, there are several "pain points" in this year's Budget where the prices of some goods and services have to be adjusted to reflect the cost of providing those services or to increase social awareness about environmental sustainability.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But these "pain points", however, are also mitigated by the various grants and subsidies that that Government will implement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These policies will ensure that those in our society who need an extra helping hand should not be in a significantly worse off position after the adjustments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We all agree that SMEs form the bulk of the number of businesses in our economy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite their significant contributions to our economy, however, our SMEs do face serious challenges moving forward.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, many continue to lack in their digital capabilities and the ability to tap on newer technologies to improve productivity and service delivery.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, they lack the resources and expertise to truly internationalise.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that the Government is cognisant of these challenges and the Budget has targeted programmes to help our SMEs overcome them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is crucial that we help our SMEs scale up their digital capabilities in the era of e-commerce and "click 'n' mortar" businesses.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should, however, go beyond this baseline assistance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The crux to a successful digital transformation is to have a talent pool that businesses can tap into.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially important for SMEs since SMEs are traditionally not the first choice of employment for many of our graduates.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Government can help to nurture a pool of digital talent, I believe SMEs themselves need to ensure that they can provide a good career path for these talents.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The career paths in SMEs can be increased by potentially increasing their level of internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An SME with regional or global presence is definitely in a better position to offer attractive careers to digital talents and also other professionals, as the scope and nature of their operations will offer the requisite job challenge and development opportunities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The devil, of course, is in the details of implementation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government is not in the business of picking winners and losers, so guidelines and assessment processes must be put in place to ensure that the funds that are set aside are used to support SMEs that have the best potential to internationalise.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The assessment criteria and methods must be appropriate and transparent, and support must be given to high-potential SMEs regardless of their size.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government has, in recent years, implemented a number of different measures to help Singaporeans own their own homes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that this year's Budget has continued on this trajectory by providing greater financial support to Singaporeans who wish to purchase a flat in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This group of Singaporeans are typically those who wish to start their family and also want to live near their parents for the supportive network.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I appreciate the rationale that the Government would not want to subsidise those who purchase bigger flats too much, as they are likely be from a higher income group, I think we cannot ignore that some consumers might choose to purchase a 4-room flat due to the fact that it is more expensive than a 5-room flat because of its location, age and other factors.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Conversely, some consumers with a lower income might have to purchase a 5-room flat, as opposed to a more expensive 4-room flat in other locations, due to their family requirements as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The recent Budget saw increases in the prices of water and diesel, and soon, Town Councils will be increasing their S&CC rates to meet rising costs, especially with regard to servicing and eventually replacing lifts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans are concerned that that is too many bullets to bite at a go.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, some segments of the population are concerned that the recent increases would pose additional constraints on their finances, and these concerns are somewhat justified.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am thus heartened to know that the Budget has provided various avenues of support through the form of GST Vouchers, S&CC rebates, and personal income tax rebates.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singapore's economy enters a period of low growth and more employees are at risk of losing their job due to structural changes in the economy, I hope that the Government will review its existing assistance schemes from time to time so that it remains responsive to the needs of the people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rather than having a broad-based Budget that hopes to raise all boats by lifting the overall level of the tide, the Budget is measured and its initiatives are targeted at giving specific help to those that need help the most.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More importantly, it reflects the Singapore ethos of fiscal prudence and the belief that the future of Singapore depends on the strong partnership between Government, business and people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I stress again, we are people that are not cowering in the dark or in the cold and the wet, we are people that are getting ready and preparing ourselves, whatever may come next.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not so much wait and see but being prepared.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that implemented well, this year's Budget, together with the recommendations of the Committee on the Future Economy, will form a roadmap that will help us to navigate the global uncertainty and possible economic headwinds that Singapore will face.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I conclude my speech in support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, in connection with the Government's measures to support businesses, I wish to highlight the cash flow problems faced by some SMEs arising from big companies holding back on prompt settlement of their invoices.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From feedback received, some big companies leverage on their economic power against SMEs by delaying payment on invoices for goods and services.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If the shoe was on the other foot, these big companies may not hesitate to impose interest for late payment in addition to the principal amounts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Micro SMEs are in particular vulnerable because, on one hand, they do not want to upset the commercial relationship with the big companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Yet, on the other hand, especially in a period of slow economic growth, the delay in payment may tip the SMEs to cash flow difficulties, higher litigation risk and even insolvency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To ameliorate the effect on these SMEs, I have two suggestions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would give SMEs more flexibility in managing their cash flow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst factoring arrangements may be available to SMEs, this comes at a cost and means a further erosion of their profit margin.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, SMEs may, in appropriate situations, utilise the framework to obtain payment on overdue invoices.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The next point I wish to make concerns the Wage Credit Scheme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As may be recalled, the Wage Credit Scheme was introduced in Budget 2013.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The purpose behind the Scheme is to help businesses cope with rising wage costs in a tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The idea is to encourage businesses to invest in and make productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These gains are to be shared with the employees.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In light of the Government's decision to extend the Scheme, may I please ask if the assessment in this economic climate is still that the businesses are continuing to face a tight labour market vis-à-vis employees at the 50th percentile of wages and below?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, I would be grateful if the Minister could please let us know whether the effort to improve productivity amongst the businesses participating in the Scheme is paying off.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate it may be difficult to get details or data on a specific industry basis, but perhaps, at least at the general level.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Without the linkage to productivity and sharing of the gains with the employees, we run the danger of providing just a wage subsidy which, given the second extension of this Scheme, may become a crutch for the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that the industry consultation on the proposed carbon tax will take place from March 2017 with the final carbon tax and exact implementation schedule decided thereafter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In principle, I support the premise behind the imposition of a carbon tax; that Singapore should do her part to address climate change, to create a sustainable environmental future for our children and generations after.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indicating a carbon tax range, as opposed to a specific rate, however, may create some uncertainty as companies would not be in a position to properly make business decisions in anticipation of the precise carbon tax rate which can be anywhere between 10% and 20% per year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may have knock-on effects, for example, companies prematurely passing costs to consumers in advance of the implementation of the tax, something we must certainly guard against, or not provisioning or investing sufficiently to mitigate the effects of the carbon tax on their businesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a comparison, with respect to the GST, the Government issued a White Paper on GST on 9 February 1993, in which the 3% rate was stated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Thereafter, the GST Bill was introduced later in the same month with the rate of 3% also stipulated in the Bill itself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Further, during the debate of the GST Bill in Parliament the following month, the Government gave an undertaking that the GST rate of 3% would not be changed for at least five years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the uncertainty removed, the companies will be able to focus on the improvements they need to make to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding the points that I have made, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my view, the hon Minister for Finance has, in his speech, properly identified the main economic challenges that we face as a country and clearly outlined a rigorous plan to strengthen our economy and allow us, as a nation, to continue to move forward together.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I respectfully disagree with the hon Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Assoc Prof Goh's categorisation of this Budget as a minimalist Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A cursory review of these Budget details will reveal otherwise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, this is far from being a static Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a Budget that would allow us to reposition ourselves and focus on the opportunities for the future.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the week of the CFE report and also the Budget Statement delivered by the Finance Minister last week, there has been much discussion on the economy in the lead-up to this particular debate.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are three central questions that we need to think about.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The first is where the opportunities are; the second, how do we position ourselves to seize them, and the third, what do we need to do to deal with some of the short-term challenges.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These are questions that several Members have echoed today.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Between 2011 and 2016, we averaged 3.1% which is comparable to other advanced and regional economies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This may be less than what we have been accustomed to in the past, but it is totally consistent with our stage of economic development, our demographic profile.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we need to ensure that within the context of where we are today, we continue to emphasise productivity and innovation as part of the basis for our continued growth.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because even at these levels of economic growth, which are not insignificant by international comparisons, it will continue to allow us to create opportunities for our businesses and jobs for our people.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This point is further enhanced when we consider the context that we are in, that is the region.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are in the heart of a region that is an important driver of global economic growth.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Their growth emanates not just from the key regions and main cities or metros that we are all quite familiar with but, in fact, they come from the next tier of cities and regions with which we might be less familiar.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In China, from the Central and Western regions; in India, from secondary cities like Coimbatore, Pune and Jaipur; and in Indonesia, cities like Semarang and Medan offer interesting opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, the recent data that the Singapore Tourism Board (STB) put out on visitor arrivals, which was strong last year, were actually significantly supported by the efforts that STB made in the secondary markets and regions with the consequential response from the markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we need to go beyond traditional spaces and we need to deepen our knowledge and acquire a more nuanced understanding of these new markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In tandem with this growth in the region, we are seeing rapid urbanisation and the rise of the Asian middle class with greater disposable incomes and sophisticated demand in sectors like retail, lifestyle, F&B, education and healthcare.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These opportunities play to our strengths, those that we have developed over the years.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One example I want to cite is in the area of infrastructure and urban solutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: China's Belt and Road initiative has heightened interest in regional infrastructure projects, whether it is road, rail, ports, airports.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: India's plan to build 100 smart cities needs adaptable and high quality urban solutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our infrastructure and urban solutions companies are generally held in very high regard and they can participate in these opportunities, in partnerships with their Chinese, Indian and Southeast Asian counterparts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is not just an opportunity for the big players in this space.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, it extends to SMEs like Memiontec and WaterTech Private Limited, who tapped into the demand for small-scale water and energy solutions in the region, and there are many of these that are emerging.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is one of the reasons why in this Budget, in particular, there was an effort to enhance the measures that we have already taken to support infrastructure.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If Members would recall, when the Economic Strategies Committee concluded its findings, this was about six, seven years ago, one of the initiatives was to set up the Clifford Capital which is just to finance many of our infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I will elaborate on that but, essentially, it is aimed to help our smaller businesses who are in this space to go regional, to seek out new opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The other area I want to emphasise is the digital economy which also presents unprecedented opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The smallest company can now seek out customers in the furthest markets as long as there is digital access.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What it means also is that through the digital platform, they can transact with their business partners, they can coordinate logistics and they can effect payment systems.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is literally transformative and it is transforming industries and offering new ways to overcome our constraints and seek out new opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why in the CFE, we have emphasised the importance of enabling our companies to harness digital technologies and platforms.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I can just give Members one example from a somewhat traditional sector − HipVan.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is a company in the furniture business but they have inverted the traditional furniture business model by going online.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Customers transact with them over the Internet and then they work through logistics and delivery, and this is a new model for this company, quite different from what we understand to be furniture businesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, companies are already moving and similarly, we are seeing good collaborative initiatives from big players and others coming on board.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, just today, Singtel, which is a co-founder of the 99% SME movement, announced a partnership with Lazada to set up an SME e-marketplace.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That will help SMEs step into a wider online customer base.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I can go on and give Members many other examples, whether it is in advanced manufacturing and Internet of things, and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our challenge is ensuring that our companies, especially our SMEs, are geared up for the longer term, so that they can seize these opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is especially important if we are to sustain our competitiveness because others around us have also seen this and are also adapting.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But we think it is a race that we can compete in quite effectively.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, a key focus of the Government's economic efforts is, indeed, in how we bring about such transformation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They are the key modality with three broad areas.
