speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: First, to grow top-line and scale, through support for companies and internationalising and financing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Second, to stay competitive by supporting capability development, both to innovate and to raise their productivity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Third, to develop deep skills in our workers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In all of these efforts, the primary focus and beneficiaries are our SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They account for about half of our GDP, two-thirds of employment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If you are really going to effect change and transformation in industry in the economy, the SMEs are key change agents.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They have to accept the reality, embrace the change and be change agents.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As they scale, SMEs will create more opportunities and jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, the Government is resolute in our commitment to help our SMEs make this transformation successfully.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Large companies do not necessarily need this breadth and depth of support.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, it is the small companies that need them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If you are a company taking the first steps towards internationalisation, you can tap on International Enterprise's Market Readiness Assistance and Global Company Partnership Scheme, and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Essentially, the aim is to help our businesses go international.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some are taking tentative steps, others are a little bit more experienced.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But they have to go into newer and more risky markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In general, we are trying to help them to take that move forward.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to stress here that the Government can be an enabler, but we cannot make the decision for the company.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But once a company makes the decision ‒ the leadership and the people ‒ we can support them in the effort.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is a co-investment effort with firms as they expand overseas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In other words, beyond loans and financial assistance and grants, the Government is prepared to come in through equity as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is an important commitment on the part of the Government, and we are putting our money where our mouth is, quite literally.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I do not want to get into a laundry list, but it includes, for example, the SME Equipment and Factory Loan, which is for expansion overseas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, if you are going overseas, you have done your market studies, you have decided you want to go, but there is capital expenditure (capex), this scheme helps you.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The MAS has also recently reviewed regulations that will enhance the ability of finance companies to provide financing to SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This scheme is designed to encourage financial institutions to provide non-recourse loans to SMEs once projects move into the post-construction stage, so that SMEs can free up their balance sheets to take on new projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The constraint today is that, if you are a small business going in for a $50 million or $100 million project in the region, you will have to tie up your resources either through personal guarantees or corporate guarantees, and it limits your ability to take on new projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This scheme is targeted to help our businesses do more and do it in an effective way.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I am talking here about the small businesses, not the big players.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want SMEs to create new products and services ‒ that is what they want to do as well ‒ to differentiate themselves in the market, but they are constrained by resources that are available.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think several Members talked about this earlier.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And to help them build up their innovation capabilities, we also have the secondment of our public sector researchers through our SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They go there, they help them come up with their research and development (R&D) blueprint, and they also, in many cases, end up joining the SMEs, sometimes to the chagrin of the research centre's director.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But, in general, we are supportive of this because it is an important productive flow of talent between the public and the private sectors.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In this Budget, there are two specific ideas which have been mooted and pushed out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Basically, it is to help SMEs access the more costly specialised equipment and to also get training and advice.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In other words, this may be in our research institutes, and SMEs cannot afford to have it on their own, but they can go in there and use it under certain arrangements.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The SMEs can tap on this grant ‒ Capability Development Grant ‒ for larger scale projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, if it is automation, there is the Automation Support Package, and I think Members are familiar with the scheme that was introduced last year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There is also the Innovation and Capability Voucher.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Importantly, the point I want to stress is, we have what we call the Partnerships for Capability Transformation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is where SMEs collaborate with big companies in order to develop new capabilities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is key, because many of our SMEs are an integral part of a cluster.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They work with the core company ‒ a big player ‒ international, local or foreign.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And the SMEs' capabilities reinforce the competitiveness of the cluster as a whole and its sustainability in our environment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Many Members have talked about the Go Digital Programme.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I do not propose to elaborate on it other than to observe that this is, again, a key plank.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Big companies do not need a Go Digital Programme.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is the SMEs that need it, and that is why we are doing it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are making significant investment in developing the skills of our people.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Members are very familiar with this through SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The SMEs can tap on these, whether it is SkillsFuture initiatives like the SME Talent Programme, SkillsFuture Mentors Scheme, and the SkillsFuture Earn and Learn programme.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have taken Members on a tour of the kind of things that we are doing with our companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Sometimes, the criticism is "Oh, it is all too complicated and so on".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not so much that there is too little, but there is too much and too variegated.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If you are an SME, you have a need in these areas, go to an SME Centre or go to one of the economic agencies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They will help you navigate and sort it out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The key point is we have this plethora of support.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I am surprised when Mr Leon Perera earlier said that we have missed an opportunity to strengthen local enterprises.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have just given Members a complete ‒ and this is not an exhaustive ‒ list of the various initiatives that we have undertaken.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Perhaps, the key point the Member was trying to make is that the Government should get into the business of picking more winners, because I think the Member described it as a bold initiative.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If it fails or does not meet up to expectations, pull out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is an interesting idea, but Mr Perera has omitted important details and how we would execute this and why the Government would be the right party to do this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because if the Government backs a company, it goes with whatever initiative, and then the initiative goes south, and then Government decides that it is going to withdraw the support, I think we can anticipate the kind of debate we would have and, indeed, the kind of questions that Mr Leon Perera will then pose on "Why did you do it in this way?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Why did you waste your funds here?" or "Why did you withdraw your support?" So, I think we have to have a sense of perspective and balance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government is taking a view on certain industries and directions that we want to go.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But, fundamentally, what we are trying to say is this: you are in an inherently more uncertain environment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Therefore, the emphasis on the broad range of capabilities that I have outlined and the broad scheme of measures that we have, are going to be the key platforms to raise the industry as a whole.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Sure, the companies that are prepared to move further and go faster will receive more support.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But that does not mean that we are picking winners.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The winners are picking themselves and adapting to our schemes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to emphasise that the impact of such schemes is really significantly amplified when we can get a collaborative effort going.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why we have stressed the role of trade associations and chambers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We do not want to substitute business judgement or trade associations' and chambers' assessment of market conditions with bureaucratic views.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want it to be a complementary exercise.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One example I want to just share with Members is the logistics industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is an initiative that the CDAS came up with.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They worked with SPRING Singapore and they got this executed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want to see more of this because they understand the need, their members tell them what their issues are, we can appreciate that there may not be enough resources, but that is where we come in and may complement.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Similarly, Singapore Logistics Association (SLA) has made initiatives in terms of going into a new market overseas and how they can help smaller businesses do that and also in the training of our workers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I hope Members would agree with me that there is actually no lack of Government resolve or resources that are available to support our companies, especially our SMEs, make the transformation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I know that there is a view ‒ and I think many of us have echoed that sentiment here ‒ that the current reality is the issue.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have challenges because of the cost and the pain and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The reality is also that the economic situation is variegated.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: How do you come up with a programme that is supposed to help SMEs in all of these, beyond the measures that we have already undertaken?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, these variations are there because the different sectors face diverse cyclical and structural challenges.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, lower oil prices ‒ and some might argue that this might be a permanent shift ‒ have changed the demand patterns for the marine and offshore industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It does not mean that they cannot do business, but they may have to adapt and also look at new opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The retail industry is going through a major change because of disruptive technology, in particular, e-commerce.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, the adoption of e-commerce in Singapore is at a lower rate, compared to many markets around the world.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, if anything, the challenge is going to get greater, not lesser.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It would really be quite futile for us to argue that we should resist such an overwhelming system level change, which, in fact, in aggregate, will bring benefits to consumers through businesses that respond to it and adapt to it and to the economy as a whole.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Having said that, I think we are very clear that we recognise that there are immediate challenges that our SMEs are facing and we will continue to provide certain forms of short-term relief where they are necessary and through the system of broad-based support that we have built up over the years.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One example is the Wage Credit, the Special Employment Credit and the extension of the additional SEC in this Budget to end of 2019.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If you go beyond that, and you look at the broader pattern, I think there was some reference to rental and other business costs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I know that this is an area of concern.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It comes up in many of our industry engagement exercises.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the reality also is that industrial, retail and office rentals have all deep fallen, and they fell in 2016 as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we, on our part, will continue to maintain a steady pipeline of industrial land and space to ensure that there is competitive pressure in the market and rentals remain affordable.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, let me put it together to say that we have not introduced further broad-based measures because they are not quite warranted and properly not even appropriate for the circumstances that we are in.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But have sustained what we already do − in some cases, extended down − and at the same time, put in place additional customised support for specific industries because of the circumstances that are quite divergent.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As many Government leaders have said, we will continue to track the situation closely and to intervene where necessary.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, if I can just give you an example − Marine and Offshore Engineering sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Last December, we introduced the bridging loans and international finance scheme.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not a panacea; it is not going to prevent consolidation which will occur to some extent in the industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But what it will do is help address some of the liquidity issues that some of the strong companies are facing and potentially, also help them get financing for expansion when they go for new projects overseas because there was a general tightening for financing in the sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It has been weighed down by the property market slowdown and economic uncertainties but we are bringing forward $700 million of public sector infrastructure projects which will start in financial year (FY)2017 and FY2018.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These measures are an illustration of the Government responding with a more targeted response and support for SMEs and other businesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is a complement to the broad-based measures we already have in place, in response to the varied needs in the economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And importantly, it is one aspect, even as we look at the longer term challenge and how we need to gear up for that.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But to seize them, we have to invest in the capabilities of our economy, of our people and our enterprises, and especially so, with our SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The most durable solution really lies in moving up the value chain, innovating, offering products and services that others are not offering, and adopting methods and techniques that will allow us to close some of the big gaps in productivity that we see when compared to international best practices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Straits Times noted that the Government feedback channel, Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH), had identified cost of living as a key pre-Budget concern among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a few questions for the Government to understand the decision-making processes around the latest round of increases in water prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government has stated in previous parliamentary replies that it prices water according to its Long-Run Marginal Cost (LMRC).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the water tariff, water conservation tax and used water charges or waterborne fees are priced to reflect the cost of producing the next drop of potable water, which is, I quote, "is likely to come from desalination and NEWater." In announcing the opening of the fifth NEWater plant last month, the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources noted that there has been upward pressure on costs because of increases associated with asset replacement, energy and manpower.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government share details on how the components of LMRC for water pricing are computed by PUB and how it assesses when to increase the price of water?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government also clarify if the maintenance and upkeep, and the associated manpower costs of current PUB assets, including thousands of kilometres of transmission networks and so forth, would have already been factored into the calculation of LRMC before the latest round of price hikes?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, it would be helpful to understand which variables of LRMC have changed from 1997 when the last price hike was announced, what is the range within each variable, and how often is the LRMC determined or re-determined?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government also share how much it costs each desalination and NEWater plant to produce water today, especially since some of these plants operate on a private-public partnership basis?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How do they compare with plants directly run by the PUB?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Are we looking at 2061 when the Water Agreement with Malaysia comes to an end, or is it when the PUB expects a doubling of Singapore's consumption in absolute terms for a much larger population and when 85% of our needs are projected to be met by NEWater and desalination?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2003, a Straits Times article quoted then Prime Minister Goh assuring Singaporeans that, and I quote, "the price of PUB water, which now costs $1.52 a cubic metre, would stay below $2 for some time, reversing all earlier projections.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The sums were redone because desalinating sea water was cheaper than thought; and NEWater, even cheaper to produce." The same year, it was reported that the Tuas desalination plant desalinates water at the cost of $0.78 per cubic metre.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This compared very favourably against about $0.90 per cubic metre produced by the Ashkelon desalination plant in Israel, considered in 2003 to be the one of the cheapest producers of desalinated water.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A 2011 Business Times' report also noted that Singapore would produce the world's cheapest desalinated water by 2013.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the PUB adjust its LMRC projections with the advent of new technology so as to keep water prices affordable and to keep its profits within reasonable limits, on an on-going basis?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From Parliamentary replies in the past, it would appear that energy is the real cost variable that can be difficult to track with a sufficient degree of accuracy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the lower cost of producing water over the years, can the Government reveal how much NEWater and desalination costs have fluctuated over the years as a result of energy prices?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2008, the Siemens Water Technologies Team was awarded a $4 million grant from the Environment and Water Industry Development Council (EWI) for successfully designing a more energy efficient desalinisation technique which produced a cubic metre of drinking water on 1.5 kilowatt hour (kWh) of power as compared to PUB's current desalination method using 3.5 kWh per cubic metre.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, the 2015 PUB annual report highlights PUB's collaboration with a US water technology company which has piloted electro-deionisation technology which has achieved reductions in energy consumption in the desalination process by more than 50%, and this pilot would be expanded in 2016.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government share details of this project and its prospects going forward?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, Mr Deputy Speaker, the announcement of an increase in water tariffs bookends a two-odd year period when Singaporeans were repeatedly reminded of water scarcity issues as a result of very low water levels in the Linggui reservoir in Malaysia, a water supply source five times the size of all of Singapore's reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, what role, if any, have the low water levels in the Linggui Reservoir played in the latest water price revision especially since the Government's position as late as 2013 confirmed no need to raise water prices?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the middle of last year, on the back of the Singapore International Water Week, a PUB official stated that should the Linggui Reservoir fail, there ought to be no cause for panic in Singapore as there were new and indigenous capacities in Singapore to meet such a contingency in the form of NEWater and desalination.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the Minister of Foreign Affairs only last month stated that the failure of the Linggui Reservoir would cause severe problems for Singapore and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government elaborate what are its contingency plans in the event of such an eventuality?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Do these contingencies include the possibility of another rise in water prices, especially the water conservation tax since its policy rationale is aimed at reminding the taxpayer about the importance of saving water and separately, to account for the LMRC of desalination and NEWater?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That would also prompt a corollary question as to whether the latest water price revision was set with a view to account for the complete failure of the Linggui Reservoir.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, in the middle of 2016, it was reported that Johor was studying plans to divert water from two rivers into the Linggui Reservoir.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the end of the last Leaders Retreat between Prime Ministers Lee and Najib in December last year, it was reported that Malaysia was looking at measures to increase the supply of water at the Linggui Reservoir.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government comment, in the event Malaysia successfully diverts water to the Linggui Reservoir allowing Singapore to draw its full entitlement of 250mgd or more, would such an outcome end up reducing the price of water for consumers in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And if so, would Singapore consider co-funding the diversion of the two rivers or re-negotiating some aspects of the Water Agreement with a win-win prospect in mind especially since Singapore has not hesitated to supply Malaysia with more treated water than it is required to in its time of need particularly in times of drought and over the Ramadan period last year?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This brings me to my final point about the public messaging on water conservation policies and the outcomes the Government seeks from the water conservation tax and how these outcomes can be improved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: About a month before the 2015 General Elections, the Prime Minister said, "In Singapore, water will always be a precious resource.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Never take it for granted or waste it." In the middle of last year, on the back of the Singapore International Water Week in a piece entitled "How Singapore Will Never Go Thirsty", the PUB chief executive officer announced that Singapore, in spite of being water-poor, had "significantly overcome the challenge of water scarcity" and later that "Singapore is not short on water".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I understand the PUB official was showcasing to an international audience the good work over many decades of our water specialists, there is a risk that over amplifying self-sufficiency can have a dampening effect on efforts to encourage water conservation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fact is self-sufficiency comes at a high price for the consumer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that the answer to the question of whether we can reduce consumption without price increases is a yes − perhaps not as resounding a yes as the experts would wish for − but a yes nonetheless.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even with our hot and humid climate and cultural practice of not using dishwashers, perhaps as a result of the spices, sauces and seasonings in Asian cooking, progress on water conservation has been steady and continuous.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Rather than to look solely at water pricing to promote conservation, the Government should look at new policies further tightening regulations on the sale of sanitary appliances such as mixers and shower heads which discharge excessive water, so as to nudge consumers to use more water-saving appliances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some experts have also proposed pricing strategies used elsewhere like in Spain which hosts a price structure that provides for a 10% rebate should a household's water consumption pattern show a 10% decrease compared to the year before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What these creative pricing strategies suggest is the prospect of a different approach towards water conservation taxes to promote a more efficient usage of water.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We already see PUB nudging Singaporeans in this direction by informing consumers of the consumption patterns of their neighbours and the national average in our monthly bills.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mr Deputy Speaker, a piece in The Straits Times last week argued that the water price only reflected the reality of increasing water stress worldwide and that bigger hikes were needed to curb wastage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The comments to that story were unexpectedly, rather animated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There remain concerns among Singaporeans who fear the knock-on effect of the water price hike on daily necessities and I hope the Government will address this point too.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leon Perera, you wish to raise a clarification?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: You are asking to raise a clarification about the Minister's speech?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Please note that you are not supposed to raise new matters in the speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My first point is really on the results of these schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There are many and various schemes and some of these schemes have had precursors, for example —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: You are not supposed to raise new matters.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My third point is really on the issue of long-termism, which I raised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: People will not become entrepreneurs if they feel that, structurally and culturally, the environment is not conducive to SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There are many schemes, there have been in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Some of the current schemes will be phased out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That may affect the willingness of the people to become entrepreneurs because there may be many schemes on the table now, but in 10 years, those schemes may be phased out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Deputy Speaker, I thank the Member for his range of questions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If I may take the last one first.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If somebody becomes an entrepreneur because he wants Government schemes and support, then that is probably the wrong starting point, if I may respectfully suggest.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think the starting point for any entrepreneur is really in deciding that he or she has a strong value proposition, a passion to grow something and then, they go out there and make it happen.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Indeed, we have many outstanding examples of entrepreneurs who have done exactly that.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Along the way, yes, they benefit from certain Government support schemes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I think we should not put the cart before the horse.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It has to come from the individuals who have the motivation to make it happen.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our schemes can enable but they can never be a fool-proof support system for this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think the other points that the Member has made − what are the results of the various schemes?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If there is one thing that we do rigorously is that we track the take-up rates, the outcomes, the key performance indicators (KPIs) associated with any programme that we introduce.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I would say that the Member raised the point − how many take up the scheme, how many globally competitive companies were created, and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, let me take a couple of those points.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We can create channels and make it easier for companies to find out about the schemes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Thomas Chua will tell Members that the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry has got one of the most active SME Centres in Singapore, and we find a plethora of ways of communicating.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But at the end of the day, the take-up rate rests with the individual companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Minimally, you have to make the effort to find out what it is that is available, what are my needs, where is the match, and how do I get it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And you do not need to do it alone because we have the SME Centres.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Even our economic agencies are prepared to work with them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Whether we will actually hit 1,000 or not, I think it remains to be seen, because there are many factors beyond our control.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the general directional push is very clear and we have in fact seen that grow.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ultimately, whether we end up having a local enterprise that becomes a global champion, again, cannot rest just with the Government, because we have many instances where companies grow and when they reach a certain stage, they get a very tempting offer from either a fund or some larger company and they sell out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Do we then say that our effort has failed or do we say then that, well, this is the realities of the market and we have to live with it because there will be some of this development?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In Israel, for example, they are known as a startup nation because they generate tremendous amount of knowledge which generate in many startup companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In Israel, is it a scale-up nation and how far do they go in scaling up?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, I think the Israelis themselves will tell you that this is one of their main focal points − how do we get our companies to scale up − because that creates the next level of depth in the economy and the capabilities that we seek.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As for funding needs, my general point would be this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have never been in a conversation where companies or enterprises tell me that funding is completely met because the need is always there, there are different kinds of needs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: You have a spectrum of funding providers in the market, whether it is Government schemes and grants, obviously, and then Government-supported schemes, whether it is venture capital, angel funding and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And it goes right through to private equity and then larger scale and, of course, you can then tap public markets, and now we got a lot more crowd-funding platforms.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, actually, there are a lot of mechanisms available but there will always be mismatches or gaps because the needs and the market situation keep changing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is why, ultimately, what is required is not so much about Government intervening by providing the lending solution per se, but it is to keep track of the situation, understanding whether this is a regulatory impediment, or a market failure, or is this because we are not getting the relevant players around the table to understand the issues and then deal with it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A case in point is what we are doing with the infrastructure financing I elaborated on, because for the smaller businesses in the infrastructure space, this was a real issue.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Big banks and other funds, when they typically do financing for infrastructural projects, they do project financing, but they need big ticket numbers, they need a billion dollar project and above because it does not justify the level of work.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we will have to see whether it takes off, how successful it would be and whether there is a need to recalibrate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Labour Movement, representing working people of all collars and ages, looks at this Budget with keen interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We strongly believe that if we as a country and as tripartite partners set our sights high, put our shoulders to the wheel, persist through difficulties and setbacks with courage and not lose heart, we will get lead our people to a better future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That said, we must indeed expect significant difficulties in the economic and job transformation journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Over the decades, the economy, job types and workforce structure of Singapore have all become more diverse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Consequently, the needs, hopes, fears and prospects of the working people in Singapore have become more segmented as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The traditional blue-collar and white-collar workers are increasingly joined by highly skilled professionals on one hand, and workers of the gig economy on the other.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The typical workforce comprise workers across widening age bands and multiple nationalities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The lines between these different groups have become more porous, sometimes due to choice and at other times, owing to circumstances such as restructuring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This renders social mobility more fluid in both directions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Both the corporate sector and Singaporeans at large tended to read and rely on the choices and signals by Government to guide their education and career decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is fine when things are stable and predictable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In an environment that is more likely uncertain and fast-changing, how should companies and workers sensibly decide on their steps and paths?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: My fellow labour Members will elaborate on the various segments of the working population that they are championing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Thus, when the CFE issued its report earlier this month, we hear comments that the strategies sounded somewhat generic, and that there were no clear magic bullets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They then pinned their hopes on the Budget.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: When the Budget was announced last week, we again hear people saying that they wished for more painkillers for the immediate strain and that the path toward transformation is still not set out clearly enough.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I believe this reaction reflects a mismatch of expectations, mindset and capability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Last Friday, I attended the third annual Projects of the Year Awards presented by the Singapore Chapter of the Project Management Institute (SPMI), a body whose membership comprise project management professionals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The leadership of the SPMI shared with me developments in their profession.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They told me that if one goes back in time, project managers are deemed good if they are able to execute to a given plan, within time and budget.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For that, they would be deemed to be good.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Clients today look for much more from project managers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They expect such managers to not only execute well, within time and budget, but also be able to add value and create value up and downstream from their traditional work − in areas of coordination, integration and unleashing synergy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Those who can do so have developed capabilities and connections both broadly and deeply, which they then leverage to good effect.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They are valuable to clients and are in strong demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On the other hand, those who can still only execute conscientiously to a plan given to them will see their relative value decline, and the need for their services progressively supplanted by re-design and technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This account mirrors that heard in many other forums, across different professions and industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To me, this means that life will no longer get better just by executing someone's plan conscientiously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That was value, but that was past value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Going forward, we must focus on leadership that can skillfully and effectively work the white space between boxes marked "Funding", "Schemes", "Regulations", "New Technology" and the such, bring them together in order to develop the critical partnership capabilities and reflexes needed to produce innovative and valuable new platforms, products and services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If we understand this, then we will also understand that much needs to be done to move us from a traditional "execute to a given plan" mindset to a leadership mindset.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Indeed, we must see ITMs as Dynamic ITMs, ever changing, never ending, always adjusting, because the underlying forces are such.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The point I want to emphasise is, many Members have spoken about the different schemes, whether or not there is a plethora of them, whether or not any particular one is sufficient or not.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But I think it is really in how you draw all these boxes together, whether as an individual, as a firm, across clusters, in partnership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That is the one that will create that value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Thus, "Building Agility through Capabilities and Partnerships" as highlighted in the Budget Speech, especially through strengthening sectoral tripartism, would be critical.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this regard, the scope of the SkillsFuture Leadership Development Initiative should not only build skills for operating internationally, but also build "white space leadership and partnership capabilities", which I deem to be equally important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They see that in industries where demand has dropped significantly, companies had begun to shed workers, both foreign and local.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They therefore worry if they would be axed next and whether they would be unfairly targeted for termination or retrenchment on account of their age or because they are deemed to be more costly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this regard, the Labour Movement and tripartite partners are monitoring the situation closely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Companies tackling excess manpower are to abide by the relevant Tripartite Guidelines, which emphasised that such action should be based on how workers demonstrate capability and value on the job, rather than on age, gender or other arbitrary non-work criteria.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As stated by the Finance Minister in his Budget speech, "To help firms with rising wages, more than $600 million will be paid out in March 2017 under the on-going Wage Credit Scheme, while more than $300 million will be paid out in FY2017 to benefit 370,000 workers under the Special Employment Credit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Additional Special Employment Credit will also be extended till 31 December to provide wage offsets of up to 3% to help older workers stay employed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Older workers who feel that they have been unfairly targeted for retrenchment or job termination can seek help from the unions, the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) or the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Every effort will be made by the tripartite partners to help displaced workers of all ages find new jobs, whether in the current line of work or, through conversion, to other lines of work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must not under-estimate the ability and will of mature workers to adapt and grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Many have shown by example their resilience, and have demonstrated reliability and openness to learning new skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Those who adopted a flexible attitude helped themselves seize opportunities faster.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Government has also introduced or enhanced initiatives that help displaced mature workers get back into work more quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These included improvements to the Adapt and Grow Programme and related schemes such as the Career Support Programme, the Professional Conversion Programme, the Work Trial Programme and the Attach and Train Programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I draw attention especially to two elements in these programmes which are very important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The first is developing a keener sense of where the jobs are today and where they will be in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The second is the wage and training support within these programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These are critical ingredients especially when helping middle age workers transit and adapt to structural shifts in the economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While displaced mature workers want to get back into work quickly, they also have many commitments to meet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In such a situation, many risk becoming structurally unemployed or underemployed, if they hold out for too long or if they do not get the offers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The help with adaption and job matching must seek to minimise such risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On the Labour Movement's part, the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) has set up a unit called the Future Jobs, Skills and Training (FJST) Unit to integrate and maximise our efforts, as well as to complement those of our tripartite partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As an example, we believe that as the mature workforce will be a growing part of the local working population, it is important for ITMs to include plans to fully utilise and continual sharpen this resource − and to do so within the ITMs as part of strategy, rather than as an accommodation or afterthought.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, companies must be reminded that should they lose experienced manpower because of lowered demand, they will find it harder to recruit such manpower quickly when the demand returns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They will then constrain their own prospects for growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That same future is also full of opportunity, promise and prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The paths we choose and the actions we take, individually and jointly, will decide our chances of success.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, during the earlier debate, Mr Dennis Tan could have given the impression that with the increase in water tariffs, the additional U-Save rebates could only help the minority of Singaporeans, while middle income Singaporeans, in particular, might not receive much help from the U-Save rebates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In reality, however, the U-Save rebates will indeed help to buffer the impact of higher water tariffs for most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope the above explanation can clarify our understanding about U-Save rebates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, please allow me to continue in English.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This year's Budget seeks to position Singapore to be "future-ready" to meet the challenges of a future filled with uncertainties and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Together with the Committee on the Future Economy report, it identifies how Singapore and Singaporeans can navigate the seismic economic and technological shifts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Being nimble and adaptable to change are the names of the new game.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But the breakneck pace of change is almost unforeseen for many.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Fourth Industrial Revolution is well under way.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The race for artificial intelligence had actually started quite a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The speed of innovation brings the "future" much closer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our workers and companies need to be future-ready.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, for some of them, they actually need to be "now-ready".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How do we gear them up for this so that they can seize the opportunities of tomorrow today?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Whether we succeed in this economic transformation or not, we cast our lot with our millennials and Generation Z.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are at the threshold of opportunities unseen in a century.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, the job search has also become more trying.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In essence, what to invest their time in.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In short, how do they go about navigating the shifting turbulence of the new job market?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thirdly, businesses are placing greater importance on work experience, on top of academic qualifications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The latter is what new graduates and first career Singaporeans would not have.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that there are three ways to tackle these challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that helping younger Singaporeans and workers is no longer about a massively sophisticated blueprint.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The speed of change certainly defeats the best intents of such blueprints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It should be a system where young workers help one another to navigate in this new economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Allow me to share the story of 23-year-old Yam Su Xian who was looking for a job and 38-year-old Zuhaina Ahmad who heads business support in her company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Su Xian was a Business Management major who was finding it difficult to land her first job.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: She sent out many job applications but could not find any positive responses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Zuhaina was a pioneer career guide in Young NTUC's Youth Career Network (YCN) programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: She volunteered to pay-it-forward to help others who might have struggled as she did in her earlier years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Through the YCN engagement sessions, Su Xian better understood the different jobs that would suit her skills and personality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Zuhaina then helped Su Xian to build and enhance her resume.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They worked together to create a LinkedIn profile to boost her visibility to prospective employers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Every day, she suggested to Su Xian on how to expand her network to enhance her job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They worked together on boosting Su Xian's self-confidence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: She recounted, after getting a job, "I was alone by myself with friends on different paths.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some of them had already found jobs, some were holidaying and others were still studying.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I was on my own until I found out about career mentoring with the Youth Career Network." YCN empowers youths to take up ownership in charting their own career journey.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can see from Su Xian's story that we saw neither blueprint nor career counsellors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The programme worked because Zuhaina wanted to pay-it-forward and Su Xian found help that was current, personal and approachable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can and should invest in such mutual help platforms to unleash the collective strength and potential of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The system is almost future-proof because there will always be people like Zuhaina and Su Xian who are leaders in their own industries keen to help, and young people who need them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A networked system of mentors like Zuhaina could potentially serve more students and Singaporeans than physical career centres would ever do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If we can expand this programme, it would be more than building mentoring networks but also about the strengthening of community bonds amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In doing so, we can continue to leverage on the extensive network of the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Then, it can truly be the Singapore Career Network.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Now, let me move on to the National Jobs Bank and the National Talent Bank.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The National Jobs Bank has helped many Singaporeans to find work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It puts in one convenient location, the job vacancies available in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also allows for the analysis of jobs and skills trends.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This system should also include networking features like those on LinkedIn and Facebook.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The National Talent Bank also allows us to analyse the deficit between national skills, competencies and what is required in our economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As we go global, international companies should now know where a good place is to reach out for Singaporean talent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The current job sites are specific industry-focused and tend to be used mostly by professionals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Hence, I encourage the Government to work with private sector companies, such as LinkedIn and Monster.com, for example, to develop such solutions on a national level.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, I would like to turn our attention to the "gig economy" as the third leg of the proposals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The recent Graduate Employment Survey showed a growing emergence of a "gig economy".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These part-time and freelance jobs will increasingly become more prevalent as both employer and employee can react to economic changes better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This "gig economy" can be an important feature in managing structural changes in the economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also helps in continuous learning and being entrepreneurial.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it cannot develop without stronger workplace protection and retirement support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need a robust network to protect freelancers and the employers hiring them, giving them a sustaining ecosystem to grow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the three proposals above, I believe that we can better help our younger Singaporeans navigate in these times of rapid technological and economic changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I applaud the Government for announcing the Attach and Train Programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I think that it can be a real boost for back-to-work women.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Most of them would like to start immediately if there is a trial work option.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: That is immense latent talent waiting to be tapped upon.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC recommends a Returnship Programme as a bridge to help women get back to work again.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It provides a trial for both the employee and the employer to ascertain job fit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The goal is to place them in a permanent role in the same company or another company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The chances of a good match would be much higher if we have work flexibility built in the system as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We should start with companies which have vacancies, or even a company whose workers are on temporary leave and need workers for the interim period, for example, employees on maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As the largest employer in Singapore, we hope that the Public Service Division can take the lead in actively looking at offering these back-to-work individuals career trial opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We also hope that the Government Linked Companies can also answer the nation's call.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: No one entity can claim to have the monopoly of knowledge in this complex world to drive this change on its own anymore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But, together, we can build good platforms to nurture higher probabilities of good outcomes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I have been making rounds in my constituency in the last couple of weeks and have been reading the local and regional news with regard to the water tariff.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The concerns of our people and businesses are understandable, given the current economic challenge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And much has been said about this issue, both in and outside of the Chamber.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, it is sometimes useful to take a view from outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, how do our competitors see us?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The South China Morning Post, widely seen as Hong Kong's flagship English newspaper and not always a fan of Singapore, recently carried this headline: "Can Hong Kong follow Singapore's lead in water tariffs?" In its sub headline, the report noted: "Among Asia's metropolises, Hong Kong is stuck with frozen tariff rates that are hurting water conservation efforts".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The report said experts are calling for Hong Kong and other Asian cities to follow Singapore's lead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The South China Morning Post quoted experts from the United Nations and think tanks, who called for countries to invest more in water infrastructure, reduce water wastage by reflecting the real cost of water, while insulating the vulnerable from the impact ‒ all of which the Singapore Government is doing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The South China Morning Post's views are also shared by leading water experts, such as Prof Asit Biswas and Robert Brears.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, the challenges of pricing water right to ensure access amidst climate change are not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must deal with them decisively while taking care of our vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And in this debate on this issue today, it is important that we separate facts from fiction and reality from perception.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I am heartened to hear our Government's recent clarification which directly addresses the hon Member Mr Dennis Tan's concern that the additional usage rebates will limit the impact on low-income and middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am also concerned about the impact on the hawkers in my constituency, which affects the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, I took a look at their water bills.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I saw today a bill for an entire coffee shop with six stalls.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: On average, each stall is using around 50 cubic meters of water a month, which costs around $100.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, I call for the Government to continue monitoring the situation, both for individuals and businesses, to see whether further tweaks are necessary.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, I had breakfast with a senior retired official who worked for Mr Goh Keng Swee.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I asked him what did he learn working for Mr Goh Keng Swee.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: He thought for a while and quoted Mr Goh, "Don't tell me the why.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Tell me how you are going to get this done." Indeed, many retired senior officials whom I spoke to shared the same view ‒ what separates Singapore from the rest is our focus on getting things done quietly, efficiently and quickly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This coordinating body, like the CFE Committee, should comprise not just our civil service officials, but also key union leaders, business leaders and educators.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This coordinating body will serve as a strong centre to oversee our Ministries' efforts to translate broad strategies into detailed plans, regularly review the progress made, incorporate good ideas, seek out industry proposals along the way and communicate to all stakeholders annually on where we are, and where we must go.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The current National Productivity Council could serve as a basis for this coordinating body.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Why is this high level of coordination and communication necessary?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To fundamentally transform our economy, we need to go beyond the whole of Government approach.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, we need our Government to move as one, we need a whole of nation effort.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The premise of the ITMs is this: each industry requires bespoke solutions to achieve deep transformation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, I hope that we must be fully prepared to remove policy sacred cows when necessary.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If the new plans for the industries end up not differing from existing plans, and if many of our ITMs look too similar, then we should question whether we are fully stretching our imagination and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some say there is no Big Bang in the CFE.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But I feel that it is no longer sufficient to push for a single Big Bang industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our Government must, however, light 23 bright sparks with each of the 23 ITMs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And our industries must turn these bright sparks into a brighter future for all.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The ITMs are supposed to rally their respective industries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many businesses, stuck in the trenches of disruption, are looking for direction amidst the storm.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Not all of them found clarity for their sector, in the measures provided in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But it does not mean that help for them is lacking.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When we can translate this significant budgetary firepower, into concrete policies industry by industry, policies that our businesses and people can touch and feel, they will naturally gain the quiet confidence that the future is bright for all.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Also, rolling out our ITMs quickly provide much needed clarity to the supporting CFE's efforts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, in this Chamber, we frequently talk about using our SkillsFuture funds efficiently.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But it is not easy for our officials in SkillsFuture, or any other CPE supporting efforts, to make concrete plans until they know the precise direction that we want to take each industry to.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, therefore, a quick rollout of our ITMs is critical.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In summary, to execute our plans, we need a strong centre to pull everybody together, we need bold plans to transform each and every of the 23 industries, and we must provide our industries with quick and clear directions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When I spoke to our seniors about the CFE, they are not sure how they fit in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, we already have forward-looking policies for our senior workers, such as our Senior Employment Credit, and our Retirement and Re-employment Act.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I think there is room for our Government to catalyse a gig economy for our seniors, by creating micro-jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Despite legislation, it is hard for us to fully remove ageism, especially towards seniors above 67.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many companies, especially in tough times, are not willing to take the risk of hiring, or even retaining senior workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This issue would be more serious over time as we continue our restructuring and as our workforce continues to age.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The gig economy can help us combat ageism.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Compared to companies, consumers using the gig economy are far less willing to discriminate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Through technology, Uber empowers hearing-impaired drivers to work in the car using Uber app.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Other examples include delivery services such as Honest Bee, Foodpanda and Deliveroo, show that our consumers are less interested in discriminating, on who shows up on the door, as long as that person can do that one-off "micro-job" well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, how can the Government create a gig economy for our seniors?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, we sometimes send two nurses to visit patients, many of whom are bedridden or have mobility challenges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Why can we not cut down to one nurse instead, and then hire a trained senior, living in a nearby block or street, to assist such as carrying the patient and assist in wound dressing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are many seniors living in our midst who can qualify to do such micro-jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Through a gig economy app that the Government creates, perhaps by working with our start-ups.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How do we prepare our seniors for these micro-jobs?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How do we ensure quality of service by these seniors?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Through the apps that ask for feedback from the nurses, and may be even the patient.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What if we certify some of our able grandmothers to provide infant care service for a few infants at their home, or retired teachers to provide after school care for a few students at home?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What if we equip our seniors to provide caregiving or respite care to their neighbours?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How many purpose built infant care, after school care centres, and respite care centres can we end up not building?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When I talk to public officials or VWO leaders about this idea, they get it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can even extend this to the private sector, for example in food service.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is already a company that hires retired prata-makers today, and deploy them to meet shift gaps throughout Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, we can also help our seniors to find micro-jobs in the food service industry in their own neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can also even extend this to stay-at-home mothers and special-needs workers to find micro-jobs nearby.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What about meeting the practical realities like CPF contributions, or verifying who is eligible for what micro-jobs?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These can be easily done, by inserting lines of code, to wire micro-contributions to one's CPF account and to check out our seniors' SkillsFuture individual learning portfolio.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In short, in this digital age, data is the new invisible hand.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We should fully tap on data, combine it with our social policies, to orchestrate our economy and society of the future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In closing, creating a gig economy for our seniors benefits Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It can put money directly in the hands of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It can cut down on unnecessary manpower including foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I stand in full support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: These programmes dovetail closely with CFE's first strategy to "deepen and diversify our international connections".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: It also recommends us sending more young Singaporeans to overseas internships and leadership development.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Despite the fact that close to 10 million Singaporeans travel overseas every year, that these programmes are still introduced says something about our realisation that we cannot afford to slacken in inculcating in especially our young, the ability to understand and appreciate the world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The world is like a vast ocean, constantly waving currents and under-currents.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Singapore can only steer forward safely if only we have up-to-date weather charts and topographical maps.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Speaking of unpredictability of events, 2016 was nothing short of surprises and shocks.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Uncertainties are still unfolding in ways which have profound implications for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: As Prime Minister Theresa May laid out her 12-point plan for Brexit, the European Union (EU) is now increasingly worried about the prospect of a "Frexit" as the French presidential elections draws near.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Meanwhile, right-wing populist parties campaigning on anti-immigration and anti-globalisation are gaining ground in Europe.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: If EU, the world's largest single market breaks up, world trade will be in disarray.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: What ensues may be trade wars leading to ultimate shrinkages in trade volume causing job losses and destabilising economies.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Given that two-third of our economy is externally driven, a trade-hampered world will spell great hardship for us.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: From the rising popularity of far-right political parties in Europe, one has to conclude that more and more voters are taking in their campaign promises which are premised not on reasons, research and facts but on impulses, emotions and anger.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Their prescriptions to economic and social woes ignore the very complex nature of economy and trade, of global supply chain and relative competitive advantages.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: They promise a magic wand which solves all problems merely by building walls around one-self, for instance.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: David Rothkopf, the chief editor of The Foreign Policy, coined the term "the shallowness of the state" to describe politician's tactics to over-simplify issues to win votes.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: He reminded us that "experience, skills and know-how require time, work and study.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Thirdly, news-reporting and consumption tend to be local.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: That most people will be concerned with things happening in their backyard is perfectly understandable.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In fact, survey has shown that those who follow local news closely also tend to be more civically engaged in and volunteer for the local community, which is a good thing for citizenry.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: But we also must be aware that there are a few orders of magnitude of difference when one says "local news" in continental-size countries such as the US and China, and that in our tiny Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While people in these large countries may take comfort in being contended with local news, we in Singapore cannot afford to think and behave the same.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Lest we unknowingly wear blinkers to see a very narrow world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: A number of businessmen I met commented to me that many Singaporeans are surprisingly insular and inward-looking.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: They told me two manifestations of this psyche.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: One is Singaporean's unwillingness to leave their comfort zones and take up foreign postings; two is that being very sheltered, Singaporeans become unsure and very risk adverse in poorly defined and uncertain environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: They believe that such lack of adaptability will hold Singaporeans back from many opportunities in the emerging world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: When I travel, I like to tune into news stations and see what is being reported.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: When I tuned into China Central Television or Phoenix news, I often found their reports of world affairs very insightful and comprehensive, covering a wide range of geographies far beyond the Chinese borders.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Over the years, I have also found CNN and other American news reporting to be more globally informed, often although accompanied by distinctive American view of the world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Singapore news and our public discourse must, by definition, be a keen observer of the world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This is because we do not have a continental size economy or geography to buffer us from any shocks.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: But I just realised that in this House, it is the topic that every Member has addressed.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: I think it is perfectly understandable how many people had found the jump of 30% abrupt and drastic.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: But if we consider the subject in context, that despite the very same dry season brought by El Nino in 2016 sweeping across Southeast Asia, Singapore unlike a number of Malaysian states such as Perlis, Pahang, Malacca, Johore and Sabah, did not have to impose water rationing because of the severe drought.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
